    Section 1 — Functions

    Skills to know firstArithmetic & SignsCore AlgebraCoordinate-plane basics
    SkillsFunction notation, evaluating functions, domain and range, reading functions, transformations, even/odd functions, and average rate of change.

    Function notation

    f(x) means “the output of function f when the input is x.”

    f(x)=2x+3 f(4)=2(4)+3=11
    Substitution shortcut: replace x using parentheses, especially for negative inputs.

    Domain

    The two most common restrictions:

    • denominators cannot equal zero
    • the inside of an even root must be greater than or equal to zero

    Worked examples — function basics

    Example 1 — evaluating, including a negative input

    f(x) = x² - 3x + 1. Find f(-2) and f(a + 1).

    Replace every x with the input IN PARENTHESES. f(-2) = (-2)² - 3(-2) + 1 = 4 + 6 + 1 = 11 f(a + 1) = (a + 1)² - 3(a + 1) + 1 = a² + 2a + 1 - 3a - 3 + 1 ← distribute the -3 to BOTH terms = a² - a - 1
    Without parentheses you would write -2² = -4 and -3 · -2 as -6. Two sign errors from one skipped habit.
    Example 2 — difference quotient

    f(x) = x². Simplify [f(x + h) - f(x)] / h.

    f(x + h) = (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h² Numerator: (x² + 2xh + h²) - x² = 2xh + h² Factor h out of the numerator so it can cancel: h(2x + h) / h = 2x + h

    This is the setup calculus opens with. Getting comfortable with it now pays off later.

    Example 3 — domain with both restriction types

    Find the domain of f(x) = √(2x - 6) / (x - 5).

    Restriction 1 — even root, inside must be ≥ 0: 2x - 6 ≥ 0 2x ≥ 6 x ≥ 3 Restriction 2 — denominator cannot be 0: x - 5 ≠ 0 x ≠ 5 Combine: start at 3 and include it, exclude 5, go to infinity. Domain: [3, 5) ∪ (5, ∞)
    Bracket vs parenthesis: a value that is allowed gets a square bracket; a value that is excluded (or is infinity) gets a round parenthesis.
    Example 4 — domain of a rational function

    Find the domain of g(x) = (x + 1)/(x² - 4).

    Set the denominator to zero and exclude those values. x² - 4 = 0 (x - 2)(x + 2) = 0 x = 2 or x = -2 Domain: (-∞, -2) ∪ (-2, 2) ∪ (2, ∞)

    Quick check — function basics

    1. f(x) = 3 - x²; find f(-4)
    2. Domain of √(5 - x)
    Answers

    1. 3 - (-4)² = 3 - 16 = -13

    f(-4) = 3 - (-4)² = 3 - 16 (-4)² = 16, in parentheses = -13

    2. 5 - x ≥ 0 → x ≤ 5 → (-∞, 5]

    √(5 - x): inside ≥ 0 5 - x ≥ 0 -x ≥ -5 subtract 5 x ≤ 5 ÷ (-1), FLIP (-∞, 5]

    Practice set — function basics

    1. f(x) = 2x² - x; find f(-3) and f(2t)
    2. Difference quotient for f(x) = 3x - 5
    3. Domain of (x - 1)/(x² - 5x + 6)
    4. Domain of √(x + 4)/(x - 1)
    Answers

    1. f(-3) = 18 + 3 = 21; f(2t) = 2(2t)² - 2t = 8t² - 2t

    f(-3) = 2(-3)² - (-3) = 2(9) + 3 = 21 f(2t) = 2(2t)² - 2t = 2(4t²) - 2t = 8t² - 2t

    2. [3(x+h) - 5 - (3x - 5)]/h = 3h/h = 3

    f(x + h) = 3(x + h) - 5 = 3x + 3h - 5 f(x + h) - f(x) = 3x + 3h - 5 - 3x + 5 = 3h 3h/h = 3

    3. (x-2)(x-3) ≠ 0 → x ≠ 2, 3

    Bottom = 0: x² - 5x + 6 = 0 (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0 → x = 2, 3 Exclude both: (-∞, 2) ∪ (2, 3) ∪ (3, ∞)

    4. x ≥ -4 and x ≠ 1 → [-4, 1) ∪ (1, ∞)

    Root: x + 4 ≥ 0 → x ≥ -4 Bottom: x - 1 ≠ 0 → x ≠ 1 [-4, 1) ∪ (1, ∞)

    Vertical line test, domain and range from a graph

    Vertical line test. If any vertical line crosses a graph more than once, it is not a function. One input cannot have two outputs.
    Reading a graph. Domain is what the graph covers left to right on the x-axis. Range is what it covers bottom to top on the y-axis. Filled dot means included, open dot means excluded, arrow means it continues forever.
    Example — reading both from a description

    A graph starts at a closed dot at (-3, 1), rises to a peak at (0, 5), falls to an open dot at (4, -2).

    Left to right, x runs from -3 (included) to 4 (excluded). Domain: [-3, 4) Bottom to top, the lowest point reached is -2 but the dot is OPEN, so -2 is not attained. The highest is 5 at the peak, which is a real point. Range: (-2, 5]
    Range is not the y-values of the endpoints. It is every height the curve actually reaches, including peaks and valleys in the middle.

    Increasing, decreasing, and extrema

    TermMeaningStated as
    increasinggraph rises left to rightan interval of x
    decreasinggraph falls left to rightan interval of x
    constantflatan interval of x
    local maximuma peakthe y-value, occurring at some x
    local minimuma valleythe y-value, occurring at some x
    absolute max/minthe highest or lowest point anywherethe y-value
    Intervals use x. Extreme values use y. "Increasing on (-2, 3)" and "local maximum of 7 at x = 3." Mixing these up is the usual lost point.
    Example — describing a cubic

    A graph falls from the far left to a valley at (-1, -4), rises to a peak at (2, 5), then falls forever.

    Decreasing: (-∞, -1) and (2, ∞) Increasing: (-1, 2) Local minimum: -4, occurring at x = -1 Local maximum: 5, occurring at x = 2 Absolute max or min: NONE. Both ends run off to infinity, so no single point is highest or lowest overall.

    Average rate of change

    Average rate of change from a to b = [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a)
    This is the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)). It is the same slope formula from Coordinate Geometry, applied to two points on a curve.
    Example 1 — numeric interval

    f(x) = x² - 3x. Find the average rate of change from x = 1 to x = 4.

    f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2 f(4) = 16 - 12 = 4 ARoC = (4 - (-2))/(4 - 1) = 6/3 = 2 The secant line through (1, -2) and (4, 4) has slope 2.
    Example 2 — the connection to the difference quotient

    f(x) = x². Find the average rate of change from x to x + h.

    ARoC = [f(x + h) - f(x)] / [(x + h) - x] = [f(x + h) - f(x)] / h That IS the difference quotient. Same formula, different name. = (x² + 2xh + h² - x²)/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h

    Letting h shrink to zero turns the average rate of change into the instantaneous rate of change. That is the first thing calculus does.

    Quick check — function properties

    Items using fg, f/g, or f∘g preview operations of functions and composition from Section 2.

    1. f(x) = x - 1, g(x) = x². Find (fg)(3).
    2. Domain of (f/g) if f(x) = x and g(x) = x - 7
    3. f(x) = √x, g(x) = x - 9. Domain of (f∘g)?
    4. ARoC of f(x) = 2x + 5 from 0 to 10
    Answers

    1. f(3)g(3) = 2 · 9 = 18

    f(3) = 3 - 1 = 2 g(3) = 3² = 9 (fg)(3) = 2 · 9 = 18

    2. All reals except 7

    f/g = x/(x - 7) g(x) = 0 when x - 7 = 0 → x = 7 All reals except 7

    3. Need g(x) ≥ 0 → x - 9 ≥ 0 → [9, ∞)

    f(g(x)) = √(x - 9) x - 9 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 9 [9, ∞)

    4. (25 - 5)/10 = 2. A line's average rate of change is always its slope.

    f(0) = 5, f(10) = 2(10) + 5 = 25 (25 - 5)/(10 - 0) = 20/10 = 2

    Practice set — function properties

    Items 1–5 use function operations and composition from Section 2.

    1. f(x) = 3x - 1, g(x) = x² + x. Find all four operations.
    2. f(x) = √(x + 4), g(x) = √(6 - x). Domain of (fg)?
    3. Domain of (f/g) for f(x) = x + 1, g(x) = x² - 9
    4. f(x) = 1/x, g(x) = x - 5. Find (f∘g)(x) and its domain.
    5. f(x) = x² + 1, g(x) = √(x - 3). Find (f∘g)(x) and its domain.
    6. ARoC of f(x) = x³ from -2 to 1
    7. A graph rises to (1, 6), falls to (4, -2), then rises forever. Give increasing/decreasing intervals and all extrema.
    Answers

    1. (f+g) = x² + 4x - 1; (f-g) = -x² + 2x - 1; (fg) = 3x³ + 2x² - x; (f/g) = (3x-1)/(x²+x), x ≠ 0, -1

    f + g = 3x - 1 + x² + x = x² + 4x - 1 f - g = 3x - 1 - x² - x = -x² + 2x - 1 fg = (3x - 1)(x² + x) = 3x³ + 3x² - x² - x = 3x³ + 2x² - x f/g = (3x - 1)/(x² + x) x² + x = x(x + 1) = 0 → x = 0, -1 excluded

    2. [-4, ∞) overlapped with (-∞, 6] → [-4, 6]

    f: x + 4 ≥ 0 → x ≥ -4 → [-4, ∞) g: 6 - x ≥ 0 → x ≤ 6 → (-∞, 6] Overlap: [-4, 6]

    3. All reals except 3 and -3

    g(x) = 0: x² - 9 = 0 → x = ±3 All reals except 3 and -3

    4. 1/(x - 5), domain x ≠ 5

    f(g(x)) = 1/(x - 5) x - 5 ≠ 0 → x ≠ 5

    5. (√(x-3))² + 1 = x - 2, but the inside needs x ≥ 3. Domain [3, ∞)

    f(g(x)) = (√(x - 3))² + 1 = x - 3 + 1 = x - 2 Inside g needs x - 3 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 3 Domain [3, ∞)

    6. (1 - (-8))/(1 - (-2)) = 9/3 = 3

    f(-2) = (-2)³ = -8, f(1) = 1³ = 1 (1 - (-8))/(1 - (-2)) = 9/3 = 3

    7. Increasing (-∞, 1) and (4, ∞); decreasing (1, 4). Local max 6 at x = 1, local min -2 at x = 4. No absolute max; -2 is not absolute either since the left end also runs down.

    Rises up to x = 1 → increasing (-∞, 1) Falls from 1 to 4 → decreasing (1, 4) Rises after 4 → increasing (4, ∞) Peak (1, 6) → local max 6 at x = 1 Valley (4, -2) → local min -2 at x = 4 Left end runs down, right end runs up → no absolute max or min

    Function transformations

    FormEffect
    f(x)+kup k
    f(x)-kdown k
    f(x-h)right h
    f(x+h)left h
    -f(x)reflect across x-axis
    f(-x)reflect across y-axis
    Memory trick: “inside lies.” Inside horizontal shifts act opposite the sign you see.

    The full transformation table

    FormEffectWhat happens to a point (x, y)
    f(x) + kup k(x, y + k)
    f(x) - kdown k(x, y - k)
    f(x - h)right h(x + h, y)
    f(x + h)left h(x - h, y)
    -f(x)reflect across x-axis(x, -y)
    f(-x)reflect across y-axis(-x, y)
    a·f(x), |a| > 1vertical stretch by a (taller)(x, ay)
    a·f(x), 0 < |a| < 1vertical compression(x, ay)
    f(bx), |b| > 1horizontal compression by 1/b (narrower)(x/b, y)
    f(bx), 0 < |b| < 1horizontal stretch by 1/b(x/b, y)
    Outside is honest, inside lies. Anything applied to the whole function (a, +k, the leading minus) does exactly what it says, vertically. Anything attached to x does the opposite of what it looks like, horizontally.

    Even and odd functions

    TestMeaningSymmetry
    f(-x) = f(x)evenmirror across the y-axis
    f(-x) = -f(x)odd180° rotation about the origin
    neither holdsneitherno symmetry

    Worked examples — transformations

    Example 1 — four transformations stacked

    Describe g(x) = -2f(x - 3) + 1 in terms of f, and find where the point (4, 5) on f ends up.

    Read the pieces from the inside out: (x - 3) inside → shift RIGHT 3 (inside lies: minus means right) × 2 outside → vertical stretch by 2 leading - outside → reflect across the x-axis + 1 outside → shift UP 1 Point mapping: (x, y) → (x + 3, -2y + 1) Apply to (4, 5): new x = 4 + 3 = 7 new y = -2(5) + 1 = -10 + 1 = -9 The point lands at (7, -9).
    Order matters vertically. Stretch before shifting: -2(5) + 1, not -2(5 + 1). The +1 is outside the multiplication.
    Example 2 — a concrete parabola

    f(x) = x². Graph g(x) = -2(x - 3)² + 1.

    Vertex of x² is (0, 0). Apply the mapping (x, y) → (x + 3, -2y + 1): new x = x + 3 new y = -2y + 1 (0, 0) → 0 + 3 = 3 -2(0) + 1 = 1 → (3, 1) vertex (1, 1) → 1 + 3 = 4 -2(1) + 1 = -1 → (4, -1) (-1, 1) → -1 + 3 = 2 -2(1) + 1 = -1 → (2, -1) (2, 4) → 2 + 3 = 5 -2(4) + 1 = -7 → (5, -7) (-2, 4) → -2 + 3 = 1 -2(4) + 1 = -7 → (1, -7) Shape: opens DOWN (leading negative), narrower than x² (stretch factor 2). Vertex (3, 1), axis of symmetry x = 3, maximum value 1.
    Example 3 — horizontal stretch and compression

    Compare y = f(2x) and y = f(x/3).

    f(2x): the 2 is INSIDE, so it does the opposite of "double." Horizontal COMPRESSION by 1/2 — the graph gets narrower. A point at x = 6 on f moves to x = 3. f(x/3): the 1/3 is inside, so it does the opposite of "shrink." Horizontal STRETCH by 3 — the graph gets wider. A point at x = 6 on f moves to x = 18. General rule: in f(bx), every x-coordinate is divided by b.
    Example 4 — even or odd?

    Classify f(x) = x⁴ - 3x² and g(x) = x³ - x.

    f(-x) = (-x)⁴ - 3(-x)² = x⁴ - 3x² = f(x) → EVEN g(-x) = (-x)³ - (-x) = -x³ + x = -(x³ - x) = -g(x) → ODD
    Polynomial shortcut: all-even exponents (a constant counts as x⁰) → even. All-odd exponents → odd. Mixed → neither.

    Quick check — transformations

    1. Describe y = f(x + 2) - 5
    2. Describe y = (1/3)f(x)
    3. Where does (2, -6) go under y = -f(x) + 4?
    4. Is f(x) = x² + x even, odd, or neither?
    Answers

    1. Left 2, down 5

    f(x + 2): inside +2 → LEFT 2 - 5 outside → DOWN 5

    2. Vertical compression by 1/3

    (1/3) outside multiplies every y by 1/3 → vertical compression by 1/3

    3. (2, -(-6) + 4) = (2, 10)

    y = -f(x) + 4 → (x, y) → (x, -y + 4) (2, -6) → (2, -(-6) + 4) = (2, 10)

    4. Mixed exponents → neither. Check: f(-x) = x² - x, which is neither f(x) nor -f(x).

    f(-x) = (-x)² + (-x) = x² - x f(x) = x² + x → not equal -f(x) = -x² - x → not equal Neither

    Practice set — transformations

    1. Starting from y = √x, describe y = 3√(x + 1) - 2
    2. Starting from y = |x|, describe y = -|2x|
    3. Point (-3, 8) on f; where is it on y = (1/2)f(x - 4)?
    4. Write the function that shifts y = x³ left 5, reflects over the x-axis, and moves up 2
    5. Classify h(x) = 5/x
    Answers

    1. Left 1, vertical stretch by 3, down 2

    y = 3√(x + 1) - 2 (x + 1) inside → LEFT 1 × 3 outside → vertical stretch by 3 - 2 outside → DOWN 2

    2. Horizontal compression by 1/2, reflect across the x-axis

    y = -|2x| 2 inside → horizontal compression by 1/2 leading - → reflect across the x-axis

    3. (-3 + 4, 8/2) = (1, 4)

    y = (1/2)f(x - 4) → (x, y) → (x + 4, y/2) (-3, 8) → (-3 + 4, 8/2) = (1, 4)

    4. y = -(x + 5)³ + 2

    Left 5: (x + 5)³ Reflect x-axis: -(x + 5)³ Up 2: -(x + 5)³ + 2

    5. h(-x) = -5/x = -h(x) → odd

    h(-x) = 5/(-x) = -5/x = -h(x) → odd

    The graphs you must know cold

    Every transformation problem starts from one of these. If you do not know the base shape, the transformation rules have nothing to act on.

    FunctionShapeDomainRangeAnchor points
    y = xline through origin, 45°all realsall reals(-1,-1) (0,0) (1,1)
    y = x²parabola opening upall reals[0, ∞)(-2,4) (-1,1) (0,0) (1,1) (2,4)
    y = x³S-curve through originall realsall reals(-2,-8) (-1,-1) (0,0) (1,1) (2,8)
    y = √xhalf parabola, opens right[0, ∞)[0, ∞)(0,0) (1,1) (4,2) (9,3)
    y = ³√xsideways Sall realsall reals(-8,-2) (-1,-1) (0,0) (1,1) (8,2)
    y = |x|V with vertex at originall reals[0, ∞)(-2,2) (-1,1) (0,0) (1,1) (2,2)
    y = 1/xtwo hyperbola branchesx ≠ 0y ≠ 0(-2,-1/2) (-1,-1) (1,1) (2,1/2)
    y = 1/x²two branches, both above the axisx ≠ 0(0, ∞)(-1,1) (1,1) (2,1/4)
    y = bˣ, b > 1exponential growthall reals(0, ∞)(-1,1/b) (0,1) (1,b)
    y = logbxexponential flipped over y = x(0, ∞)all reals(1/b,-1) (1,0) (b,1)
    The three-point method. Memorize just (-1, ?), (0, ?), (1, ?) for each parent. Apply the point mapping from the transformation table, plot the three images, and the shape follows.
    Example — transforming a parent graph by its anchor points

    Graph y = -2√(x + 1) + 3.

    Parent: y = √x with anchors (0,0), (1,1), (4,2), (9,3) Read the transformations: (x + 1) inside → shift LEFT 1 × 2 outside → vertical stretch 2 leading - → reflect over the x-axis + 3 outside → shift UP 3 Mapping: (x, y) → (x - 1, -2y + 3) new x = x - 1 new y = -2y + 3 (0,0) → 0 - 1 = -1 -2(0) + 3 = 3 → (-1, 3) start (1,1) → 1 - 1 = 0 -2(1) + 3 = 1 → ( 0, 1) (4,2) → 4 - 1 = 3 -2(2) + 3 = -1 → ( 3, -1) (9,3) → 9 - 1 = 8 -2(3) + 3 = -3 → ( 8, -3) Domain: [-1, ∞) Range: (-∞, 3]

    Section 2 — Function Composition and Rational & Inverse Functions

    Skills to know firstFunction notationDomainFractionsFactoringQuadraticsPolynomial SkillsEquation solving
    SkillsComposition, inverse functions, function operations, rational functions, holes, asymptotes, intercepts, and rational-function graphing.

    Composition

    (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x))
    Composition: inside function first.

    Inverse functions

    To find an inverse:

    1. write y=f(x)
    2. swap x and y
    3. solve for y
    4. rename y as f-1(x)
    Inverse notation does not mean reciprocal.

    Guided function routine

    1For f(a), replace every x with (a).
    2For domain, look for denominator zeros and even-root restrictions.
    3Composition → inside function first.
    4Inverse → swap x and y, solve for y.
    Shortcut: always use parentheses around substituted negative values.

    Worked examples — composition and inverses

    Example 1 — composition, both orders

    f(x) = 2x - 1, g(x) = x² + 3. Find (f∘g)(x) and (g∘f)(x).

    (f∘g)(x) means f(g(x)) — g runs FIRST, its whole output goes into f's x slot. f(g(x)) = 2(x² + 3) - 1 = 2x² + 6 - 1 = 2x² + 5 (g∘f)(x) means g(f(x)) — f runs first. g(f(x)) = (2x - 1)² + 3 = 4x² - 4x + 1 + 3 = 4x² - 4x + 4
    Composition is not commutative. The two answers above are completely different functions. Read the notation right to left.
    Example 2 — composition at a number

    Same f and g. Find (f∘g)(2) two ways.

    Way 1 — inside first: g(2) = 2² + 3 = 7 f(7) = 2(7) - 1 = 13 Way 2 — use the composed formula from Example 1: (f∘g)(x) = 2x² + 5 (f∘g)(2) = 2(4) + 5 = 13 ✓
    Example 3 — inverse of a rational function

    Find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = (3x - 1)/(x + 2).

    Step 1 Write y = f(x). y = (3x - 1)/(x + 2) Step 2 Swap x and y. x = (3y - 1)/(y + 2) Step 3 Solve for y. Clear the fraction first. x(y + 2) = 3y - 1 xy + 2x = 3y - 1 Step 4 Get every y term on one side, everything else on the other. xy - 3y = -1 - 2x ← 3y moved left (became -3y), 2x moved right (became -2x) Step 5 Factor y out of the left side. y(x - 3) = -(2x + 1) Step 6 Divide. y = -(2x + 1)/(x - 3) Step 7 Clean up the sign by distributing -1 into the denominator instead. y = (2x + 1)/(3 - x) Answer: f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 1)/(3 - x)
    Step 5 is the move people miss. When y appears in two terms you cannot divide it out — you have to factor it out first.
    Example 4 — inverse with a cube

    Find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 2x³ + 5.

    y = 2x³ + 5 x = 2y³ + 5 (swap) x - 5 = 2y³ (x - 5)/2 = y³ y = ³√[(x - 5)/2] f⁻¹(x) = ³√[(x - 5)/2]
    Two facts the inverse section usually leaves out. (1) A function has an inverse function only if it passes the horizontal line test (it must be one-to-one). (2) The inverse swaps domain and range: the domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f.

    Quick check — composition and inverses

    1. f(x) = x + 4, g(x) = 1/x; find (g∘f)(x) and its domain
    2. Inverse of f(x) = (x - 7)/3
    Answers

    1. g(f(x)) = 1/(x + 4), domain x ≠ -4

    g(f(x)) = 1/(f(x)) = 1/(x + 4) x + 4 ≠ 0 → x ≠ -4

    2. x = (y - 7)/3 → 3x = y - 7 → y = 3x + 7

    y = (x - 7)/3 Swap: x = (y - 7)/3 3x = y - 7 y = 3x + 7

    Practice set — composition and inverses

    1. f(x) = x², g(x) = x - 3; find both compositions
    2. Inverse of f(x) = 5/(x + 1)
    Answers

    1. (f∘g)(x) = (x - 3)²; (g∘f)(x) = x² - 3

    f(g(x)) = (g(x))² = (x - 3)² g(f(x)) = f(x) - 3 = x² - 3

    2. x = 5/(y+1) → x(y+1) = 5 → y + 1 = 5/x → y = 5/x - 1

    y = 5/(x + 1) Swap: x = 5/(y + 1) x(y + 1) = 5 y + 1 = 5/x y = 5/x - 1

    Operations of functions

    OperationRuleDomain
    (f + g)(x)f(x) + g(x)overlap of both domains
    (f - g)(x)f(x) - g(x)overlap of both domains
    (fg)(x)f(x) · g(x)overlap of both domains
    (f/g)(x)f(x)/g(x)overlap, and g(x) ≠ 0
    Example 1 — all four operations

    f(x) = x² - 4, g(x) = x + 2. Find all four combinations and their domains.

    Both are polynomials, so both domains are all real numbers. (f + g)(x) = x² - 4 + x + 2 = x² + x - 2 domain: all reals (f - g)(x) = x² - 4 - (x + 2) = x² - 4 - x - 2 ← distribute the minus = x² - x - 6 domain: all reals (fg)(x) = (x² - 4)(x + 2) = x²·x + x²·2 - 4·x - 4·2 ← each times each = x³ + 2x² - 4x - 8 domain: all reals (f/g)(x) = (x² - 4)/(x + 2) = (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x + 2) = x - 2, but x ≠ -2 domain: all reals EXCEPT -2
    The restriction survives the cancelling. (f/g) simplifies to a line, but x = -2 is still excluded because it made the original denominator zero. Same idea as a hole in a rational function.
    Example 2 — when the domains do not match

    f(x) = √(x - 1), g(x) = √(5 - x). Find (f + g)(x) and (f/g)(x) with domains.

    Domain of f: x - 1 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 1 [1, ∞) Domain of g: 5 - x ≥ 0 → x ≤ 5 (-∞, 5] OVERLAP: [1, 5] (f + g)(x) = √(x - 1) + √(5 - x) domain [1, 5] (f/g)(x) = √(x - 1)/√(5 - x) Now also require g(x) ≠ 0: 5 - x ≠ 0 → x ≠ 5 domain [1, 5)

    Domain of a composite function

    This is the most commonly missed domain question in the course. The domain of (f∘g)(x) is not just the domain of the simplified formula. You need both: x must be in the domain of g, and g(x) must be in the domain of f.
    Example 1 — the restriction that disappears from the formula

    f(x) = 1/x, g(x) = x + 3. Find (g∘f)(x) and its domain.

    (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) = 1/x + 3 Test 1 x must be in the domain of the INSIDE function f. f(x) = 1/x needs x ≠ 0. Test 2 f(x) must land in the domain of g. g accepts everything, so no new restriction. Domain: x ≠ 0 The formula 1/x + 3 shows the restriction here, so this one is easy.
    Example 2 — the restriction that vanishes and must be restored

    f(x) = x², g(x) = 1/(x - 4). Find (f∘g)(x) and its domain.

    (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)) = [1/(x - 4)]² = 1/(x - 4)² Test 1 x in the domain of g: x ≠ 4 Test 2 g(x) in the domain of f: f accepts everything, no new restriction Domain: x ≠ 4 Here the formula still shows it. Now watch the hard case.
    Example 3 — the hard case, where the formula lies

    f(x) = √x, g(x) = x². Find (f∘g)(x), then f(x) = x², g(x) = √(x - 2) and find (f∘g)(x).

    CASE A: f(g(x)) = √(x²) = |x| Test 1 x in domain of g = x²: all reals Test 2 g(x) = x² must be ≥ 0 for the square root: always true Domain: all reals. The |x| formula agrees. CASE B: f(g(x)) = (√(x - 2))² = x - 2 The simplified formula "x - 2" looks like it works for every x. It does NOT. Test 1 x must be in the domain of g = √(x - 2): x - 2 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 2 Test 2 g(x) is a square root output, always ≥ 0, and f = x² accepts it. Domain: [2, ∞) The answer is the LINE y = x - 2, but only from x = 2 rightward.
    Why this matters. Squaring undid the square root algebraically, but it cannot undo the fact that you could never have entered a number below 2 in the first place. Always run Test 1 on the inside function before you simplify.

    Rational functions

    General form:

    f(x)= N(x)D(x)

    The full order

    1. Factor numerator completely.
    2. Factor denominator completely.
    3. Record original denominator restrictions.
    4. Cancel common factors.
    5. Canceled denominator factors create holes.
    6. Remaining denominator factors create vertical asymptotes.
    7. Remaining numerator zeros create x-intercepts.
    8. Set x = 0 for y-intercept.
    9. Compare degrees for horizontal/slant behavior.
    Fast rational-function scan. Factor first. A denominator zero from a canceled factor is a hole; a denominator zero that remains is a vertical asymptote. For end behavior, compare degrees before doing any long division: bottom degree larger → y = 0; equal degrees → ratio of leading coefficients; top degree exactly one larger → divide for a slant asymptote. This saves work without skipping the domain restrictions.

    Cancel factors, not terms

    You may cancel: x(x+3)x = x+3 But you may not cancel x in: x+3x

    Hole coordinates

    Use the canceled x-value in the simplified function to find the y-coordinate.

    Guided rational-function graphing — full procedure

    FACTOR→RESTRICTIONS→CANCEL→CLASSIFY→ASYMPTOTES→POINTS→SHAPE
    1Factor top and bottom completely. Do not label holes or VAs yet.
    2Write all original denominator restrictions. Those x-values can never be in the domain.
    3Cancel common factors. Canceled denominator factor = hole. Remaining denominator factor = vertical asymptote.
    4Hole coordinate: solve canceled factor = 0 for x, then plug that x into the simplified function for y.
    5End behavior: compare degrees for horizontal/slant asymptotes.
    6Intercepts: remaining numerator = 0 for x-intercepts; x = 0 for y-intercept.
    7Points: vertical asymptotes split the graph into pieces. Pick easy x-values on each piece.
    8Shape: use signs to decide +∞/−∞ near VAs and above/below end-behavior asymptotes.
    Example 1 — hole + VA + HA
    g(x)=-3x-15x2+7x+10

    Factor the numerator:

    -3x-15=-3(x+5)

    Factor the denominator: find two numbers multiplying to 10 and adding to 7 → 5 and 2.

    x2+7x+10=(x+5)(x+2)

    Original restrictions: x ≠ −5, −2.

    Cancel:

    g(x)=-3x+2,x≠-5
    Classify: x+5 canceled → hole at x=−5. x+2 stayed → VA at x=−2.

    Hole y-value:

    g(-5)=-3-5+2=1

    Hole = (−5,1).

    Horizontal asymptote: simplified top degree 0, bottom degree 1 → bottom bigger → y=0.

    Classic mistake: calling x=−5 a VA because it made the original denominator zero. Its factor canceled, so it is a hole.
    TI-30XIIS: use the simplified function −3/(x+2) to calculate ordinary graph points. Never evaluate x=−2, and remember x=−5 is still missing.

    Second and third worked examples

    Example 2 — hole, VA, and a nonzero horizontal asymptote

    Analyze h(x) = (x² - 4)/(x² - x - 6) completely.

    FACTOR Numerator: x² - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) difference of squares Denominator: x² - x - 6 = (x - 3)(x + 2) mult to -6, add to -1 → -3 and 2 RESTRICTIONS (from the ORIGINAL denominator, before any cancelling) x - 3 = 0 → x ≠ 3 x + 2 = 0 → x ≠ -2 CANCEL (x + 2) appears top and bottom → it cancels. h(x) = (x - 2)/(x - 3), x ≠ -2 CLASSIFY (x + 2) CANCELLED → HOLE at x = -2 (x - 3) STAYED downstairs → VERTICAL ASYMPTOTE at x = 3 HOLE COORDINATE Plug x = -2 into the SIMPLIFIED function: (-2 - 2)/(-2 - 3) = -4/-5 = 4/5 Hole at (-2, 4/5) END BEHAVIOR Top degree 1, bottom degree 1 → equal → divide leading coefficients: 1/1 HORIZONTAL ASYMPTOTE y = 1 INTERCEPTS x-intercept: set the simplified numerator to 0 → x - 2 = 0 → (2, 0) y-intercept: h(0) = (0 - 2)/(0 - 3) = -2/-3 = 2/3 → (0, 2/3)
    Two traps in one problem. (1) x = -2 is not a vertical asymptote even though it zeroes the original denominator — its factor cancelled. (2) The hole's y-value comes from the simplified function; the original gives 0/0.
    Example 3 — everything cancels except a line

    Analyze k(x) = (2x² + x - 6)/(x + 2).

    FACTOR the numerator with AC: a·c = 2(-6) = -12, add to 1 → 4 and -3 2x² + 4x - 3x - 6 2x(x + 2) - 3(x + 2) (2x - 3)(x + 2) RESTRICTIONS: x ≠ -2 CANCEL (x + 2): k(x) = 2x - 3, x ≠ -2 CLASSIFY The denominator factor cancelled entirely. NO vertical asymptote. NO horizontal asymptote. The graph is the LINE y = 2x - 3 with a hole punched in it. HOLE: y = 2(-2) - 3 = -7 → hole at (-2, -7)
    Why this matters. A rational function does not have to have an asymptote. Factoring first is the only way to find out.
    Example 4 — a slant case from start to finish

    Analyze m(x) = (x² - 4)/(x + 1).

    FACTOR: (x - 2)(x + 2) / (x + 1) RESTRICTIONS: x ≠ -1 CANCEL: nothing cancels VERTICAL ASYMPTOTE x = -1 No hole. END BEHAVIOR: top degree 2, bottom degree 1. Difference is exactly 1 → SLANT. Long division of x² + 0x - 4 by x + 1: D x² ÷ x = x M x(x + 1) = x² + x S (x² + 0x) - (x² + x) = -x B bring down -4 → -x - 4 D -x ÷ x = -1 M -1(x + 1) = -x - 1 S (-x - 4) - (-x - 1) = -4 + 1 = -3 (subtracting -1 ADDS 1) Quotient x - 1, remainder -3 m(x) = x - 1 + (-3)/(x + 1) SLANT ASYMPTOTE y = x - 1 INTERCEPTS x-intercepts: x² - 4 = 0 → (2, 0) and (-2, 0) y-intercept: m(0) = -4/1 = -4 → (0, -4) ABOVE OR BELOW the slant? The remainder piece is -3/(x + 1). For large positive x it is negative → graph sits BELOW y = x - 1 on the right. For large negative x, (x + 1) is negative, so -3/(negative) is positive → ABOVE on the left.

    Quick check — rational functions

    1. Hole or VA at x = 1 for (x - 1)/(x² - 1)?
    2. Can you cancel the x in (x + 5)/x?
    3. y-intercept of (2x - 6)/(x + 4)
    4. Simplify (x² - 9)/(x² + 6x + 9) and give the restrictions
    Answers

    1. (x-1)/[(x-1)(x+1)] = 1/(x+1); the (x-1) cancels → HOLE at x = 1, y-value 1/2. VA is at x = -1.

    (x - 1)/(x² - 1) = (x - 1)/[(x - 1)(x + 1)] (x - 1) cancels → 1/(x + 1) → HOLE at x = 1 Hole y: 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2 → (1, 1/2) (x + 1) stays → VA x = -1

    2. No. x is a term in the numerator, not a factor. Only factors cancel.

    (x + 5)/x: the top is a SUM. x is a term of the top, not a factor. Only factors cancel → no

    3. -6/4 = -3/2

    y-int: x = 0 (2(0) - 6)/(0 + 4) = -6/4 = -3/2

    4. (x-3)(x+3)/(x+3)² = (x-3)/(x+3), x ≠ -3. Since one (x+3) remains downstairs, x = -3 is a VA, not a hole.

    Top: x² - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3) Bottom: x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)² Cancel one (x + 3): (x - 3)/(x + 3) Restriction from original: x ≠ -3 One (x + 3) still downstairs → x = -3 is a VA

    Practice set — rational functions

    For each, give holes, vertical asymptotes, end-behavior asymptote, and both intercepts.

    1. f(x) = (x² - 25)/(x² - 3x - 10)
    2. f(x) = (4x + 8)/(x² - 4)
    3. f(x) = (3x² + 1)/(x² - 9)
    4. f(x) = (x² + 2x - 8)/(x - 1)
    Answers

    1. (x-5)(x+5)/[(x-5)(x+2)] = (x+5)/(x+2), x ≠ 5. Hole at (5, 10/7); VA x = -2; HA y = 1; x-int (-5, 0); y-int (0, 5/2)

    Top (x - 5)(x + 5); bottom (x - 5)(x + 2) Cancel (x - 5): (x + 5)/(x + 2), x ≠ 5 Hole: (5 + 5)/(5 + 2) = 10/7 → (5, 10/7) VA x = -2 Degrees equal 1/1 → HA y = 1 x-int: x + 5 = 0 → (-5, 0) y-int: 5/2 → (0, 5/2)

    2. 4(x+2)/[(x-2)(x+2)] = 4/(x-2), x ≠ -2. Hole at (-2, -1); VA x = 2; HA y = 0; no x-intercept; y-int (0, -2)

    Top 4(x + 2); bottom (x - 2)(x + 2) Cancel (x + 2): 4/(x - 2), x ≠ -2 Hole: 4/(-2 - 2) = -1 → (-2, -1) VA x = 2 Top degree 0 < 1 → HA y = 0 x-int: 4 = 0 never → none y-int: 4/(0 - 2) = -2 → (0, -2)

    3. Nothing cancels. VA x = 3 and x = -3; HA y = 3; no x-intercept (3x² + 1 is never 0); y-int (0, -1/9)

    Bottom x² - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3); top 3x² + 1 does not factor Nothing cancels → VA x = 3 and x = -3 Degrees equal 3/1 → HA y = 3 x-int: 3x² + 1 = 0 → x² = -1/3 → none y-int: 1/(-9) = -1/9

    4. (x+4)(x-2)/(x-1), nothing cancels. VA x = 1. Degrees 2 and 1 → slant. Division gives x + 3 + (-5)/(x - 1), so slant y = x + 3. x-int (-4, 0) and (2, 0); y-int (0, 8)

    Top: multiply -8, add 2 → 4, -2 → (x + 4)(x - 2) Bottom (x - 1), nothing cancels → VA x = 1 Degrees 2 and 1 → slant. Synthetic c = 1: 1 | 1 2 -8 | 1 3 +-------------- 1 3 -5 x + 3 + (-5)/(x - 1) → slant y = x + 3 x-int (-4, 0), (2, 0) y-int: (-8)/(-1) = 8 → (0, 8)

    Asymptotes

    How to use this note: If a step feels rusty, use the links above before continuing. For example, vertical asymptotes depend on factoring, rational-function cancellation, and domain restrictions; slant asymptotes also depend on polynomial degree/division.

    Vertical asymptote

    After cancellation: set the remaining denominator equal to zero.
    Best memory shortcut:
    Canceled downstairs factor → hole
    Factor that stays downstairs → vertical asymptote

    Horizontal asymptote: compare degrees

    Top degreeBottom degreeResult
    smallerlargery=0
    equalequalratio of leading coefficients
    largersmallerno horizontal asymptote — divide instead: gap of 1 gives a slant, a larger gap gives a polynomial asymptote
    Memory: Bottom bigger → zero. Same → divide. Top bigger → divide polynomials.

    Slant asymptote

    If the numerator degree is exactly one more than the denominator degree, use polynomial long division.

    Quotient = slant asymptote. Ignore the remainder for the asymptote.

    Worked example — slant asymptote with messy coefficients

    f(x)= -4x2-18x+6 6x+9

    Vertical asymptote:

    6x+9=0 ⇒ x=-32

    y-intercept:

    f(0) = 69 = 23

    x-intercepts:

    x= -9±105 4

    Slant asymptote:

    y= -23x-2

    Guided asymptote decision tree

    Degree comparisonAction
    top < bottomHA: y = 0
    top = bottomHA: divide leading coefficients
    top = bottom + 1slant: polynomial division
    top > bottom + 1polynomial asymptote: divide
    Memory: Bottom bigger → 0. Same → divide. Top 1 higher → divide polynomials.

    Slant asymptote — repeatable routine

    1Confirm top degree is exactly one larger.
    2DMSB: Divide → Multiply → Subtract → Bring down.
    3Quotient = slant line.
    4Keep the remainder fraction for branch direction.
    Draw the line: put quotient in y=mx+b. Plot b, use slope m = rise/run, connect with a dashed line.
    Above/below shortcut: f(x) = slant + remainder fraction. Remainder fraction positive → graph above slant; negative → below.
    DMSB danger: when subtracting the multiplied polynomial, distribute the negative to every term.

    More asymptote examples

    Example 1 — a denominator with no real zeros

    Find all asymptotes of f(x) = (3x² - 5)/(x² + 1).

    Vertical: set x² + 1 = 0 → x² = -1 → no real solution. NO vertical asymptote at all. Horizontal: degrees are equal (2 and 2), so divide the LEADING coefficients. 3/1 = 3 → y = 3
    Leading coefficients only. The -5 and the +1 are irrelevant to the horizontal asymptote. They matter for intercepts, not end behavior.
    Example 2 — degree gap of 2, so neither HA nor slant

    Find the end-behavior asymptote of f(x) = (x³ + 1)/(x - 2).

    Top degree 3, bottom degree 1. The gap is 2, not 1, so it is NOT a slant. Divide anyway — the quotient is still the asymptote, it is just a curve. Synthetic division, c = 2, coefficients 1, 0, 0, 1: 2 | 1 0 0 1 | 2 4 8 +--------------------- 1 2 4 9 Quotient x² + 2x + 4, remainder 9. f(x) = x² + 2x + 4 + 9/(x - 2) As x runs off to ±∞, 9/(x - 2) → 0, so the graph hugs the PARABOLA y = x² + 2x + 4 Vertical asymptote: x = 2.
    The general rule. Divide. The quotient is always the end-behavior asymptote: a constant when degrees are equal, a line when the gap is 1, a parabola when the gap is 2, and so on. "No horizontal asymptote" does not mean "no asymptote."
    Example 3 — reading direction near a vertical asymptote

    For f(x) = (x + 3)/(x - 1), which way does the graph go on each side of x = 1?

    You only need SIGNS, not values. Test just left and just right. x = 0.9: numerator 0.9 + 3 = +3.9 denominator 0.9 - 1 = -0.1 (tiny NEGATIVE) positive ÷ tiny negative = large NEGATIVE → goes DOWN to -∞ x = 1.1: numerator 1.1 + 3 = +4.1 denominator 1.1 - 1 = +0.1 (tiny POSITIVE) positive ÷ tiny positive = large POSITIVE → goes UP to +∞ Left branch dives down, right branch shoots up.
    Never substitute the asymptote value itself. Pick a number a tenth away on each side. The sign is the whole answer.

    Quick check — asymptotes

    1. HA of (2x + 1)/(5x - 3)
    2. HA of (x + 4)/(x² - 1)
    3. What kind of asymptote does (x² + 1)/(x - 3) have?
    4. Does (x³)/(x² + 4) have a vertical asymptote?
    Answers

    1. Equal degrees → y = 2/5

    (2x + 1)/(5x - 3): degrees equal (1 and 1) Ratio of leading coefficients: y = 2/5

    2. Bottom bigger → y = 0

    (x + 4)/(x² - 1): top degree 1 < bottom 2 → y = 0

    3. Degree gap of 1 → slant. Division gives x + 3 + 10/(x - 3), so y = x + 3

    (x² + 1)/(x - 3): gap of 1 → slant 3 | 1 0 1 | 3 9 +-------------- 1 3 10 x + 3 + 10/(x - 3) → y = x + 3

    4. No. x² + 4 = 0 has no real solution. It does have a slant asymptote y = x.

    VA needs bottom = 0: x² + 4 = 0 → x² = -4 → no real x → no vertical asymptote Divide x³ by x² + 4: x³ ÷ x² = x, x(x² + 4) = x³ + 4x, remainder -4x → slant y = x

    Practice set — asymptotes

    1. All asymptotes of (7x³ - 2)/(2x³ + x)
    2. All asymptotes of (x² - 1)/(x² + 2x - 8)
    3. Slant asymptote of (2x² - 3x + 1)/(x - 2)
    4. End-behavior asymptote of (x⁴)/(x² - 1)
    Answers

    1. Denominator x(2x² + 1) = 0 → x = 0 only → VA x = 0. Equal degrees → HA y = 7/2

    Bottom: 2x³ + x = x(2x² + 1) = 0 x = 0 (2x² + 1 is never 0) → VA x = 0 Degrees equal (3 and 3) → HA y = 7/2

    2. (x-1)(x+1)/[(x+4)(x-2)], nothing cancels. VA x = -4 and x = 2; HA y = 1

    Top (x - 1)(x + 1); bottom: multiply -8, add 2 → 4, -2 → (x + 4)(x - 2). Nothing cancels. VA x = -4 and x = 2 Degrees equal 1/1 → HA y = 1

    3. Divide: 2x + 1 + 3/(x - 2) → slant y = 2x + 1

    2 | 2 -3 1 | 4 2 +-------------- 2 1 3 2x + 1 + 3/(x - 2) → slant y = 2x + 1

    4. Divide x⁴ by x² - 1: quotient x² + 1, remainder 1. Parabolic asymptote y = x² + 1; VAs at x = ±1

    x⁴ ÷ (x² - 1): x⁴ ÷ x² = x²; x²(x² - 1) = x⁴ - x²; subtract → x² x² ÷ x² = 1; 1(x² - 1) = x² - 1; subtract → 1 Quotient x² + 1, remainder 1 → y = x² + 1 VA: x² - 1 = 0 → x = ±1

    Rational-function graphing

    Recognize the graph family first

    After factoring/simplifyingFeature
    denominator factor cancelshole
    denominator factor remainsvertical asymptote
    top degree smallerhorizontal asymptote y=0
    same degreehorizontal asymptote = leading coefficient ratio
    top degree exactly 1 largerslant asymptote

    Two points on each piece

    1Draw vertical asymptotes first; they split the x-axis into intervals.
    2Choose easy integer x-values inside each interval. Never choose the VA itself.
    3Use the simplified form when it makes point arithmetic easier.
    4Plot the points, then shape the curve so it obeys the VA and HA/slant behavior.

    How to decide up/down near a vertical asymptote

    Test one x-value just left and one just right. You only need the sign. A tiny positive denominator and positive numerator gives +∞; a tiny negative denominator flips the sign.

    Never plug the VA itself in. That is division by zero. Nearby values reveal the direction.

    How to decide above/below a slant asymptote

    After division, write:

    function = slant line + remainder fraction

    Positive remainder fraction → above. Negative remainder fraction → below.

    Full paper routine: FACTOR → RESTRICTIONS → CANCEL → HOLES/VAs → DEGREE RULE → INTERCEPTS → TWO POINTS PER PIECE → SIGN/DIRECTION → DRAW.

    Quiz 1

    CoverageSections 1–2
    FocusFunctions, domain, transformations, average rate of change, composition, inverses, and rational-function features.
    Directions: Work without notes if you can. Show enough algebra to make your method clear. TI-30XIIS use is allowed, but these questions are designed to be solvable mostly by hand.

    Quiz 1 — 8 questions

    1. g(x) = 2x² - 3x + 4; find g(-3) and g(a - 1)
    2. Domain of h(x) = √(6 - 2x)/(x + 1) in interval notation
    3. Starting from y = √x, describe y = -2√(x - 3) + 4, then give its domain and range
    4. Average rate of change of f(x) = x² - 4x from x = 1 to x = 5
    5. f(x) = √(x + 5), g(x) = x² - 9. Find (f∘g)(x) and its domain
    6. Inverse of f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x - 3)
    7. For r(x) = (x² + x - 6)/(x² - 4), find any hole, the vertical and horizontal asymptotes, and both intercepts
    8. Slant asymptote and vertical asymptote of f(x) = (x² + 3x - 1)/(x - 1)
    Quiz 1 answer key + worked solutions
    1. g(-3) = 18 + 9 + 4 = 31. g(a - 1) = 2(a² - 2a + 1) - 3(a - 1) + 4 = 2a² - 4a + 2 - 3a + 3 + 4 = 2a² - 7a + 9
      g(-3) = 2(-3)² - 3(-3) + 4 = 2(9) + 9 + 4 = 31 g(a - 1) = 2(a - 1)² - 3(a - 1) + 4 (a - 1)² = a² - 2a + 1 = 2a² - 4a + 2 - 3a + 3 + 4 = 2a² - 7a + 9
    2. 6 - 2x ≥ 0 → x ≤ 3, and x ≠ -1 → (-∞, -1) ∪ (-1, 3]
      Root: 6 - 2x ≥ 0 → -2x ≥ -6 → x ≤ 3 (FLIP) Bottom: x + 1 ≠ 0 → x ≠ -1 (-∞, -1) ∪ (-1, 3]
    3. Right 3, vertical stretch by 2, reflect over the x-axis, up 4. Domain [3, ∞); range (-∞, 4]
      (x - 3) inside → right 3; × 2 → stretch; - → reflect; + 4 → up 4 Domain: x - 3 ≥ 0 → [3, ∞) Range: √ gives [0, ∞); × (-2) → (-∞, 0]; + 4 → (-∞, 4]
    4. f(1) = -3, f(5) = 5 → (5 - (-3))/(5 - 1) = 8/4 = 2
      f(1) = 1 - 4 = -3 f(5) = 25 - 20 = 5 (5 - (-3))/(5 - 1) = 8/4 = 2
    5. f(g(x)) = √(x² - 9 + 5) = √(x² - 4). Need x² - 4 ≥ 0 → (-∞, -2] ∪ [2, ∞)
      f(g(x)) = √(g(x) + 5) = √(x² - 9 + 5) = √(x² - 4) x² - 4 ≥ 0 → (x - 2)(x + 2) ≥ 0 x = -3: (-5)(-1) = 5 + x = 0: (-2)(2) = -4 - x = 3: (1)(5) = 5 + (-∞, -2] ∪ [2, ∞)
    6. Swap: x = (2y + 1)/(y - 3) → xy - 3x = 2y + 1 → xy - 2y = 3x + 1 → y(x - 2) = 3x + 1 → f⁻¹(x) = (3x + 1)/(x - 2)
      Swap: x = (2y + 1)/(y - 3) x(y - 3) = 2y + 1 xy - 3x = 2y + 1 xy - 2y = 3x + 1 y(x - 2) = 3x + 1 y = (3x + 1)/(x - 2)
    7. (x + 3)(x - 2)/[(x - 2)(x + 2)] = (x + 3)/(x + 2), x ≠ 2. Hole (2, 5/4); VA x = -2; HA y = 1; x-int (-3, 0); y-int (0, 3/2)
      Top: multiply -6, add 1 → 3, -2 → (x + 3)(x - 2) Bottom: (x - 2)(x + 2) Cancel (x - 2): (x + 3)/(x + 2), x ≠ 2 Hole: (2 + 3)/(2 + 2) = 5/4 → (2, 5/4) VA x = -2; HA 1/1 → y = 1 x-int (-3, 0); y-int 3/2 → (0, 3/2)
    8. Synthetic with c = 1: 1, 4, 3 → x + 4 + 3/(x - 1). Slant y = x + 4; VA x = 1
      1 | 1 3 -1 | 1 4 +-------------- 1 4 3 x + 4 + 3/(x - 1) → slant y = x + 4 VA x = 1 (top at 1 is 3, not 0)

    Section 3 — Exponential & Logarithmic Functions

    Skills to know firstExponents & RadicalsCore AlgebraFunction notationFunctions
    SkillsExponential functions, growth and decay, exponential equations, logarithms, log rules, change of base, and related calculator use.

    Exponential form

    y=abx

    b > 1 → growth.   0 < b < 1 → decay.

    Growth factor = 1 + rate.
    Decay factor = 1 - rate.

    Compound interest

    A=P (1+rn) nt

    Continuous compounding

    A=Pert

    Logs are inverse exponents

    logb(x)=y ⇔ by=x

    Log rules

    log(ab) = log(a) + log(b)
    log(ab) = log(a) - log(b)
    log(ak) = klog(a)
    You cannot split log(a+b).

    Change of base

    logb(x) = log(x)log(b)

    Guided exponential/log equation routine

    1Try to rewrite both sides with the same base.
    2If you cannot, isolate the exponential and take log or ln.
    3Use the power rule to move the exponent down.
    4Solve the remaining algebra.
    TI-30XIIS: LOG is base 10; LN is base e; arbitrary base = LOG(value) ÷ LOG(base).
    Fast exponential/log path. Before touching LOG or LN, ask whether both sides can be rewritten with the same base. If yes, equate exponents. If not, isolate the exponential first, then take a log. For log equations, condense only when it makes the equation simpler, convert to exponential form, solve, and finally reject any answer that makes an original log input nonpositive.

    Domain of a logarithm

    You can only take the log of a positive number. For logb(expression), the expression must be > 0. This is what creates extraneous solutions, and checking for them is usually worth points on its own.

    Worked examples — exponentials and logarithms

    Example 1 — same-base method

    Solve 4ˣ⁺¹ = 8ˣ⁻².

    Both 4 and 8 are powers of 2. Rewrite everything base 2. 4 = 2² so 4ˣ⁺¹ = (2²)ˣ⁺¹ = 2²⁽ˣ⁺¹⁾ = 2²ˣ⁺² 8 = 2³ so 8ˣ⁻² = (2³)ˣ⁻² = 2³ˣ⁻⁶ Same base, so the exponents must be equal: 2x + 2 = 3x - 6 2 + 6 = 3x - 2x x = 8
    Try same base first, always. It gives an exact answer with no logarithm and no calculator.
    Example 2 — when bases will not match

    Solve 5ˣ = 40.

    40 is not a power of 5, so take the log of both sides. log(5ˣ) = log(40) x · log 5 = log 40 ← power rule brings the exponent down in front x = log 40 / log 5 Exact answer: x = log 40 / log 5 (this IS the answer) Decimal: x ≈ 2.2920
    TI-30XIIS. LOG 40 ) ÷ LOG 5 ) ENTER → 2.292029674 LOG opens a parenthesis for you. Close it before dividing, or the calculator reads log(40 ÷ log(5)) and you get the wrong number.
    Example 3 — isolate the exponential first

    Solve 3e²ˣ = 21.

    Divide by 3 BEFORE touching the exponent. e²ˣ = 7 Base is e, so use ln (they undo each other exactly). ln(e²ˣ) = ln 7 2x = ln 7 x = (ln 7)/2 ≈ 0.9730
    Do not take the log while the 3 is still attached. ln(3e²ˣ) is ln 3 + 2x, which is a longer road to the same place and a common source of dropped terms.
    Example 4 — log equation with an extraneous root

    Solve log₂(x) + log₂(x - 2) = 3.

    Step 1 Condense the left side with the product rule. log₂[x(x - 2)] = 3 Step 2 Rewrite as an exponential: log_b(A) = y means bʸ = A 2³ = x(x - 2) 8 = x² - 2x Step 3 Solve the quadratic. x² - 2x - 8 = 0 (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0 x = 4 or x = -2 Step 4 CHECK both against the domain. x = 4: log₂(4) and log₂(2) — both inputs positive ✓ x = -2: log₂(-2) — negative input ✗ REJECT Answer: x = 4 only
    Why the fake root appears. Condensing two logs into one widens the domain: x(x-2) is positive when x = -2 even though the original logs are not defined there. Condensing creates the extra root, so you have to throw it back out.
    Example 5 — expanding a log

    Expand log(x³√y / z²) fully.

    Division bar → subtraction: log(x³√y) - log(z²) Multiplication → addition: log(x³) + log(√y) - log(z²) Exponents → coefficients out front. Remember √y = y⁽¹⁄²⁾: 3 log x + (1/2) log y - 2 log z
    Example 6 — condensing a log

    Write 2 ln x - (1/3) ln y as a single logarithm.

    Coefficients go back up as exponents first: ln(x²) - ln(y⁽¹⁄³⁾) Subtraction becomes a quotient: ln( x² / ³√y )
    There is no rule for log(a + b). It does not split into log a + log b. Sums inside a log stay put.
    Example 7 — compound interest

    $2,500 is invested at 4.5% compounded monthly for 6 years. Find the balance.

    A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ P = 2500 r = 0.045 (percent → decimal: divide by 100) n = 12 (monthly) t = 6 r/n = 0.045/12 = 0.00375 nt = 12 · 6 = 72 A = 2500(1.00375)⁷² A ≈ 2500(1.3093027) A ≈ $3,273.26
    TI-30XIIS. 2500 × ( 1 + .045 ÷ 12 ) ^ 72 ENTER The parentheses around 1 + .045 ÷ 12 are mandatory. Without them the calculator raises only the 12 to the 72nd power.
    Example 8 — the same money, compounded continuously

    Same $2,500 at 4.5% for 6 years, compounded continuously.

    A = Peʳᵗ A = 2500 e^(0.045 · 6) A = 2500 e⁰·²⁷ A ≈ 2500(1.3099645) A ≈ $3,274.91
    TI-30XIIS. 2500 × 2nd LN .27 ) ENTER 2nd LN is eˣ. Close its parenthesis.

    Continuous compounding earns $1.65 more over six years. That gap is the whole point of the comparison problems.

    Quick check — exponentials and logs

    1. Rewrite log₃(81) = 4 in exponential form
    2. Evaluate log₅(125) without a calculator
    3. Solve 2ˣ = 32
    4. Solve ln(x + 1) = 0
    Answers

    1. 3⁴ = 81

    log_b(A) = c means bᶜ = A log₃(81) = 4 → 3⁴ = 81

    2. 5³ = 125 → 3

    5^? = 125 125 = 5 · 5 · 5 = 5³ log₅(125) = 3

    3. 2ˣ = 2⁵ → x = 5

    32 = 2⁵ 2ˣ = 2⁵ → x = 5

    4. e⁰ = x + 1 → 1 = x + 1 → x = 0

    ln(x + 1) = 0 → e⁰ = x + 1 1 = x + 1 x = 0 (check: ln 1 = 0 ✓)

    Practice set — exponentials and logs

    1. 9ˣ = 27ˣ⁻¹
    2. 7ˣ = 250 (exact and to 4 decimals)
    3. 4eˣ⁄² - 6 = 18
    4. log(x) + log(x - 3) = 1
    5. log₃(2x + 1) - log₃(x - 1) = 1
    6. Expand ln(√x / (y³z))
    7. Condense 3 log a + log b - 2 log c
    8. $1,200 at 6% compounded quarterly for 10 years
    Answers

    1. 3²ˣ = 3³ˣ⁻³ → 2x = 3x - 3 → x = 3

    9 = 3², 27 = 3³ 3²ˣ = 3³⁽ˣ⁻¹⁾ = 3³ˣ⁻³ 2x = 3x - 3 x = 3

    2. x = log 250 / log 7 ≈ 2.8375

    log both sides: x log 7 = log 250 x = log 250 / log 7 ≈ 2.397940/0.845098 ≈ 2.8375

    3. 4eˣ⁄² = 24 → eˣ⁄² = 6 → x/2 = ln 6 → x = 2 ln 6 ≈ 3.5835

    4eˣ⁄² - 6 = 18 4eˣ⁄² = 24 add 6 eˣ⁄² = 6 ÷ 4 x/2 = ln 6 ln both sides x = 2 ln 6 ≈ 2(1.791759) ≈ 3.5835

    4. log[x(x-3)] = 1 → x² - 3x = 10 → (x-5)(x+2) = 0. Reject -2. x = 5

    log[x(x - 3)] = 1 product rule x(x - 3) = 10¹ x² - 3x - 10 = 0 (x - 5)(x + 2) = 0 → x = 5 or -2 x = -2 makes log(-2): reject x = 5

    5. log₃[(2x+1)/(x-1)] = 1 → (2x+1)/(x-1) = 3 → 2x + 1 = 3x - 3 → x = 4. Check: both inputs positive. Valid.

    log₃[(2x + 1)/(x - 1)] = 1 quotient rule (2x + 1)/(x - 1) = 3¹ 2x + 1 = 3(x - 1) = 3x - 3 4 = x Check: 2(4) + 1 = 9 > 0, 4 - 1 = 3 > 0 ✓

    6. (1/2)ln x - 3 ln y - ln z

    ln(√x/(y³z)) = ln √x - ln(y³z) = ln x^(1/2) - (ln y³ + ln z) = (1/2)ln x - 3 ln y - ln z

    7. log(a³b / c²)

    3 log a + log b - 2 log c = log a³ + log b - log c² powers up = log(a³b) - log c² sum → product = log(a³b/c²) difference → quotient

    8. 1200(1 + .06/4)⁴⁰ = 1200(1.015)⁴⁰ ≈ $2,176.82

    A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ r/n = 0.06/4 = 0.015, nt = 4 · 10 = 40 A = 1200(1.015)⁴⁰ ≈ 1200(1.814018) ≈ $2,176.82

    Graphing exponential functions

    Parent y = bˣ with b > 0, b ≠ 1. Horizontal asymptote y = 0. Domain all reals, range (0, ∞). Anchor points (-1, 1/b), (0, 1), (1, b). b > 1 rises left to right; 0 < b < 1 falls.
    Example 1 — exponential with transformations

    Graph y = 3⁽ˣ⁻¹⁾ - 4. Give domain, range, and the asymptote.

    Parent y = 3ˣ, anchors (-1, 1/3), (0, 1), (1, 3), asymptote y = 0 Transformations: (x - 1) inside → shift RIGHT 1 - 4 outside → shift DOWN 4 Mapping: (x, y) → (x + 1, y - 4) (-1, 1/3) → (-1 + 1, 1/3 - 4) = (0, 1/3 - 12/3) ← write 4 as 12/3 = (0, -11/3) ← this is the y-intercept ( 0, 1) → (0 + 1, 1 - 4) = (1, -3) ( 1, 3) → (1 + 1, 3 - 4) = (2, -1) The ASYMPTOTE moves with the vertical shift: y = 0 → y = -4 Domain: all reals Range: (-4, ∞)
    Only the vertical shift moves the asymptote. A horizontal shift slides the curve sideways along the same asymptote. A reflection over the x-axis flips the range to (-∞, -4) but keeps the line at y = -4.
    Example 2 — reflected and decaying

    Graph y = -2(1/2)ˣ + 1.

    Parent y = (1/2)ˣ is DECAY, anchors (-1, 2), (0, 1), (1, 1/2) × 2 → vertical stretch 2 leading - → reflect over x-axis + 1 → shift up 1 Mapping: (x, y) → (x, -2y + 1) (-1, 2) → (-1, -3) ( 0, 1) → ( 0, -1) ← y-intercept ( 1, 1/2) → ( 1, 0) ← x-intercept Asymptote: y = 0 shifted up 1 → y = 1 Because of the reflection the curve sits BELOW the asymptote. Domain: all reals Range: (-∞, 1)

    Graphing logarithmic functions

    Parent y = logbx is the exponential reflected across y = x. Vertical asymptote x = 0. Domain (0, ∞), range all reals. Anchor points (1/b, -1), (1, 0), (b, 1).
    The log's asymptote is vertical, and only a horizontal shift moves it. This is the exact mirror image of the exponential rule above, and swapping the two is a common error.
    Example 1 — log with a horizontal shift

    Graph y = log₂(x + 3). Give domain, range, and the asymptote.

    Parent y = log₂x, anchors (1/2, -1), (1, 0), (2, 1), asymptote x = 0 (x + 3) inside → shift LEFT 3 Mapping: (x, y) → (x - 3, y) (1/2, -1) → (-5/2, -1) ( 1, 0) → (-2, 0) ← x-intercept ( 2, 1) → (-1, 1) Asymptote moves left too: x = 0 → x = -3 Domain: x + 3 > 0 → (-3, ∞) Range: all reals
    Find the domain by setting the inside > 0. That single inequality also hands you the vertical asymptote.
    Example 2 — reflected log

    Graph y = -ln(x - 2) + 1.

    Parent y = ln x (base e ≈ 2.718), anchors (1/e, -1), (1, 0), (e, 1) (x - 2) inside → shift RIGHT 2 leading - → reflect over x-axis + 1 → shift up 1 Mapping: (x, y) → (x + 2, -y + 1) (1/e, -1) → (1/e + 2, -(-1) + 1) ≈ (0.37 + 2, 1 + 1) = (2.37, 2) ( 1, 0) → (1 + 2, -(0) + 1) = (3, 1) ( e, 1) → (e + 2, -(1) + 1) ≈ (2.72 + 2, 0) = (4.72, 0) ← x-intercept Asymptote: x = 0 → x = 2 Domain: (2, ∞) Range: all reals The reflection makes it fall instead of rise, but it still hugs x = 2.

    Exponential growth and decay models

    ModelUse it for
    A = A₀eᵏᵗcontinuous growth (k > 0) or decay (k < 0)
    A = A₀(1 + r)ᵗgrowth by a fixed percent per period
    A = A₀(1 - r)ᵗdecay by a fixed percent per period
    A = A₀(1/2)t/hhalf-life, where h is the half-life
    Example 1 — finding k, then predicting

    A bacteria culture grows from 500 to 1,800 in 6 hours. Assume continuous growth. Find k, then the population at 10 hours.

    A = A₀eᵏᵗ with A₀ = 500 Use the known pair to solve for k: 1800 = 500 eᵏ⁶ 3.6 = e⁶ᵏ ← divide FIRST, before taking any log ln 3.6 = 6k k = (ln 3.6)/6 k ≈ 1.280934/6 ≈ 0.213489 At t = 10: A = 500 e^(0.213489 · 10) = 500 e^2.13489 ≈ 500(8.45605) ≈ 4228 bacteria
    TI-30XIIS. 500 × 2nd LN LN 3.6 ) ÷ 6 × 10 ) ENTER → 4228.0... Doing it in one expression keeps every digit of k. Rounding k to three decimals first and retyping it shifts the answer by several bacteria.
    Example 2 — half-life, both directions

    Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. (a) How much of a 200 g sample remains after 10,000 years? (b) When will only 25 g remain?

    A = 200(1/2)^(t/5730) (a) t = 10000 A = 200(1/2)^(10000/5730) = 200(1/2)^(1.74520) ≈ 200(0.29829) ≈ 59.7 g (b) Set A = 25 and solve for t. 25 = 200(1/2)^(t/5730) 0.125 = (1/2)^(t/5730) Notice 0.125 = 1/8 = (1/2)³, so bases match: 3 = t/5730 t = 17190 years (Three half-lives: 200 → 100 → 50 → 25.)
    Check for a clean power of one half first. If the remaining fraction is 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, or 1/16, you can count half-lives instead of taking a log.
    Example 3 — percent decay, when the base is not 1/2

    A car worth $32,000 depreciates 15% per year. What is it worth after 7 years, and when does it drop below $10,000?

    Decay factor = 1 - 0.15 = 0.85 V(t) = 32000(0.85)ᵗ After 7 years: V(7) = 32000(0.85)⁷ ≈ 32000(0.320577) ≈ $10,258 Below $10,000: 10000 = 32000(0.85)ᵗ 0.3125 = 0.85ᵗ ln 0.3125 = t ln 0.85 t = ln(0.3125)/ln(0.85) ≈ (-1.163151)/(-0.162519) ≈ 7.157 years So it crosses below $10,000 early in year 8.
    The rate is not the base. 15% decay means multiply by 0.85, not 0.15. Multiplying by 0.15 would be an 85% loss every year.

    Practice set — exponential and log graphs and models

    1. Domain, range, asymptote, and y-intercept of y = 2ˣ⁺³ - 5
    2. Domain, range, asymptote of y = -eˣ + 2
    3. Domain and asymptote of y = log(x - 6)
    4. Domain and asymptote of y = ln(4 - x)
    5. A population of 8,000 grows continuously at 3.2% per year. Value after 15 years.
    6. An isotope decays from 90 g to 60 g in 4 days. Find k for the continuous model.
    7. Half-life 12 years. What fraction of a sample remains after 36 years?
    8. A $1,400 laptop loses 22% of its value per year. Value after 5 years.
    Answers

    1. Domain all reals; asymptote y = -5; range (-5, ∞); y-intercept 2³ - 5 = 3, so (0, 3)

    y = 2ˣ⁺³ - 5 Domain: all reals (exponents never restrict) Asymptote: parent y = 0 moved down 5 → y = -5 2ˣ⁺³ > 0, so y > -5 → range (-5, ∞) y-int: 2³ - 5 = 8 - 5 = 3 → (0, 3)

    2. Domain all reals; asymptote y = 2; reflected so the curve is below it, range (-∞, 2)

    y = -eˣ + 2 Domain all reals eˣ > 0 → -eˣ < 0 → -eˣ + 2 < 2 Asymptote y = 2, range (-∞, 2)

    3. x - 6 > 0 → domain (6, ∞), asymptote x = 6

    x - 6 > 0 → x > 6 Domain (6, ∞), asymptote x = 6

    4. 4 - x > 0 → domain (-∞, 4), asymptote x = 4. The graph is also reflected left-to-right because of the -x

    4 - x > 0 -x > -4 x < 4 FLIP Domain (-∞, 4), asymptote x = 4

    5. 8000e⁽⁰·⁰³²⁾⁽¹⁵⁾ = 8000e⁰·⁴⁸ ≈ 8000(1.61607) ≈ 12,929

    A = 8000e^(rt), r = 0.032, t = 15 rt = 0.032 · 15 = 0.48 A = 8000e⁰·⁴⁸ ≈ 8000(1.61607) ≈ 12,929

    6. 60 = 90e⁴ᵏ → 2/3 = e⁴ᵏ → k = ln(2/3)/4 ≈ -0.10137 per day

    60 = 90e⁴ᵏ 2/3 = e⁴ᵏ ÷ 90 ln(2/3) = 4k k = ln(2/3)/4 ≈ -0.405465/4 ≈ -0.10137 per day

    7. 36/12 = 3 half-lives → (1/2)³ = 1/8

    36 ÷ 12 = 3 half-lives (1/2)³ = 1/8 remains

    8. 1400(0.78)⁵ ≈ 1400(0.288717) ≈ $404.20

    Keep 100% - 22% = 78% each year → factor 0.78 V = 1400(0.78)⁵ 0.78⁵ ≈ 0.288717 V ≈ 1400(0.288717) ≈ $404.20

    Test 1 Study Guide

    CoverageSections 1–3
    GoalRecognize the skill, choose the right method, and carry the algebra through cleanly.

    Know how to

    Section 1 — Functions





    Section 2 — Composition, Inverses & Rational Functions





    Section 3 — Exponentials & Logs





    Must-know formulas and rules

    Average rate of change: (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a)
    Composition: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x))
    Compound interest: A = P(1 + r/n)nt    Continuous: A = Pert
    Log rules: log(MN)=log M+log N;   log(M/N)=log M-log N;   log(Mp)=p log M
    Change of base: logb(x) = log(x)/log(b)

    Common mistakes

    Inverse is not reciprocal. f⁻¹(x) means reverse the function, not 1/f(x).
    Factor before deciding hole vs. VA. A canceled denominator factor creates a hole; an uncanceled denominator zero creates a vertical asymptote.
    Log inputs must be positive. Check every logarithm after solving.
    Composition order matters. f∘g means do g first.

    Calculator reminders

    • Use parentheses around full numerators, denominators, and exponents.
    • For an exponential equation such as 7ˣ = 250, use log(250)/log(7) or ln(250)/ln(7).
    • Use ln with e-based models and keep extra digits until the final rounding step.

    Test 1

    CoverageSections 1–3
    Format20 mixed problems. Some questions tell you the skill directly; others require you to recognize the method.
    Directions: Show your setup and algebra. TI-30XIIS use is allowed. Give exact answers unless a decimal or rounding direction is requested.

    Test 1 — 20 questions

    1. f(x) = -x² + 5x; find f(-2) and f(x + h)
    2. Simplify the difference quotient of f(x) = 3x² - x
    3. Domain of k(x) = (x + 2)/(x² - 7x + 12)
    4. Domain of m(x) = 1/√(10 - 5x)
    5. Describe y = (1/2)f(x - 4) + 3 and find where the point (-2, 6) on f moves
    6. Classify as even, odd, or neither: f(x) = x³ - 2x and g(x) = x² + x
    7. Average rate of change of f(x) = 2ˣ from x = 0 to x = 3
    8. f(x) = x² + 1, g(x) = √(x - 2). Find (f∘g)(x) and its domain
    9. f(x) = 3x - 4, g(x) = x². Find (g∘f)(2) and (f∘g)(-1)
    10. Inverse of f(x) = ∛(x - 1) + 2
    11. Full analysis of f(x) = (2x² - 8)/(x² + x - 2): holes, asymptotes, intercepts
    12. Slant asymptote and vertical asymptote of f(x) = (2x² + 5x - 4)/(x + 3)
    13. For r(x) = (x - 3)/(x + 1)², describe the behavior as x approaches -1 from each side
    14. Solve 9^(x - 1) = 27^(2x)
    15. Solve 5^(2x) = 40 exactly and to four decimals
    16. Expand ln(x³/(y²√z))
    17. Condense 2 log x + log(x + 1) - (1/2) log y
    18. Solve log₂(x + 2) + log₂(x - 4) = 4
    19. $3,000 is invested at 5.2% for 8 years. Find the balance compounded monthly and compounded continuously.
    20. A sample decays continuously from 250 mg to 180 mg in 6 hours. Find k and the half-life.
    Test 1 answer key + worked solutions
    1. f(-2) = -4 - 10 = -14; f(x + h) = -x² - 2xh - h² + 5x + 5h
      f(-2) = -(-2)² + 5(-2) = -4 - 10 = -14 f(x + h) = -(x + h)² + 5(x + h) = -(x² + 2xh + h²) + 5x + 5h = -x² - 2xh - h² + 5x + 5h
    2. [3(x + h)² - (x + h) - 3x² + x]/h = (6xh + 3h² - h)/h = 6x + 3h - 1
      f(x + h) = 3(x + h)² - (x + h) = 3x² + 6xh + 3h² - x - h Subtract f(x) = 3x² - x: 6xh + 3h² - h Divide by h: 6x + 3h - 1
    3. (x - 3)(x - 4) ≠ 0 → (-∞, 3) ∪ (3, 4) ∪ (4, ∞)
      x² - 7x + 12 = 0: multiply 12, add -7 → -3, -4 (x - 3)(x - 4) = 0 → x = 3, 4 excluded (-∞, 3) ∪ (3, 4) ∪ (4, ∞)
    4. Root in a denominator, so strictly positive: 10 - 5x > 0 → x < 2 → (-∞, 2)
      Root on the bottom → strictly > 0 10 - 5x > 0 -5x > -10 x < 2 ÷ (-5), FLIP (-∞, 2)
    5. Right 4, vertical compression by 1/2, up 3. (x, y) → (x + 4, y/2 + 3), so (-2, 6) → (2, 6)
      (x - 4) → right 4; 1/2 → compression; + 3 → up 3 (x, y) → (x + 4, y/2 + 3) (-2, 6) → (-2 + 4, 6/2 + 3) = (2, 6)
    6. f(-x) = -x³ + 2x = -f(x) → odd. g(-x) = x² - x, neither g(x) nor -g(x) → neither
      f(-x) = (-x)³ - 2(-x) = -x³ + 2x = -(x³ - 2x) = -f(x) → odd g(-x) = (-x)² + (-x) = x² - x ≠ g(x) = x² + x, ≠ -g(x) = -x² - x → neither
    7. (2³ - 2⁰)/(3 - 0) = (8 - 1)/3 = 7/3
      f(0) = 2⁰ = 1, f(3) = 2³ = 8 (8 - 1)/(3 - 0) = 7/3
    8. (√(x - 2))² + 1 = x - 1, but the inside needs x ≥ 2. Domain [2, ∞)
      f(g(x)) = (√(x - 2))² + 1 = x - 2 + 1 = x - 1 Inside: x - 2 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 2 Domain [2, ∞)
    9. f(2) = 2, g(2) = 4. g(-1) = 1, f(1) = -1
      (g∘f)(2): f(2) = 3(2) - 4 = 2; g(2) = 2² = 4 (f∘g)(-1): g(-1) = (-1)² = 1; f(1) = 3(1) - 4 = -1
    10. Swap: x = ∛(y - 1) + 2 → (x - 2)³ = y - 1 → f⁻¹(x) = (x - 2)³ + 1
      Swap: x = ∛(y - 1) + 2 x - 2 = ∛(y - 1) (x - 2)³ = y - 1 cube both sides y = (x - 2)³ + 1
    11. 2(x - 2)(x + 2)/[(x + 2)(x - 1)] = 2(x - 2)/(x - 1), x ≠ -2. Hole (-2, 8/3); VA x = 1; HA y = 2; x-int (2, 0); y-int (0, 4)
      Top: 2(x² - 4) = 2(x - 2)(x + 2) Bottom: multiply -2, add 1 → 2, -1 → (x + 2)(x - 1) Cancel (x + 2): 2(x - 2)/(x - 1), x ≠ -2 Hole: 2(-4)/(-3) = 8/3 → (-2, 8/3) VA x = 1; HA 2/1 → y = 2 x-int (2, 0); y-int 2(-2)/(-1) = 4 → (0, 4)
    12. Synthetic with c = -3: 2, -1, -1 → 2x - 1 - 1/(x + 3). Slant y = 2x - 1; VA x = -3
      -3 | 2 5 -4 | -6 3 +-------------- 2 -1 -1 2x - 1 - 1/(x + 3) → slant y = 2x - 1 VA x = -3 (top at -3 is -1, not 0)
    13. Near x = -1 the numerator is about -4 (negative), and (x + 1)² is a tiny positive number from both sides. So r(x) → -∞ from the left and from the right
      Near x = -1: top ≈ -1 - 3 = -4 (negative) Bottom (x + 1)² is squared → tiny POSITIVE on both sides x = -1.1: -4.1/0.01 = -410 x = -0.9: -3.9/0.01 = -390 negative ÷ tiny positive → -∞ from the left and the right
    14. 3^(2x - 2) = 3^(6x) → 2x - 2 = 6x → x = -1/2
      9 = 3², 27 = 3³ 3²⁽ˣ⁻¹⁾ = 3³⁽²ˣ⁾ 2x - 2 = 6x -2 = 4x x = -1/2
    15. 2x log 5 = log 40 → x = log 40/(2 log 5) ≈ 1.1460
      log both sides: 2x log 5 = log 40 x = log 40/(2 log 5) ≈ 1.602060/(2 · 0.698970) ≈ 1.602060/1.397940 ≈ 1.1460
    16. 3 ln x - 2 ln y - (1/2) ln z
      ln(x³/(y²√z)) = ln x³ - ln(y²√z) = 3 ln x - (2 ln y + (1/2)ln z) = 3 ln x - 2 ln y - (1/2)ln z
    17. log[x²(x + 1)/√y]
      2 log x + log(x + 1) - (1/2) log y = log x² + log(x + 1) - log √y = log[x²(x + 1)] - log √y = log[x²(x + 1)/√y]
    18. (x + 2)(x - 4) = 2⁴ = 16 → x² - 2x - 24 = 0 → (x - 6)(x + 4) = 0. x = -4 makes both log inputs negative, reject. x = 6
      log₂[(x + 2)(x - 4)] = 4 (x + 2)(x - 4) = 2⁴ = 16 x² - 2x - 8 = 16 x² - 2x - 24 = 0 (x - 6)(x + 4) = 0 → x = 6 or -4 x = -4: log₂(-2) undefined → reject x = 6
    19. Monthly: 3000(1 + .052/12)⁹⁶ ≈ $4,543.57. Continuous: 3000e^(0.416) ≈ $4,547.66
      Monthly: r/n = 0.052/12 ≈ 0.0043333, nt = 96 3000(1.0043333)⁹⁶ ≈ $4,543.57 Continuous: rt = 0.052 · 8 = 0.416 3000e⁰·⁴¹⁶ ≈ 3000(1.515886) ≈ $4,547.66
    20. 180 = 250e^(6k) → k = ln(0.72)/6 ≈ -0.05475 per hour. Half-life ln 2/0.05475 ≈ 12.66 hours
      180 = 250e⁶ᵏ 0.72 = e⁶ᵏ ÷ 250 ln 0.72 = 6k k = ln(0.72)/6 ≈ -0.328504/6 ≈ -0.05475 per hour Half-life: 1/2 = eᵏᵗ → t = ln(0.5)/k t ≈ -0.693147/-0.05475 ≈ 12.66 hours

    Section 4 — Right-Triangle Trigonometry

    Tags#trigonometry#SOHCAHTOA
    Skills to know firstFractionsExponents & RadicalsCore Algebra
    RelatedSection 5 — Coterminal and Reference AnglesSection 6 — Trig on xy-plane & Special Angles
    TI-30XIISTrig modeInverse trig

    SOH–CAH–TOA

    FunctionRatio
    sinesin(θ)=oppositehypotenuse
    cosinecos(θ)=adjacenthypotenuse
    tangenttan(θ)=oppositeadjacent

    Guided right-triangle trig routine

    1Circle the angle being used.
    2Label opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse relative to that angle.
    3Choose SOH, CAH, or TOA from the sides known/needed.
    4Finding a side → algebra. Finding an angle → inverse trig.
    TI-30XIIS: confirm DEG or RAD before trig.

    Worked examples — right-triangle trig

    Example 1 — all six ratios from one triangle

    A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. Angle θ sits opposite the side of length 5. Find all six trig values.

    Hypotenuse first: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 → hyp = 13 Relative to θ: opposite = 5, adjacent = 12, hypotenuse = 13 sin θ = opp/hyp = 5/13 csc θ = 13/5 cos θ = adj/hyp = 12/13 sec θ = 13/12 tan θ = opp/adj = 5/12 cot θ = 12/5
    Reciprocals flip the fraction. Once you have sin, cos, tan, the other three are free.
    Example 2 — solving for a missing side

    A ladder leans against a wall at 37° to the ground. The ladder is 20 ft long. How high up the wall does it reach?

    The wall height is OPPOSITE the 37° angle. The ladder is the HYPOTENUSE. opp and hyp → SOH → use sine. sin 37° = h/20 h = 20 sin 37° ← the 20 moved across by multiplying h ≈ 20(0.601815) h ≈ 12.04 ft
    TI-30XIIS. Confirm DEG first: press DRG, underline DEG, press ENTER. Then 20 × SIN 37 ) ENTER → 12.03604...
    Example 3 — solving for a missing angle

    A ramp rises 7 ft over a horizontal run of 10 ft. What angle does it make with the ground?

    opposite = 7, adjacent = 10 → TOA → tangent. tan θ = 7/10 = 0.7 To undo tangent, use INVERSE tangent. θ = tan⁻¹(0.7) θ ≈ 34.99°
    TI-30XIIS. 2nd TAN 7 ÷ 10 ) ENTER → 34.99202... 2nd TAN is TAN⁻¹. It opens its own parenthesis; the single ) after the 10 closes it.
    tan⁻¹ is not 1/tan. The reciprocal of tangent is cotangent. The superscript -1 on a trig function means "the inverse function," never an exponent.

    Solving a right triangle completely

    "Solve the triangle" means find every missing side and every missing angle. In a right triangle you always know one angle (90°), so you need just two more facts, at least one of them a side.

    Three tools, in this order of preference. The two acute angles add to 90°. The sides obey a² + b² = c². Any one side plus one acute angle gives the rest through SOH–CAH–TOA.
    Example 4 — one angle and the hypotenuse

    Right triangle with C = 90°, A = 32°, hypotenuse c = 15. Solve the triangle.

    Missing angle first. It costs nothing: B = 90° - 32° = 58° Side a is OPPOSITE A, and c is the hypotenuse → sine. sin 32° = a/15 a = 15 sin 32° ≈ 15(0.529919) ≈ 7.95 Side b is ADJACENT to A → cosine. cos 32° = b/15 b = 15 cos 32° ≈ 15(0.848048) ≈ 12.72 Check with Pythagoras: 7.95² + 12.72² ≈ 63.2 + 161.8 = 225 = 15² ✓
    TI-30XIIS (DEG). 15 × SIN 32 ) ENTER → 7.948788963 15 × COS 32 ) ENTER → 12.72072144
    Example 5 — two legs, no angles

    Right triangle with legs a = 9 and b = 14. Solve the triangle.

    Hypotenuse: c = √(9² + 14²) = √(81 + 196) = √277 ≈ 16.64 Angle A is opposite the 9, and 14 is adjacent → tangent. tan A = 9/14 A = tan⁻¹(9/14) ≈ 32.74° B = 90° - 32.74° = 57.26°
    TI-30XIIS (DEG). 2nd TAN 9 ÷ 14 ) ENTER → 32.73522627 Use the unrounded side lengths whenever you can, so round-off does not pile up.

    Angles of elevation and depression

    An angle of elevation is measured up from a horizontal line of sight. An angle of depression is measured down from a horizontal line of sight. Both are always measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical.

    Depression = elevation. The angle of depression from the top observer equals the angle of elevation from the bottom observer. They are alternate interior angles between two horizontal lines, so you can put the angle at whichever end makes the right triangle easiest to label.
    Example 6 — angle of elevation

    From a point 120 ft from the base of a building, the angle of elevation to the top is 38°. How tall is the building?

    Sketch: horizontal ground 120 ft, vertical building h, angle 38° at the observer. Relative to the 38° angle: h is OPPOSITE, 120 is ADJACENT → tangent. tan 38° = h/120 h = 120 tan 38° ≈ 120(0.781286) ≈ 93.75 ft
    TI-30XIIS (DEG). 120 × TAN 38 ) ENTER → 93.75427518
    Example 7 — angle of depression

    A lighthouse keeper 85 ft above the water sees a boat at an angle of depression of 14°. How far is the boat from the base of the lighthouse?

    Move the 14° down to the boat: the angle of elevation from the boat is also 14°. Relative to that angle: 85 is OPPOSITE, distance d is ADJACENT → tangent. tan 14° = 85/d d = 85/tan 14° ≈ 85/0.249328 ≈ 340.9 ft
    The unknown is in the denominator. From tan 14° = 85/d, multiply both sides by d, then divide by tan 14°. Writing d = 85 tan 14° is the most common slip here.
    Example 8 — two angles, one unknown distance

    From a point on level ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a tree is 40°. After walking 25 ft straight toward the tree, the angle is 55°. How tall is the tree?

    Let h = height and d = distance from the CLOSER point to the tree. Closer point: tan 55° = h/d → h = d tan 55° Farther point: tan 40° = h/(d + 25) → h = (d + 25) tan 40° Both equal h, so set them equal: d tan 55° = (d + 25) tan 40° d tan 55° = d tan 40° + 25 tan 40° ← distribute tan 40° d tan 55° - d tan 40° = 25 tan 40° ← subtract d tan 40° d(tan 55° - tan 40°) = 25 tan 40° d = 25 tan 40° / (tan 55° - tan 40°) ≈ 25(0.839100)/(1.428148 - 0.839100) ≈ 35.61 ft h = d tan 55° ≈ 35.61(1.428148) ≈ 50.86 ft

    Two right triangles share the same height. Writing h two ways and setting them equal is the standard move for every "two angles of elevation" problem.

    Cofunctions and complementary angles

    The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, and the side that is opposite one of them is adjacent to the other. That swaps the ratios:

    Cofunction identityIn radians
    sin θ = cos(90° - θ)sin θ = cos(π/2 - θ)
    tan θ = cot(90° - θ)tan θ = cot(π/2 - θ)
    sec θ = csc(90° - θ)sec θ = csc(π/2 - θ)
    Use it to rewrite an angle. sin 25° = cos 65°, tan 10° = cot 80°, and if cos θ = sin 52° with θ acute, then θ = 38°. The "co" in cosine literally means "sine of the complement."

    Quick check — right-triangle trig

    1. A right triangle has opposite side 7 and hypotenuse 25. Find cos θ.
    2. sin 50° = cos ___
    3. The side opposite a 30° angle in a right triangle with hypotenuse 18. No calculator.
    4. Find θ if tan θ = 1.2, to the nearest hundredth of a degree.
    Answers

    1. Adjacent = √(625 - 49) = √576 = 24, so cos θ = 24/25

    Adjacent² + 7² = 25² Adjacent = √(625 - 49) = √576 = 24 cos θ = adj/hyp = 24/25

    2. 40°, the complement of 50°

    Cofunction: sin θ = cos(90° - θ) 90° - 50° = 40° → sin 50° = cos 40°

    3. 18 sin 30° = 18(1/2) = 9

    Opposite 30°, hypotenuse 18 → sine sin 30° = O/18 O = 18 · (1/2) = 9

    4. θ = tan⁻¹(1.2) ≈ 50.19°

    tan θ = 1.2 θ = tan⁻¹(1.2) ≈ 50.19° (DEG mode)

    Practice set — right-triangle trig

    1. Solve the right triangle: C = 90°, A = 27°, b = 20.
    2. Solve the right triangle: C = 90°, a = 5, c = 13.
    3. A 30-ft ladder makes a 70° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
    4. A kite string 150 ft long makes a 48° angle of elevation. How high is the kite?
    5. From the top of a 200-ft cliff, the angle of depression to a boat is 22°. How far is the boat from the base of the cliff?
    6. A ramp must rise 2.5 ft, and its angle cannot exceed 4.8°. What is the shortest horizontal run allowed?
    7. Legs 20 and 21: all six trig ratios for the angle opposite the 20.
    8. From two points 50 ft apart on the same side of a pole, the angles of elevation to the top are 45° (closer) and 30° (farther). Find the height exactly.
    Answers

    1. B = 63°; a = 20 tan 27° ≈ 10.19; c = 20/cos 27° ≈ 22.45

    B = 90° - 27° = 63° b = 20 is ADJACENT to A; a is OPPOSITE A → tangent tan 27° = a/20 → a = 20 tan 27° ≈ 20(0.509525) ≈ 10.19 c is the hypotenuse → cosine cos 27° = 20/c → c = 20/cos 27° ≈ 20/0.891007 ≈ 22.45

    2. b = 12; A = sin⁻¹(5/13) ≈ 22.62°; B ≈ 67.38°

    b = √(13² - 5²) = √(169 - 25) = √144 = 12 sin A = 5/13 → A = sin⁻¹(5/13) ≈ 22.62° B = 90° - 22.62° = 67.38°

    3. 30 sin 70° ≈ 28.19 ft

    Height is OPPOSITE 70°, ladder is the hypotenuse → sine sin 70° = h/30 → h = 30 sin 70° ≈ 30(0.939693) ≈ 28.19 ft

    4. 150 sin 48° ≈ 111.47 ft

    Height OPPOSITE 48°, string is the hypotenuse → sine h = 150 sin 48° ≈ 150(0.743145) ≈ 111.47 ft

    5. 200/tan 22° ≈ 495.02 ft

    Depression 22° = elevation from the boat (alternate angles) 200 is OPPOSITE, distance d is ADJACENT → tangent tan 22° = 200/d → d = 200/tan 22° ≈ 200/0.404026 ≈ 495.02 ft

    6. 2.5/tan 4.8° ≈ 29.77 ft

    Rise 2.5 OPPOSITE, run ADJACENT → tangent tan 4.8° = 2.5/run → run = 2.5/tan 4.8° run ≈ 2.5/0.083971 ≈ 29.77 ft (a smaller run means a steeper angle)

    7. Hypotenuse 29. sin 20/29, cos 21/29, tan 20/21, csc 29/20, sec 29/21, cot 21/20

    Hypotenuse √(20² + 21²) = √(400 + 441) = √841 = 29 opp 20, adj 21, hyp 29 sin 20/29 cos 21/29 tan 20/21 csc 29/20 sec 29/21 cot 21/20

    8. Closer point: h = d (tan 45° = 1). Farther: h = (d + 50)/√3. So √3 d = d + 50, d = 50/(√3 - 1) = 25(√3 + 1). Height 25(√3 + 1) ≈ 68.30 ft

    Closer: tan 45° = h/d → h = d (tan 45° = 1) Farther: tan 30° = h/(d + 50) → h = (d + 50)/√3 Set equal: d = (d + 50)/√3 √3 d = d + 50 d(√3 - 1) = 50 d = 50/(√3 - 1) · (√3 + 1)/(√3 + 1) = 50(√3 + 1)/2 = 25(√3 + 1) h = d = 25(√3 + 1) ≈ 68.30 ft

    Section 5 — Coterminal and Reference Angles

    Tags#degrees#radians#reference-angles#quadrants
    Skills to know firstCoordinate GeometryFractionsSection 4 — Right-Triangle Trigonometry
    RelatedSection 6 — Trig on xy-plane & Special Angles
    TI-30XIISTrig mode

    Degrees and radians

    180°=π radians

    Degrees → radians:

    degrees·π180

    Radians → degrees:

    radians·180π
    Example 1 — degrees to radians

    Convert 135° and 210° to radians.

    Multiply by π/180. The degree unit cancels. 135° · π/180 = 135π/180 divide top and bottom by 45 → 3π/4 210° · π/180 = 210π/180 divide top and bottom by 30 → 7π/6
    Example 2 — radians to degrees

    Convert 5π/6 and 7π/4 to degrees.

    Multiply by 180/π. The π cancels. 5π/6 · 180/π = 5 · 180/6 = 5 · 30 = 150° 7π/4 · 180/π = 7 · 180/4 = 7 · 45 = 315°
    Memorize the denominators. π/6 = 30°, π/4 = 45°, π/3 = 60°, π/2 = 90°. Then 5π/6 is just five thirty-degree steps.

    Angles in standard position

    Vertex at the origin, initial side along the positive x-axis, and the terminal side wherever the rotation ends. Counterclockwise is positive, clockwise is negative. The quadrant of the terminal side is what decides every sign.
    Coterminal angles share a terminal side. Add or subtract 360° (or 2π) as many times as needed. Quadrantal angles land on an axis: 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°.
    Example — finding coterminal angles both ways

    Find one positive and one negative angle coterminal with -495°, and name its quadrant.

    -495 + 360 = -135 still negative, keep going -135 + 360 = 225 positive, in [0, 360) Positive coterminal: 225° Negative coterminal: -135° 225° is between 180° and 270° → Quadrant III

    Degrees, minutes, and seconds

    1 degree = 60 minutes ('). 1 minute = 60 seconds ("). So 1° = 3600". This is the same structure as hours and minutes on a clock.
    Example 1 — DMS to decimal degrees

    Convert 38° 24' 45" to decimal degrees.

    Divide each smaller unit down to degrees and add. 24' → 24/60 = 0.4° 45" → 45/3600 = 0.0125° 38 + 0.4 + 0.0125 = 38.4125°
    Example 2 — decimal degrees to DMS

    Convert 72.316° to degrees, minutes, and seconds.

    Whole degrees: 72 Take the decimal part and multiply by 60 to get minutes. 0.316 × 60 = 18.96 → 18 whole minutes Take THAT decimal part and multiply by 60 to get seconds. 0.96 × 60 = 57.6 → ≈ 58 seconds 72° 18' 58"

    Arc length, sector area, and velocity

    Every formula in this block requires θ in RADIANS. Plugging degrees in gives an answer that is wrong by a factor of about 57. Convert first, every time.
    QuantityFormulaUnits
    Arc lengths = rθsame as r
    Sector areaA = (1/2)r²θsquare units
    Angular velocityω = θ/tradians per unit time
    Linear velocityv = rω or v = s/tdistance per unit time
    Example 1 — arc length and sector area

    A circle has radius 9 cm. Find the arc length and sector area cut off by a central angle of 140°.

    Convert to radians FIRST. 140 · π/180 = 7π/9 ≈ 2.44346 rad Arc length: s = rθ = 9(7π/9) = 7π ≈ 21.99 cm (the 9s cancel, which is why exact form is worth keeping) Sector area: A = (1/2)r²θ = (1/2)(81)(7π/9) = (81 · 7π)/18 = 63π/2 ≈ 98.96 cm²
    Example 2 — angular and linear velocity

    A bicycle wheel of radius 14 inches spins at 220 revolutions per minute. Find the angular velocity in radians per minute and the bike's speed in miles per hour.

    Angular velocity: one revolution is 2π radians. ω = 220 · 2π = 440π rad/min ≈ 1382.3 rad/min Linear velocity: v = rω = 14(440π) = 6160π in/min ≈ 19352.2 in/min Convert to mph: inches → miles: ÷ 63360 minutes → hours: × 60 19352.2 × 60 / 63360 = 1161132 / 63360 ≈ 18.33 mph
    Revolutions are not radians. Multiply rev/min by 2π before using v = rω. Skipping that undercounts the speed by a factor of about 6.28.

    Practice set — angles, DMS, and circular motion

    1. Positive and negative coterminal angles for 410°, and its quadrant
    2. Positive coterminal angle for -7π/4
    3. Convert 15° 42' 30" to decimal degrees
    4. Convert 104.85° to DMS
    5. Arc length for r = 6 ft, θ = 5π/6
    6. Sector area for r = 10 m, θ = 72°
    7. A wheel of radius 20 cm turns at 5 rad/s. Find the linear speed.
    8. A record spins at 33 rpm. Angular velocity in rad/min?
    Answers

    1. 410 - 360 = 50°; 50 - 360 = -310°; Quadrant I

    Positive: 410° - 360° = 50° Negative: 50° - 360° = -310° 50° is between 0° and 90° → Quadrant I

    2. -7π/4 + 2π = π/4

    -7π/4 + 2π = -7π/4 + 8π/4 = π/4

    3. 42/60 = 0.7, 30/3600 = 0.008333 → 15.70833°

    42' → 42/60 = 0.7° 30" → 30/3600 ≈ 0.008333° 15 + 0.7 + 0.008333 = 15.70833°

    4. 0.85 × 60 = 51 exactly → 104° 51' 0"

    Degrees: 104 0.85 × 60 = 51.0 → 51 minutes, nothing left over 0 seconds → 104° 51' 0"

    5. s = 6(5π/6) = 5π ≈ 15.71 ft

    s = rθ = 6(5π/6) = 5π ≈ 15.71 ft (6s cancel)

    6. 72° = 2π/5; A = (1/2)(100)(2π/5) = 20π ≈ 62.83 m²

    72 · π/180 = 72π/180 = 2π/5 (÷ 36) A = (1/2)r²θ = (1/2)(100)(2π/5) = 20π ≈ 62.83 m²

    7. v = 20(5) = 100 cm/s

    v = rω = 20 · 5 = 100 cm/s

    8. 33 × 2π = 66π ≈ 207.3 rad/min

    1 revolution = 2π radians ω = 33 · 2π = 66π ≈ 207.3 rad/min

    Reference angles

    Use the acute reference angle to find the magnitude, then use the quadrant to determine signs.

    Terminal side inReference angle (degrees)Reference angle (radians)
    Quadrant Iθθ
    Quadrant II180° - θπ - θ
    Quadrant IIIθ - 180°θ - π
    Quadrant IV360° - θ2π - θ
    Get the angle into one turn first. The formulas above assume 0 ≤ θ < 360°. A negative angle or an angle past one full turn must be made coterminal before you use them.
    Example — reference angles in every situation

    Find the reference angle for 300°, 5π/4, -210°, 17π/6, and 1000°.

    300° QIV (270° to 360°) 360° - 300° = 60° 5π/4 5π/4 = 225°, QIII 5π/4 - π = π/4 -210° coterminal: -210° + 360° = 150°, QII 180° - 150° = 30° 17π/6 coterminal: 17π/6 - 2π = 5π/6, QII π - 5π/6 = π/6 1000° 1000° - 2(360°) = 280°, QIV 360° - 280° = 80°

    Practice set — reference angles

    1. 145°
    2. -60°
    3. 11π/4
    4. 7π/5
    5. 520°
    6. 2 radians (give a decimal)
    Answers

    1. QII → 35°

    145° is between 90° and 180° → QII Reference = 180° - 145° = 35°

    2. coterminal 300°, QIV → 60°

    -60° + 360° = 300° → QIV Reference = 360° - 300° = 60°

    3. coterminal 3π/4, QII → π/4

    11π/4 - 2π = 11π/4 - 8π/4 = 3π/4 → QII Reference = π - 3π/4 = π/4

    4. QIII → 7π/5 - π = 2π/5

    π = 5π/5 < 7π/5 < 3π/2 = 7.5π/5 → QIII Reference = 7π/5 - π = 2π/5

    5. coterminal 160°, QII → 20°

    520° - 360° = 160° → QII Reference = 180° - 160° = 20°

    6. 2 is between π/2 ≈ 1.571 and π ≈ 3.142, so QII → π - 2 ≈ 1.1416

    π/2 ≈ 1.571 < 2 < π ≈ 3.142 → QII Reference = π - 2 ≈ 3.1416 - 2 = 1.1416

    Coterminal angles

    Add or subtract full turns (360° or 2π) until the angle lands in [0°, 360°). The trig values are identical.
