    Special triangles

    45–45–90

    Side ratio:

    1:1:2
    30–60–90

    Side ratio:

    1:3:2
    Example — special triangles, no calculator

    (a) A 30-60-90 triangle has a short leg of 6. Find the other two sides. (b) A 45-45-90 triangle has a hypotenuse of 10. Find the legs.

    (a) Ratio is 1 : √3 : 2 (short leg : long leg : hypotenuse) Short leg 6 means the scale factor is 6. long leg = 6√3 hypotenuse = 12 (b) Ratio is 1 : 1 : √2 (leg : leg : hypotenuse) Hypotenuse 10 means leg · √2 = 10 leg = 10/√2 rationalize: 10√2/2 = 5√2
    On the unit circle: (x,y) = (cosθ,sinθ)

    Core first-quadrant values

    AngleRadianssincos
    0°001
    30°π/61/2√3/2
    45°π/4√2/2√2/2
    60°π/3√3/21/2
    90°π/210
    Sine generation shortcut: √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2.
    Cosine is the same list reversed.

    Quadrant signs

    All Students Take Calculus

    QuadrantPositive functions
    Iall
    IIsine
    IIItangent
    IVcosine

    Reciprocal trig functions

    cscθ=1sinθ
    secθ=1cosθ
    cotθ=1tanθ
    Inverse sine sin-1 is not the same thing as csc.

    Guided unit-circle routine

    1Find the reference angle.
    2Use the first-quadrant exact value.
    3Use ASTC to attach the correct sign.
    4Cosine = x-coordinate; sine = y-coordinate.
    Shortcut: sine values at 0°,30°,45°,60°,90° are √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2; cosine is reversed.

    First-quadrant table, with tangent

    AngleRadianssincostan
    0°0010
    30°π/61/2√3/2√3/3
    45°π/4√2/2√2/21
    60°π/3√3/21/2√3
    90°π/210undefined
    Tangent comes free. tan = sin/cos. At 30°: (1/2) ÷ (√3/2) = 1/√3 = √3/3. You never have to memorize the tangent row.

    Worked examples — unit circle

    Example 1 — a Quadrant III cosine

    Find cos(210°) exactly.

    Step 1 Which quadrant? 180° < 210° < 270° → Quadrant III Step 2 Reference angle: distance to the nearest x-axis. In QIII: θ - 180° = 210° - 180° = 30° Step 3 First-quadrant value: cos 30° = √3/2 Step 4 Sign from ASTC. In QIII only TANGENT is positive. Cosine is NEGATIVE there. Answer: cos(210°) = -√3/2
    Example 2 — a Quadrant IV sine, in radians

    Find sin(5π/3) exactly.

    Step 1 5π/3 = 300°, which is between 270° and 360° → Quadrant IV Step 2 Reference angle in QIV: 2π - θ = 2π - 5π/3 = π/3 Step 3 sin(π/3) = √3/2 Step 4 In QIV only COSINE is positive, so sine is negative. Answer: sin(5π/3) = -√3/2
    Reference angle formulas. QI: θ. QII: 180° - θ. QIII: θ - 180°. QIV: 360° - θ. In radians swap 180° for π and 360° for 2π.
    Example 3 — tangent in Quadrant II

    Find tan(3π/4) exactly.

    3π/4 = 135° → Quadrant II Reference: π - 3π/4 = π/4 tan(π/4) = 1 In QII only SINE is positive, so tangent is negative. Answer: tan(3π/4) = -1
    Example 4 — a reciprocal function

    Find sec(7π/6) exactly.

    sec is 1/cos, so find the cosine first. 7π/6 = 210° → Quadrant III Reference: 7π/6 - π = π/6 cos(π/6) = √3/2, and cosine is negative in QIII cos(7π/6) = -√3/2 Now flip: sec(7π/6) = 1 ÷ (-√3/2) = 1 · (-2/√3) ← ÷ a fraction = × its flip = -2/√3 Rationalize: multiply top and bottom by √3. -2/√3 · √3/√3 = -2√3/(√3 · √3) = -2√3/3
    Example 5 — a negative angle

    Find csc(-π/6) exactly.

    Negative angles rotate clockwise. -π/6 lands in Quadrant IV. Coterminal positive angle: -π/6 + 2π = 11π/6. sin(11π/6): reference π/6, QIV, sine negative → -1/2 csc = 1/sin = 1 ÷ (-1/2) = -2
    Example 6 — coterminal cleanup

    Find cos(405°) and sin(-120°).

    405° - 360° = 45° → cos(405°) = cos(45°) = √2/2 -120° + 360° = 240° → Quadrant III, reference 240° - 180° = 60° sin 60° = √3/2, sine negative in QIII sin(-120°) = -√3/2

    Quick check — unit circle

    1. sin(150°)
    2. cos(4π/3)
    3. tan(π)
    4. sec(0)
    Answers

    1. QII, ref 30°, sine positive → 1/2

    150°: QII, reference 180° - 150° = 30° sin 30° = 1/2, sine positive in QII → 1/2

    2. QIII, ref π/3, cosine negative → -1/2

    4π/3: QIII, reference 4π/3 - π = π/3 cos(π/3) = 1/2, cosine negative in QIII → -1/2

    3. sin π / cos π = 0/(-1) = 0

    π is the point (-1, 0) tan π = sin π / cos π = 0/(-1) = 0

    4. 1/cos 0 = 1/1 = 1

    cos 0 = 1 (point (1, 0)) sec 0 = 1/cos 0 = 1/1 = 1

    Practice set — unit circle

    1. cos(135°)
    2. sin(7π/6)
    3. tan(5π/3)
    4. csc(3π/2)
    5. cot(225°)
    6. sin(-45°)
    7. sec(11π/6)
    8. cos(-π/3)
    Answers

    1. -√2/2

    135°: QII, reference 45° cos 45° = √2/2, cosine negative in QII → -√2/2

    2. -1/2

    7π/6: QIII, reference 7π/6 - π = π/6 sin(π/6) = 1/2, sine negative in QIII → -1/2

    3. ref π/3, QIV, tangent negative → -√3

    5π/3: QIV, reference 2π - 5π/3 = π/3 tan(π/3) = √3, tangent negative in QIV → -√3

    4. sin(3π/2) = -1 → -1

    3π/2 is the point (0, -1) → sin(3π/2) = -1 csc = 1/sin = 1/(-1) = -1

    5. QIII ref 45°, tangent positive → tan = 1, so cot = 1

    225°: QIII, reference 45° tan 45° = 1, tangent positive in QIII → tan 225° = 1 cot = 1/tan = 1

    6. -√2/2

    -45° + 360° = 315°: QIV, reference 45° sin 45° = √2/2, sine negative in QIV → -√2/2

    7. cos(11π/6) = √3/2 → 2/√3 = 2√3/3

    11π/6: QIV, reference 2π - 11π/6 = π/6 cos(π/6) = √3/2, cosine positive in QIV sec = 1/(√3/2) = 2/√3 = 2√3/3

    8. cosine is even, so cos(-π/3) = cos(π/3) = 1/2

    Cosine is even: cos(-θ) = cos θ cos(-π/3) = cos(π/3) = 1/2

    Review — Sections 4–6

    Quick check — trig basics

    1. Legs 8 and 15: find sin θ where θ is opposite the 8
    2. Convert 300° to radians
    3. Convert 11π/6 to degrees
    4. Short leg of a 30-60-90 is 4. Find the hypotenuse.
    Answers

    1. hyp = 17, so sin θ = 8/17

    hyp = √(8² + 15²) = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17 sin θ = opp/hyp = 8/17

    2. 300π/180 = 5π/3

    300 · π/180 = 300π/180 = 5π/3 (÷ 60)

    3. 11 · 30 = 330°

    11π/6 · 180/π = 11 · 30 = 330°

    4. 8

    30-60-90 sides 1 : √3 : 2 short leg 4 → hypotenuse 2 · 4 = 8

    Practice set — trig basics

    1. Legs 9 and 40: all six ratios for the angle opposite the 9
    2. Find x: hypotenuse 25, angle 52°, x adjacent to it
    3. Find the angle: opposite 15, hypotenuse 22
    4. Convert 225° and 40° to radians
    5. Convert 2π/3 and 7π/12 to degrees
    6. 45-45-90 with legs of 7: find the hypotenuse

    hyp = √(9² + 40²) = √(81 + 1600) = √1681 = 41 opp 9, adj 40, hyp 41 sin 9/41 cos 40/41 tan 9/40 csc 41/9 sec 41/40 cot 40/9

    2. cos 52° = x/25 → x = 25 cos 52° ≈ 15.39

    x ADJACENT, 25 hypotenuse → cosine cos 52° = x/25 x = 25 cos 52° ≈ 25(0.615661) ≈ 15.39

    Quiz 2

    CoverageSections 4–6
    FocusRight-triangle trig, angle measure and coterminal angles, circular measure, special triangles, reference-angle reasoning, and exact unit-circle values.
    Directions: Work without notes if you can. Show enough work to make your method clear. Use degree mode when a problem gives an angle in degrees. Give exact answers unless a decimal approximation is requested.

    Quiz 2 — 8 questions

    1. A right triangle has legs 7 and 24. For the acute angle θ opposite the 7, find all six trig ratios.
    2. A 16-ft ladder makes a 62° angle with the ground. How far is its base from the wall? Round to two decimals.
    3. A right triangle has the side opposite θ equal to 9 and the side adjacent equal to 13. Find θ to the nearest hundredth of a degree.
    4. Find one positive and one negative angle coterminal with -580°, and name the quadrant of its terminal side.
    5. Convert 240° to radians and 11π/9 to degrees.
    6. A sector has radius 8 cm and central angle 135°. Find the arc length and the sector area, exact and to two decimals.
    7. Find exactly: cos(5π/4), tan(150°), csc(7π/6).
    8. Find the reference angle of 300° and use it to find sec(300°) exactly.
    Quiz 2 answer key + worked solutions
    1. Hypotenuse √(49 + 576) = 25. sin θ = 7/25, cos θ = 24/25, tan θ = 7/24, csc θ = 25/7, sec θ = 25/24, cot θ = 24/7
      Hypotenuse √(7² + 24²) = √(49 + 576) = √625 = 25 opp 7, adj 24, hyp 25 sin 7/25 cos 24/25 tan 7/24 csc 25/7 sec 25/24 cot 24/7
    2. Base is adjacent: 16 cos 62° ≈ 7.51 ft
      Base is ADJACENT to 62°, ladder is the hypotenuse → cosine cos 62° = b/16 → b = 16 cos 62° ≈ 16(0.469472) ≈ 7.51 ft
    3. θ = tan⁻¹(9/13) ≈ 34.70°
      opp 9, adj 13 → tangent tan θ = 9/13 ≈ 0.692308 θ = tan⁻¹(9/13) ≈ 34.70°
    4. -580° + 720° = 140°; -580° + 360° = -220°. 140° is in Quadrant II
      Negative: -580° + 360° = -220° Positive: -220° + 360° = 140° 140° is between 90° and 180° → Quadrant II
    5. 240 · π/180 = 4π/3; 11π/9 · 180/π = 220°
      240 · π/180 = 240π/180 = 4π/3 (÷ 60) 11π/9 · 180/π = 11 · 20 = 220°
    6. 135° = 3π/4. s = 8(3π/4) = 6π ≈ 18.85 cm; A = (1/2)(64)(3π/4) = 24π ≈ 75.40 cm²
      135° = 135π/180 = 3π/4 s = rθ = 8(3π/4) = 6π ≈ 18.85 cm A = (1/2)r²θ = (1/2)(64)(3π/4) = 24π ≈ 75.40 cm²
    7. -√2/2; -√3/3; sin(7π/6) = -1/2, so csc(7π/6) = -2
      cos(5π/4): QIII, ref π/4, cosine negative → -√2/2 tan(150°): QII, ref 30°, tan 30° = √3/3, negative → -√3/3 sin(7π/6): QIII, ref π/6 → -1/2, so csc(7π/6) = 1/(-1/2) = -2
    8. Quadrant IV, reference 60°. cos 300° = +1/2, so sec 300° = 2
      300°: QIV, reference 360° - 300° = 60° cos 60° = 1/2, cosine positive in QIV → cos 300° = 1/2 sec 300° = 1/(1/2) = 2

    Section 7 — Trig Graphs

    Tags#trigonometry#graphs#amplitude#period#phase-shift
    Skills to know firstFunction transformationsRadiansUnit circle and exact trig values
    SkillsSine, cosine, tangent, cotangent, secant, cosecant, amplitude, period, phase shift, midline, graph transformations, and simple harmonic motion.
    TI-30XIISTrig modeInverse trigExact answers

    Sine and cosine form

    y=Asin(B(x-C))+D
    FeatureFormula
    Amplitude|A|
    Period (sin/cos)2π|B|
    Phase shiftC  (only when B is factored out — see the warning below)
    Midliney = D

    Tangent period

    Period=π|B|

    Guided trig-graph routine

    1Identify A, B, C, D.
    2Compute amplitude and period.
    3Find phase shift and midline.
    4Mark one period and the key quarter-points.
    TI-30XIIS: use it to check trig values; it does not graph.
    Five-point sine/cosine graph shortcut. Once you know the phase shift and period, compute period ÷ 4. Starting at the phase shift, mark five x-values one quarter-period apart. For sine, the parent y-pattern is 0, 1, 0, -1, 0; for cosine it is 1, 0, -1, 0, 1. Multiply by A and then add D. This produces one full cycle quickly and reliably.
    Parent table instead: make four columns, parent x (θ = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π), parent y (the pattern above), new x and new y. Then apply the transformations to every row: new x = θ/B + phase shift (stretch/shrink, then shift) and new y = A·(parent y) + D (stretch/reflect, then shift). For y = sin(3/4x - 4) + 4: new x = θ ÷ (3/4) + 16/3, new y = parent y + 4.

    Two forms of the same equation

    Read the form before you read the phase shift.
    In y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D the phase shift is C.
    In y = A sin(Bx - C) + D the phase shift is C/B.
    If B is not already factored out, factor it out first. Skipping this is the single most common error in this section.

    Worked examples — trig graphs

    Example 1 — factoring B out before reading the shift

    For y = 3 sin(2x - π) + 1, find amplitude, period, phase shift, and midline, then list the five quarter-points.

    Step 1 Factor the 2 out of the inside. Copy just the inside: 2x - π Write B in front: 2( ) Divide EACH term by 2: 2x ÷ 2 = x π ÷ 2 = π/2 Fill in the parenthesis: 2(x - π/2) Check by distributing: 2·x - 2·(π/2) = 2x - π ✓ Put it back in the function: y = 3 sin(2(x - π/2)) + 1 Now A = 3, B = 2, C = π/2, D = 1. Step 2 Amplitude = |A| = 3 Period = 2π/|B| = 2π/2 = π Phase shift = π/2 to the RIGHT Midline = y = 1 Step 3 Quarter-point spacing = period/4 = π/4. Start at the phase shift and step forward. x = π/2 y = 1 + 0 = 1 (midline, heading up) x = 3π/4 y = 1 + 3 = 4 (maximum) x = π y = 1 + 0 = 1 (midline) x = 5π/4 y = 1 - 3 = -2 (minimum) x = 3π/2 y = 1 + 0 = 1 (back to start of next cycle) Or with a parent table. Apply the transformations to each row: new x = θ/2 + π/2 (shrink by B = 2, then shift right π/2) new y = 3·(parent y) + 1 (stretch by 3, then up 1) parent x (θ) parent y new x new y 0 0 π/2 1 π/2 1 3π/4 4 π 0 π 1 3π/2 -1 5π/4 -2 2π 0 3π/2 1 Range: [-2, 4]
    If you had read C = π straight off the unfactored form, your graph would be shifted twice as far as it should be.
    Example 2 — negative A and a fractional B

    Describe y = -2 cos(x/3) - 4.

    A = -2 → amplitude |A| = 2, and the graph is FLIPPED vertically B = 1/3 → period = 2π/(1/3) = 2π · 3 = 6π (÷ 1/3 is × 3) C = 0 → no phase shift D = -4 → midline y = -4 Range: midline ± amplitude = [-6, -2] Quarter-point spacing = period/4 = 6π/4 = 3π/2 Step from 0: 0, 3π/2, 3π, 9π/2, 6π Because A is negative, cosine STARTS at its minimum instead of its maximum. x = 0 y = -4 - 2 = -6 (minimum) x = 3π/2 y = -4 (midline) x = 3π y = -4 + 2 = -2 (maximum) x = 9π/2 y = -4 (midline) x = 6π y = -6 (minimum, cycle complete)

    Quick check — trig graphs

    1. Period of y = sin(4x)
    2. Period of y = tan(2x)
    3. Range of y = 5 cos x - 2
    Answers

    1. 2π/4 = π/2

    Period = 2π/|B| = 2π/4 = π/2

    2. π/2 (tangent's period is π, not 2π)

    Tangent period = π/|B| = π/2

    3. midline -2, amplitude 5 → [-7, 3]

    Midline D = -2, amplitude |A| = 5 [D - |A|, D + |A|] = [-2 - 5, -2 + 5] = [-7, 3]

    Practice set — trig graphs

    1. Amplitude, period, phase shift, midline of y = 4 sin(3x + π) - 2
    2. Amplitude, period, midline of y = -cos(πx) + 3
    Answers

    1. Factor: 4 sin(3(x + π/3)) - 2. Amplitude 4, period 2π/3, shift π/3 LEFT, midline y = -2

    Factor 3: 3x + π = 3(x + π/3) y = 4 sin(3(x + π/3)) - 2 x + π/3 = x - (-π/3) → C = -π/3 Amplitude 4; period 2π/3; shift π/3 LEFT; midline y = -2

    2. Amplitude 1 (reflected), period 2π/π = 2, midline y = 3

    A = -1 → amplitude |-1| = 1, reflected B = π → period 2π/π = 2 D = 3 → midline y = 3

    Graphing tangent and cotangent

    y = tan xy = cot x
    Periodππ
    Asymptotesx = π/2 + πn (where cos = 0)x = πn (where sin = 0)
    Zerosx = πnx = π/2 + πn
    Directionincreasing, bottom left to top rightdecreasing, top left to bottom right
    Amplitudenone, the range is all realsnone
    For y = A tan(B(x - C)) + D: period is π/|B|, not 2π/|B|. A is a vertical stretch, not an amplitude. Build one cycle between two consecutive asymptotes and mark the three key points at the quarter marks.
    Example 1 — tangent with a stretch and a period change

    Graph one cycle of y = 3tan(2x).

    A = 3, B = 2, no shift. Period = π/|B| = π/2 Asymptotes: tangent's asymptotes sit half a period apart, centered on the zero. Solve 2x = ±π/2: 2x = -π/2 → x = -π/4 2x = π/2 → x = π/4 One cycle runs between x = -π/4 and x = π/4. Key points, quarter marks of that interval: x = -π/8: y = 3tan(-π/4) = 3(-1) = -3 x = 0: y = 3tan(0) = 0 ← the zero, in the middle x = π/8: y = 3tan(π/4) = 3(1) = 3 Curve rises from the left asymptote through (-π/8, -3), (0,0), (π/8, 3), up to the right asymptote.
    Example 2 — cotangent with a shift

    Graph one cycle of y = cot(x - π/4).

    B = 1, so period = π. Shift right π/4. Cotangent's asymptotes are where the inside equals 0 and π: x - π/4 = 0 → x = π/4 x - π/4 = π → x = 5π/4 Cycle runs from π/4 to 5π/4. Key points: x = π/2: inside = π/4, cot = 1 x = 3π/4: inside = π/2, cot = 0 ← the zero, in the middle x = π: inside = 3π/4, cot = -1 Curve FALLS from the left asymptote through (π/2, 1), (3π/4, 0), (π, -1), down to the right asymptote.
    Cotangent falls, tangent rises. They also have asymptotes in opposite places. Getting the direction backward is the usual error on these.

    Graphing secant and cosecant

    Always sketch the reciprocal first. Draw y = cos x lightly, then build y = sec x on top of it. Every zero of the cosine becomes a vertical asymptote of the secant, and every peak or valley of the cosine becomes the turning point of a secant branch.
    y = sec xy = csc x
    Based oncos xsin x
    Period2π2π
    Asymptoteswhere cos x = 0: π/2 + πnwhere sin x = 0: πn
    Range(-∞, -1] ∪ [1, ∞)(-∞, -1] ∪ [1, ∞)
    Zerosnone, evernone, ever
    Example — building a secant graph from its cosine

    Graph y = 2sec(x) - 1 on [0, 2π].

    Step 1 Sketch the guide curve y = 2cos(x) - 1. Amplitude 2, midline y = -1, so it runs between -3 and 1. x = 0 → 2(1) - 1 = 1 max x = π/2 → 2(0) - 1 = -1 crosses the midline x = π → 2(-1) - 1 = -3 min x = 3π/2 → 2(0) - 1 = -1 crosses the midline x = 2π → 2(1) - 1 = 1 max Step 2 Every midline crossing of the guide becomes an ASYMPTOTE. (Those are where cos x = 0.) x = π/2 and x = 3π/2 Step 3 Every max or min of the guide becomes the TURNING POINT of a branch, and the branch opens away from the midline. (0, 1) is a max → branch opens UPWARD from (0, 1) (π, -3) is a min → branch opens DOWNWARD from (π, -3) (2π, 1) is a max → branch opens UPWARD Range: (-∞, -3] ∪ [1, ∞)
    Why the branches open away. Near an asymptote the cosine is close to zero, and one over a tiny number is huge. Near a peak the cosine is at its largest, so one over it is at its smallest. The turning points are where the reciprocal is least extreme.

    Simple harmonic motion

    An object oscillating without friction follows d = a cos(ωt) if it starts at maximum displacement, or d = a sin(ωt) if it starts at equilibrium. Amplitude |a|, period 2π/ω, and frequency ω/(2π) cycles per unit time.
    Example 1 — starting at maximum displacement

    A weight is pulled 8 cm below equilibrium and released. It completes one full oscillation every 3 seconds. Write the model and find the position at t = 2 s.

    Starts at maximum displacement → use cosine. Pulled DOWN → a = -8 Period = 2π/ω, and the period is 3: 3 = 2π/ω 3ω = 2π ← multiply both sides by ω ω = 2π/3 ← divide by 3 d = -8 cos(2πt/3) At t = 2: inside: (2π/3)(2) = 4π/3 d = -8 cos(4π/3) 4π/3 is in QIII, reference π/3, cosine negative there → cos(4π/3) = -1/2 = -8(-1/2) = 4 cm 4 cm ABOVE equilibrium. Frequency = ω/(2π) = (2π/3)/(2π) = 1/3 cycle per second.
    Example 2 — starting at equilibrium

    An object starts at rest position and oscillates with amplitude 5 in and frequency 4 cycles per second, moving upward first. Write the model and find the period.

    Starts at equilibrium → use sine. Moves up first → a is positive, a = 5 Frequency = ω/(2π), and the frequency is 4: 4 = ω/(2π) ω = 4 · 2π = 8π ← multiply both sides by 2π d = 5 sin(8πt) Period = 2π/ω = 2π/(8π) = 1/4 second. Check: 4 cycles per second means each cycle takes 1/4 second. ✓

    Practice set — tangent, reciprocal graphs, and harmonic motion

    1. Period and asymptotes of y = tan(3x)
    2. Period and asymptotes of y = cot(x/2)
    3. Period and asymptotes of y = -2tan(x + π/2)
    4. Asymptotes and range of y = csc(x) + 3
    5. Asymptotes and range of y = 4sec(2x)
    6. A spring is pushed 6 in above rest and released, period 2 s. Write the model.
    7. Amplitude, period, and frequency of d = 12 sin(πt/4)
    Answers

    1. Period π/3; asymptotes where 3x = π/2 + πn → x = π/6 + πn/3

    Period π/|B| = π/3 Tangent asymptotes: inside = π/2 + πn 3x = π/2 + πn → x = π/6 + πn/3

    2. Period π/(1/2) = 2π; asymptotes where x/2 = πn → x = 2πn

    Period π/(1/2) = 2π Cotangent asymptotes: inside = πn x/2 = πn → x = 2πn

    3. Period π; asymptotes where x + π/2 = π/2 + πn → x = πn. The -2 flips it so it falls instead of rising

    B = 1 → period π x + π/2 = π/2 + πn → x = πn A = -2 < 0 → the curve falls instead of rising

    4. Asymptotes where sin x = 0 → x = πn. Guide curve is sin x + 3, so branches turn at 4 and 2. Range (-∞, 2] ∪ [4, ∞)

    csc = 1/sin → asymptotes where sin x = 0 → x = πn Guide curve sin x + 3 runs from 2 to 4 Branches turn at 4 (open up) and 2 (open down) Range (-∞, 2] ∪ [4, ∞)

    5. Asymptotes where cos 2x = 0 → 2x = π/2 + πn → x = π/4 + πn/2. Range (-∞, -4] ∪ [4, ∞)

    sec = 1/cos → asymptotes where cos 2x = 0 2x = π/2 + πn → x = π/4 + πn/2 Guide 4cos(2x) runs from -4 to 4 Range (-∞, -4] ∪ [4, ∞)

    6. Starts at max displacement, upward, so a = 6 with cosine. ω = 2π/2 = π → d = 6 cos(πt)

    Starts at max displacement → cosine Pushed UP → a = +6 ω = 2π/period = 2π/2 = π d = 6 cos(πt)

    7. Amplitude 12; period 2π/(π/4) = 8; frequency 1/8 cycle per unit time

    Amplitude |12| = 12 ω = π/4 → period 2π/(π/4) = 2π · 4/π = 8 Frequency = 1/period = 1/8

    Inverse trigonometric functions

    The calculator button is not the whole story. Sine, cosine and tangent fail the horizontal line test, so each one has to be restricted to a slice where it is one-to-one before an inverse exists. That restricted slice is the range of the inverse, and it is why your calculator hands back one angle and no others.
    FunctionDomain (what you may put in)Range (what comes out)Quadrants of the output
    sin⁻¹x[-1, 1][-π/2, π/2]I and IV
    cos⁻¹x[-1, 1][0, π]I and II
    tan⁻¹xall reals(-π/2, π/2)I and IV
    Memory hook. Arcsine and arctangent live on the right half of the circle, Q1 and Q4, so their outputs can be negative. Arccosine lives on the top half, Q1 and Q2, so its output is never negative. That single distinction answers most sign questions here.
    Example 1 — a negative input, three ways

    Find sin⁻¹(-1/2), cos⁻¹(-1/2), and tan⁻¹(-1) exactly.

    sin⁻¹(-1/2) Reference angle: sine is 1/2 at π/6. Range is [-π/2, π/2]. Negative output allowed, so go clockwise. Answer: -π/6 cos⁻¹(-1/2) Reference angle: cosine is 1/2 at π/3. Range is [0, π]. NO negative output. A negative cosine means Quadrant II. π - π/3 = 2π/3 Answer: 2π/3 tan⁻¹(-1) Reference angle: tangent is 1 at π/4. Range is (-π/2, π/2). Negative allowed. Answer: -π/4
    cos⁻¹(-1/2) ≠ -π/3. That angle is not in the range. Arccosine can never return a negative number, so a negative input must push the answer into Quadrant II.
    Example 2 — the cancellation rule, and when it fails

    Evaluate sin⁻¹(sin(π/3)) and sin⁻¹(sin(5π/6)).

    CASE A: sin⁻¹(sin(π/3)) Is π/3 inside the arcsine range [-π/2, π/2]? YES. They cancel cleanly. Answer: π/3 CASE B: sin⁻¹(sin(5π/6)) Is 5π/6 inside [-π/2, π/2]? NO. 5π/6 = 150°, way outside. You may NOT just cancel. Work it inside out instead: sin(5π/6) = 1/2 (Q2, reference π/6, sine positive) sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6 (must land in the range) Answer: π/6, not 5π/6
    The rule. f⁻¹(f(x)) = x only when x is already inside the restricted range. Otherwise evaluate the inside first, then take the inverse.
    Example 3 — composing across functions with a triangle

    Find the exact value of tan(cos⁻¹(3/5)).

    Let θ = cos⁻¹(3/5). That means cos θ = 3/5, and θ is in [0, π]. Since 3/5 is positive, θ is in Quadrant I. Draw the triangle from the cosine: adjacent = 3 hypotenuse = 5 opposite = √(25 - 9) = 4 (3-4-5) Now read off the tangent: tan θ = opposite/adjacent = 4/3 Answer: 4/3
    Example 4 — a negative input, where the quadrant decides the sign

    Find the exact value of sin(cos⁻¹(-2/3)) and cos(tan⁻¹(-5/12)).

    PART A: θ = cos⁻¹(-2/3) Arccosine range is [0, π], and the input is negative → Quadrant II. In Q2, sine is POSITIVE. adjacent = -2, hypotenuse = 3 opposite = √(9 - 4) = √5 sin θ = √5/3 (positive, as Q2 requires) PART B: θ = tan⁻¹(-5/12) Arctangent range is (-π/2, π/2), and the input is negative → Quadrant IV. In Q4, cosine is POSITIVE. opposite = -5, adjacent = 12 hypotenuse = √(25 + 144) = 13 cos θ = 12/13 (positive, as Q4 requires)
    The hypotenuse is never negative. Put the sign on the leg that carries it, then let the quadrant confirm whether your final answer should be positive or negative.
    Example 5 — a composition with a variable

    Write sin(tan⁻¹x) as an algebraic expression in x.

    Let θ = tan⁻¹x, so tan θ = x = x/1. opposite = x adjacent = 1 hypotenuse = √(x² + 1) sin θ = x/√(x² + 1) Rationalize: multiply top and bottom by √(x² + 1). x/√(x² + 1) · √(x² + 1)/√(x² + 1) = x√(x² + 1) / (x² + 1) ← √(x² + 1) · √(x² + 1) = x² + 1

    This substitution shows up again in calculus. Building the triangle is the whole technique.

    Quick check — inverse trig

    1. cos⁻¹(0)
    2. sin⁻¹(-1)
    3. tan⁻¹(√3)
    4. Why is sin⁻¹(2) undefined?
    Answers

    1. π/2

    cos⁻¹(0): angle in [0, π] with cosine 0 cos(π/2) = 0 → π/2

    2. -π/2

    sin⁻¹(-1): angle in [-π/2, π/2] with sine -1 sin(-π/2) = -1 → -π/2

    3. π/3

    tan⁻¹(√3): angle in (-π/2, π/2) with tangent √3 tan(π/3) = √3 → π/3

    4. The domain of arcsine is [-1, 1]. Sine never outputs 2, so no angle can be returned.

    Arcsine only accepts inputs in [-1, 1] 2 > 1, and sine never equals 2 → undefined

    Practice set — inverse trig

    1. sin⁻¹(√2/2)
    2. cos⁻¹(-√3/2)
    3. tan⁻¹(-√3/3)
    4. cos⁻¹(cos(4π/3))
    5. tan⁻¹(tan(3π/4))
    6. cos(sin⁻¹(7/25))
    7. tan(sin⁻¹(-3/5))
    8. sec(tan⁻¹(2))
    9. Write cos(sin⁻¹x) algebraically
    Answers

    1. π/4

    sin(π/4) = √2/2 and π/4 is in [-π/2, π/2] → π/4

    2. Negative input, arccosine range [0, π] → Q2 → π - π/6 = 5π/6

    Reference: cos(π/6) = √3/2 Negative input → QII (range [0, π]) π - π/6 = 5π/6

    3. -π/6

    Reference: tan(π/6) = √3/3 Negative allowed in (-π/2, π/2) → -π/6

    4. 4π/3 is outside [0, π], so no cancelling. cos(4π/3) = -1/2, then cos⁻¹(-1/2) = 2π/3

    4π/3 is not in [0, π] → cannot cancel Inside: cos(4π/3) = -1/2 (QIII, ref π/3) cos⁻¹(-1/2) = π - π/3 = 2π/3

    5. 3π/4 is outside (-π/2, π/2). tan(3π/4) = -1, then tan⁻¹(-1) = -π/4

    3π/4 is not in (-π/2, π/2) → cannot cancel Inside: tan(3π/4) = -1 (QII, ref π/4) tan⁻¹(-1) = -π/4

    6. 7-24-25 triangle, Q1 → 24/25

    θ = sin⁻¹(7/25): sin θ = 7/25, positive → QI opp 7, hyp 25, adj = √(625 - 49) = √576 = 24 cos θ = 24/25

    7. Arcsine range, negative input → Q4, tangent negative. 3-4-5 → -3/4

    θ = sin⁻¹(-3/5): negative → QIV opp -3, hyp 5, adj = √(25 - 9) = 4 tan θ = opp/adj = -3/4

    8. tan θ = 2/1, hypotenuse √5, Q1 → sec θ = √5/1 = √5

    θ = tan⁻¹(2): tan θ = 2/1, QI opp 2, adj 1, hyp = √(4 + 1) = √5 sec θ = hyp/adj = √5/1 = √5

    9. sin θ = x/1, adjacent √(1 - x²) → √(1 - x²)

    θ = sin⁻¹(x): sin θ = x/1 opp x, hyp 1, adj = √(1 - x²) cos θ = √(1 - x²)/1 = √(1 - x²) (positive, since θ is in [-π/2, π/2])

    Test 2 Study Guide

    CoverageSections 4–8
    GoalRecognize which trig tool fits the problem, keep exact values exact, and use the calculator only when it helps.

    Know how to

    Section 4 — Right-Triangle Trigonometry



    Section 5 — Coterminal and Reference Angles




    Section 6 — Trig on xy-plane & Special Angles




    Section 7 — Trig Graphs




    Section 8 — Inverse Trig Functions



    Must-know formulas and rules

    SOH–CAH–TOA: sin θ = opp/hyp;   cos θ = adj/hyp;   tan θ = opp/adj
    Angle conversion: 180° = π radians;   degrees · π/180;   radians · 180/π
    Circular measure: s = rθ;   A = (1/2)r²θ;   ω = θ/t;   v = rω   (θ in radians)
    Unit circle: (x, y) = (cos θ, sin θ);   tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
    Graph form: y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D or A cos(B(x - C)) + D; amplitude = |A|; period = 2π/|B|; midline y = D
    Tangent/cotangent period: π/|B|
    Principal ranges: arcsin → [-π/2, π/2];   arccos → [0, π];   arctan → (-π/2, π/2)

    Common mistakes

    Check DEG/RAD first. A correct setup with the wrong calculator mode still gives a wrong answer.
    Reference angle gives the magnitude, not the sign. Use the quadrant after finding the reference angle.
    Arc and sector formulas require radians. Convert degree measures before using s = rθ or A = (1/2)r²θ.
    Factor B before reading phase shift. For sin(3x + π), write sin(3(x + π/3)).
    Inverse trig is not reciprocal trig. sin⁻¹ means arcsine; csc means 1/sin.
    Inverse-trig compositions do not always cancel. The inside angle must already lie in the inverse function's principal range.

    Calculator reminders

    • Before right-triangle work, confirm DEG unless the problem is explicitly in radians.
    • Use 2nd with SIN/COS/TAN for inverse trig when finding an angle.
    • Keep exact unit-circle values exact; do not replace √3/2 with a decimal unless asked.
    • For graph and inverse-trig work in radians, switch to RAD before checking decimal values.

    Test 2 answer key + worked solutions
    1. A = 49°; a is adjacent to B, so b = 12 tan 41° ≈ 10.43 and c = 12/cos 41° ≈ 15.90
      A = 90° - 41° = 49° a = 12 is ADJACENT to B, b is OPPOSITE B → tangent b = 12 tan 41° ≈ 12(0.869287) ≈ 10.43 c is the hypotenuse → cosine c = 12/cos 41° ≈ 12/0.754710 ≈ 15.90
    2. 300 tan 23° ≈ 127.34 ft
      Height OPPOSITE 23°, 300 ADJACENT → tangent h = 300 tan 23° ≈ 300(0.424475) ≈ 127.34 ft
    3. cos⁻¹(11/17) ≈ 49.68°
      adj 11, hyp 17 → cosine cos θ = 11/17 ≈ 0.647059 θ = cos⁻¹(11/17) ≈ 49.68°
    4. 7π/6 and -5π/12
      210 · π/180 = 210π/180 = 7π/6 (÷ 30) -75 · π/180 = -75π/180 = -5π/12 (÷ 15)
    5. 126° and 390°
      7π/10 · 180/π = 7 · 18 = 126° 13π/6 · 180/π = 13 · 30 = 390°
    6. 23π/6 - 2π = 11π/6 (Quadrant IV); reference π/6
      23π/6 - 2π = 23π/6 - 12π/6 = 11π/6 3π/2 = 9π/6 < 11π/6 < 2π → Quadrant IV Reference = 2π - 11π/6 = π/6
    7. 47 + 15/60 + 36/3600 = 47 + 0.25 + 0.01 = 47.26°
      15' → 15/60 = 0.25° 36" → 36/3600 = 0.01° 47 + 0.25 + 0.01 = 47.26°
    8. ω = 150 · 2π = 300π ≈ 942.48 rad/min; v = 0.4(300π) = 120π ≈ 376.99 m/min
      ω = 150 rev/min · 2π = 300π ≈ 942.48 rad/min v = rω = 0.4(300π) = 120π ≈ 376.99 m/min
    9. Short leg 14/2 = 7; long leg 7√3
      30-60-90 sides 1 : √3 : 2 hyp 14 = 2 · short → short = 7 long = 7√3
    10. 3-4-5 triangle, QIII: cos θ = -4/5, tan θ = 3/4
      sin θ = y/r = -3/5 → y = -3, r = 5 x² + 9 = 25 → x = ±4; QIII → x = -4 cos θ = x/r = -4/5 tan θ = y/x = -3/(-4) = 3/4
    11. -√3/2; cosine is even so cos 225° = -√2/2; -√3/3
      sin(4π/3): QIII, ref π/3, sine negative → -√3/2 cos(-225°) = cos 225° (cosine is even): QIII, ref 45° → -√2/2 tan(5π/6): QII, ref π/6, tan(π/6) = √3/3, negative → -√3/3
    12. cos(5π/3) = 1/2 → 2; tan(3π/4) = -1 → -1
      cos(5π/3): QIV, ref π/3, cosine positive → 1/2 sec(5π/3) = 1/(1/2) = 2 tan(3π/4): QII, ref π/4 → -1 cot(3π/4) = 1/(-1) = -1
    13. r = 13: sin θ = 12/13, cos θ = -5/13, tan θ = -12/5
      r = √((-5)² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 sin θ = y/r = 12/13 cos θ = x/r = -5/13 tan θ = y/x = 12/(-5) = -12/5
    14. 3cos(2(x - π/4)) + 1: amplitude 3, period π, shift π/4 right, midline y = 1, range [-2, 4]
      Factor 2: 2x - π/2 = 2(x - π/4) y = 3cos(2(x - π/4)) + 1 Amplitude 3; period 2π/2 = π; shift π/4 right Midline y = 1; range [1 - 3, 1 + 3] = [-2, 4]
    15. B = 2π/6π = 1/3 → y = 4 sin(x/3) - 2
      Period = 2π/B = 6π → B = 2π/(6π) = 1/3 A = 4, D = -2, C = 0 y = 4 sin(x/3) - 2
    16. Period π/(1/2) = 2π; x/2 = π/2 + πn → x = π + 2πn
      Period π/(1/2) = 2π Asymptotes: x/2 = π/2 + πn → x = π + 2πn
    17. Where cos x = 0: x = π/2 + πn. Branches turn at 3 - 1 = 2 and -3 - 1 = -4: range (-∞, -4] ∪ [2, ∞)
      sec = 1/cos → asymptotes where cos x = 0 → x = π/2 + πn Guide 3cos x - 1 runs from -4 to 2 Branches turn at 2 (open up) and -4 (open down) Range (-∞, -4] ∪ [2, ∞)
    18. d = 2cos(2πt/5). d(2) = 2cos(4π/5) ≈ -1.62 ft (below equilibrium)
      Starts at highest point → cosine, a = 2 ω = 2π/5 → d = 2cos(2πt/5) t = 2: inside 4π/5 cos(4π/5) ≈ -0.809017 (RAD mode) d ≈ 2(-0.809017) ≈ -1.62 ft (below equilibrium)
    19. -π/3; 3π/4; π/6
      sin⁻¹(-√3/2): ref π/3, negative allowed → -π/3 cos⁻¹(-√2/2): ref π/4, QII → π - π/4 = 3π/4 tan⁻¹(√3/3): tan(π/6) = √3/3 → π/6
    20. cos⁻¹(-5/13) is in QII, where sine is positive: 12/13. cos(5π/3) = 1/2, and cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3
      θ = cos⁻¹(-5/13): negative → QII adj -5, hyp 13, opp = √(169 - 25) = 12 sin θ = 12/13 (positive in QII) cos⁻¹(cos(5π/3)): 5π/3 not in [0, π] cos(5π/3) = 1/2 → cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3

    Section 9 — Trig Identities — Part 1

    PaperPythagorean identitiesQuotient identities
    TI-30XIISTrig mode

    Pythagorean identities

    sin2θ + cos2θ =1
    1+tan2θ = sec2θ
    1+cot2θ = csc2θ

    Quotient identities

    tanθ = sinθcosθ
    cotθ = cosθsinθ
    Best trig simplification fallback: if stuck, rewrite everything in sine and cosine.

    Guided trig-identity routine

    1Usually transform one side only.
    2If stuck, rewrite tan/cot/sec/csc in sine and cosine.
    3Look for a Pythagorean identity.
    4Use ordinary algebra: factoring, LCDs, cancellation.
    Identity speed ladder. Start on the more complicated side. First factor or combine fractions if ordinary algebra will expose a pattern. Next use reciprocal/quotient/Pythagorean identities that move you toward the other side. If nothing is obvious, convert everything to sine and cosine. Do not work both sides at once when you are verifying an identity.

    More identities

    Even and odd

    sin(-θ) = -sin θcsc(-θ) = -csc θ
    cos(-θ) = cos θsec(-θ) = sec θ
    tan(-θ) = -tan θcot(-θ) = -cot θ

    Cosine and secant are even. Everything else is odd.

    Worked examples — identities

    Example 1 — verify, working one side only

    Verify (1 - cos²θ)/sin θ = sin θ.

    Work the LEFT side. Do not move anything across the equals sign. Pythagorean identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 Rearranged: 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ LHS = sin²θ/sin θ = sin θ ← one sin cancels LHS = RHS ✓
    Verifying is not solving. You cannot multiply both sides or cross-multiply. Transform one side until it looks like the other.
    Example 2 — the rewrite-in-sine-and-cosine fallback

    Verify sec θ - cos θ = sin θ tan θ.

    Left side, everything into sine and cosine: sec θ - cos θ = 1/cos θ - cos θ Common denominator cos θ: = 1/cos θ - cos²θ/cos θ = (1 - cos²θ)/cos θ Pythagorean: = sin²θ/cos θ Split the square to match the right side: = sin θ · (sin θ/cos θ) = sin θ tan θ ✓
    Example 3 — adding two fractions

    Simplify 1/(1 - sin θ) + 1/(1 + sin θ).

    Common denominator is the product, which is a difference of squares. (1 + sin θ) + (1 - sin θ) -------------------------------- (1 - sin θ)(1 + sin θ) Numerator: 1 + sin θ + 1 - sin θ = 2 Denominator: 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ = 2/cos²θ = 2 sec²θ
    Example 4 — factoring inside an identity

    Simplify (sin²θ - cos²θ)/(sin θ - cos θ).

    The numerator is a difference of squares with a = sin θ, b = cos θ. (sin θ - cos θ)(sin θ + cos θ) ------------------------------------------ (sin θ - cos θ) Cancel the matching factor: = sin θ + cos θ

    Ordinary algebra does most of the work in identity problems. The trig part is usually just one substitution.

    Reciprocal and cofunction identities

    ReciprocalCofunction (degrees)Cofunction (radians)
    csc θ = 1/sin θsin θ = cos(90° - θ)sin θ = cos(π/2 - θ)
    sec θ = 1/cos θtan θ = cot(90° - θ)tan θ = cot(π/2 - θ)
    cot θ = 1/tan θsec θ = csc(90° - θ)sec θ = csc(π/2 - θ)

    The reciprocal pairs multiply to 1: sin θ csc θ = 1, cos θ sec θ = 1, tan θ cot θ = 1. Every cofunction pair works in both directions.

    More verification techniques

    Example 5 — multiply by a conjugate

    Verify cos θ/(1 - sin θ) = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ.

    A "1 - sin θ" in a denominator is the signal. Multiply top and bottom of the LEFT side by its conjugate (1 + sin θ): cos θ (1 + sin θ) cos θ (1 + sin θ) --------- · ----------- = ----------------- 1 - sin θ (1 + sin θ) 1 - sin²θ Pythagorean: 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ = cos θ (1 + sin θ) / cos²θ = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ ← one cos θ cancels ✓
    Example 6 — factor a higher power

    Verify sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = sin²θ - cos²θ.

    The left side is a difference of squares, with a = sin²θ and b = cos²θ. sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = (sin²θ - cos²θ)(sin²θ + cos²θ) = (sin²θ - cos²θ)(1) = sin²θ - cos²θ ✓
    Example 7 — combine two fractions

    Verify sin θ/(1 + cos θ) + (1 + cos θ)/sin θ = 2 csc θ.

    Common denominator sin θ (1 + cos θ): sin²θ + (1 + cos θ)² ---------------------- sin θ (1 + cos θ) Expand the numerator: sin²θ + 1 + 2cos θ + cos²θ Group sin²θ + cos²θ = 1: 1 + 1 + 2cos θ = 2 + 2cos θ = 2(1 + cos θ) 2(1 + cos θ) ------------------- = 2/sin θ = 2 csc θ ✓ sin θ (1 + cos θ)
    Example 8 — even and odd in one line

    Simplify sin(-θ)/cos(-θ) + tan θ.

    Sine is odd, cosine is even: sin(-θ) = -sin θ cos(-θ) = cos θ -sin θ/cos θ + tan θ = -tan θ + tan θ = 0

    Quick check — fundamental identities

    1. Simplify sin θ csc θ
    2. Simplify (1 + tan²θ)cos²θ
    3. Write sin(π/2 - θ) as a single function of θ
    4. Simplify cos(-θ) sec θ
    Answers

    1. 1

    sin θ csc θ = sin θ · (1/sin θ) = 1

    2. sec²θ · cos²θ = 1

    1 + tan²θ = sec²θ sec²θ · cos²θ = (1/cos²θ) · cos²θ = 1

    3. cos θ

    Cofunction: sin(π/2 - θ) = cos θ

    4. cos θ · (1/cos θ) = 1

    cos(-θ) = cos θ (cosine is even) cos θ · sec θ = cos θ · (1/cos θ) = 1

    Practice set — fundamental identities

    1. Simplify (csc²θ - 1)/csc²θ
    2. Simplify sin θ + cos θ cot θ
    3. Verify sec θ - sin θ tan θ = cos θ
    4. Verify (1 + sin θ)(1 - sin θ) = cos²θ
    5. Verify (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ
    6. Verify 1/(sec θ - tan θ) = sec θ + tan θ
    7. Verify tan θ + cot θ = sec θ csc θ
    8. Simplify cos(-θ)/sin(-θ)
    Answers

    1. cot²θ/csc²θ = (cos²θ/sin²θ)(sin²θ) = cos²θ

    csc²θ - 1 = cot²θ cot²θ/csc²θ = (cos²θ/sin²θ) ÷ (1/sin²θ) = (cos²θ/sin²θ)(sin²θ/1) = cos²θ

    2. sin θ + cos²θ/sin θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/sin θ = 1/sin θ = csc θ

    sin θ + cos θ · (cos θ/sin θ) = sin θ + cos²θ/sin θ = sin²θ/sin θ + cos²θ/sin θ common denominator = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/sin θ = 1/sin θ = csc θ

    3. 1/cos θ - sin²θ/cos θ = (1 - sin²θ)/cos θ = cos²θ/cos θ = cos θ

    Left side: sec θ - sin θ tan θ = 1/cos θ - sin θ(sin θ/cos θ) = 1/cos θ - sin²θ/cos θ = (1 - sin²θ)/cos θ = cos²θ/cos θ = cos θ ✓

    4. Difference of squares: 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ

    (1 + sin θ)(1 - sin θ) = 1 - sin²θ difference of squares = cos²θ ✓

    5. sin²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ + cos²θ = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ

    (sin θ + cos θ)² = sin²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ + cos²θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ) + 2 sin θ cos θ = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ ✓

    6. Multiply by the conjugate (sec θ + tan θ): denominator sec²θ - tan²θ = 1, leaving sec θ + tan θ

    Multiply by the conjugate: 1/(sec θ - tan θ) · (sec θ + tan θ)/(sec θ + tan θ) = (sec θ + tan θ)/(sec²θ - tan²θ) sec²θ - tan²θ = 1 (from 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ) = sec θ + tan θ ✓

    7. sin θ/cos θ + cos θ/sin θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ) = 1/(sin θ cos θ) = sec θ csc θ

    tan θ + cot θ = sin θ/cos θ + cos θ/sin θ = sin²θ/(sin θ cos θ) + cos²θ/(sin θ cos θ) = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ) = 1/(sin θ cos θ) = (1/cos θ)(1/sin θ) = sec θ csc θ ✓

    8. cos θ/(-sin θ) = -cot θ

    cos(-θ) = cos θ (even), sin(-θ) = -sin θ (odd) cos θ/(-sin θ) = -cot θ
    Related skills: Section 6 — Trig on xy-plane & Special AnglesFactoringFractionsSection 10 — Trig Identities — Part 2

    Section 10 — Trig Identities — Part 2

    Skills to know firstSection 9 — Trig Identities — Part 1Exact trig valuesFactoring

    Sum and difference

    sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
    cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B
    tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B)
    Cosine flips the sign. cos(A + B) uses a minus in the middle. Sine keeps the sign you were given.
    Exact-value angle shortcut. If an angle is not on the unit circle, first ask whether it is a simple sum/difference of known angles: 15° = 45° - 30°, 75° = 45° + 30°, 105° = 60° + 45°. If it is half of a known angle, such as 22.5° = 45°/2, use a half-angle formula instead. Choose the formula from the angle pattern before doing any arithmetic.

    Double angle

    sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ
    cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ = 2cos²θ - 1 = 1 - 2sin²θ
    tan 2θ = 2 tan θ / (1 - tan²θ)

    The three versions of cos 2θ are all correct. Pick whichever one matches what you already know.

    Worked examples — advanced identities

    Example 1 — exact value from a difference formula

    Find cos 15° exactly.

    15° is not on the unit circle, but 45° - 30° is. cos(45° - 30°) = cos45 cos30 + sin45 sin30 (difference → PLUS in the middle for cosine) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) Multiply each pair, top × top and bottom × bottom: (√2 · √3)/(2 · 2) = √6/4 (√2 · 1)/(2 · 2) = √2/4 = √6/4 + √2/4 = (√6 + √2)/4 ← same denominator, add the tops
    Example 2 — double angle from a given ratio

    If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is in Quadrant I, find sin 2θ and cos 2θ.

    Find cos θ first. 3-4-5 triangle, QI so everything is positive. cos θ = 4/5 sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25 cos 2θ = 1 - 2sin²θ = 1 - 2(9/25) = 1 - 18/25 = 7/25
    Example 3 — tangent of a sum

    Find tan 105° exactly.

    105° = 60° + 45° tan(60° + 45°) = (tan 60° + tan 45°)/(1 - tan 60° tan 45°) = (√3 + 1)/(1 - √3) Rationalize: multiply top and bottom by (1 + √3). numerator: (√3 + 1)(1 + √3) = √3 + 3 + 1 + √3 = 4 + 2√3 denominator: (1 - √3)(1 + √3) = 1 - 3 = -2 tan 105° = (4 + 2√3)/(-2) = 4/(-2) + 2√3/(-2) ← divide EACH term by -2 = -2 - √3

    Sign check: 105° is in Quadrant II, where tangent is negative. -2 - √3 ≈ -3.73. ✓

    Example 4 — a sum formula from two given ratios

    If sin α = 3/5 with α in Quadrant I and cos β = -5/13 with β in Quadrant II, find sin(α + β) and cos(α + β).

    Fill in the missing ratios first, with quadrant signs. α: 3-4-5 triangle, QI → cos α = 4/5 β: 5-12-13 triangle, QII → sin β = 12/13 (sine positive in QII) sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β = (3/5)(-5/13) + (4/5)(12/13) = -15/65 + 48/65 = 33/65 cos(α + β) = cos α cos β - sin α sin β = (4/5)(-5/13) - (3/5)(12/13) = -20/65 - 36/65 = -56/65

    Check: 33² + 56² = 1089 + 3136 = 4225 = 65², so the pair sits on the unit circle. Sine positive, cosine negative puts α + β in Quadrant II.

    Example 5 — verifying with a double-angle formula

    Verify sin 2θ/(1 + cos 2θ) = tan θ.

    Pick the cos 2θ version that kills the 1: cos 2θ = 2cos²θ - 1 sin 2θ 2 sin θ cos θ 2 sin θ cos θ ---------- = ------------------ = ------------- = sin θ/cos θ = tan θ ✓ 1 + cos 2θ 1 + 2cos²θ - 1 2cos²θ

    Half-angle formulas

    sin(θ/2) = ±√[(1 - cos θ)/2]
    cos(θ/2) = ±√[(1 + cos θ)/2]
    tan(θ/2) = (1 - cos θ)/sin θ = sin θ/(1 + cos θ)
    The ± is decided by the quadrant of θ/2, not θ. Compute the half angle first, see which quadrant it lands in, then pick the sign. The two tangent versions carry their own sign automatically, so they need no ±.
    Memory hook. Sine goes with minus, cosine goes with plus. Both sit over 2, both under a radical.
    Example 1 — an exact value off the unit circle

    Find cos(22.5°) exactly.

    22.5° is half of 45°, which IS on the unit circle. θ = 45°, θ/2 = 22.5° Quadrant of 22.5°: Quadrant I → cosine POSITIVE → use + cos(22.5°) = +√[(1 + cos45°)/2] = √[(1 + √2/2)/2] Clean up the nested fraction. Top: write 1 as 2/2 1 + √2/2 = 2/2 + √2/2 = (2 + √2)/2 Divide by 2: ((2 + √2)/2) ÷ 2 = (2 + √2)/4 = √[(2 + √2)/4] Root of top over root of bottom, √4 = 2: = √(2 + √2)/√4 = √(2 + √2)/2
    Example 2 — where the sign is negative

    If cos θ = 3/5 and θ is in Quadrant IV, find sin(θ/2).

    Locate θ: Quadrant IV means 270° < θ < 360°. Halve that range: 135° < θ/2 < 180° → θ/2 is in Quadrant II In Q2, sine is POSITIVE, so take the + root: sin(θ/2) = +√[(1 - 3/5)/2] = √[(2/5)/2] = √(1/5) = 1/√5 = √5/5 Now the contrast: find cos(θ/2) for the same θ. θ/2 is in Q2, where cosine is NEGATIVE. cos(θ/2) = -√[(1 + 3/5)/2] = -√[(8/5)/2] = -√(4/5) = -2/√5 = -2√5/5
    Halving the interval is the step people skip. θ in Quadrant IV does not put θ/2 in Quadrant IV. Divide the angle bounds by 2 and see where you land.

    Product-to-sum and sum-to-product

    Product to sum
    sin A cos B = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)]
    cos A sin B = (1/2)[sin(A + B) - sin(A - B)]
    cos A cos B = (1/2)[cos(A - B) + cos(A + B)]
    sin A sin B = (1/2)[cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)]
    Sum to product
    sin A + sin B = 2 sin[(A+B)/2] cos[(A-B)/2]
    sin A - sin B = 2 cos[(A+B)/2] sin[(A-B)/2]
    cos A + cos B = 2 cos[(A+B)/2] cos[(A-B)/2]
    cos A - cos B = -2 sin[(A+B)/2] sin[(A-B)/2]
    When to reach for these. Product to sum when you are stuck with two trig functions multiplied together. Sum to product when an equation has a sum of two trig terms set to zero, because factoring it is what lets you solve it.
    Example 1 — product to sum

    Write sin(5x)cos(3x) as a sum.

    Pattern: sin A cos B = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)] A = 5x, B = 3x A + B = 8x A - B = 2x sin(5x)cos(3x) = (1/2)[sin(8x) + sin(2x)]
    Example 2 — sum to product, used to solve an equation

    Solve cos(3x) + cos(x) = 0 on [0, 2π).

    Pattern: cos A + cos B = 2 cos[(A+B)/2] cos[(A-B)/2] A = 3x, B = x (A+B)/2 = 4x/2 = 2x (A-B)/2 = 2x/2 = x cos(3x) + cos(x) = 2 cos(2x) cos(x) = 0 Now it FACTORS, so set each piece to zero. cos(2x) = 0 2x runs over [0, 4π), and cosine is 0 at π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2 x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4 cos(x) = 0 x = π/2, 3π/2 Answer: π/4, π/2, 3π/4, 5π/4, 3π/2, 7π/4
    This is the whole point of sum-to-product. A sum set to zero tells you nothing. A product set to zero lets you use the zero-product property, exactly as in Quadratics.

    Practice set — half-angle and product formulas

    1. sin(15°) exactly, using a half-angle formula
    2. tan(22.5°) exactly
    3. cos θ = -7/25, θ in QII. Find cos(θ/2).
    4. sin θ = 4/5, θ in QI. Find sin(θ/2).
    5. Write cos(7x)cos(2x) as a sum
    6. Write sin(6x) - sin(4x) as a product
    7. Solve sin(3x) + sin(x) = 0 on [0, 2π)
    Answers

    1. 15° is half of 30°, Q1 so positive: √[(1 - √3/2)/2] = √(2 - √3)/2

    15° = 30°/2, in QI → + sin(θ/2) = √[(1 - cos θ)/2], cos 30° = √3/2 √[(1 - √3/2)/2] Top: 1 - √3/2 = 2/2 - √3/2 = (2 - √3)/2 ÷ 2: (2 - √3)/4 √[(2 - √3)/4] = √(2 - √3)/√4 = √(2 - √3)/2

    2. tan(22.5°) = (1 - cos45°)/sin45° = (1 - √2/2)/(√2/2) = 2/√2 - 1 = √2 - 1

    tan(θ/2) = (1 - cos θ)/sin θ with θ = 45° (1 - √2/2)/(√2/2) × 2/2: (2 - √2)/√2 Split: 2/√2 - √2/√2 = √2 - 1 (2/√2 = √2)

    3. θ in QII means 90° < θ < 180°, so 45° < θ/2 < 90°, Q1, cosine positive: +√[(1 + (-7/25))/2] = √[(18/25)/2] = √(9/25) = 3/5

    θ in QII: 90° < θ < 180° Halve: 45° < θ/2 < 90° → QI → cosine + cos(θ/2) = √[(1 + cos θ)/2] = √[(1 - 7/25)/2] = √[(18/25)/2] = √(9/25) = 3/5

    4. sin θ = 4/5 in Q1 → cos θ = 3/5. θ/2 is in Q1: √[(1 - 3/5)/2] = √(1/5) = √5/5

    sin θ = 4/5, QI → 3-4-5 → cos θ = 3/5 θ/2 also QI → + sin(θ/2) = √[(1 - 3/5)/2] = √[(2/5)/2] = √(1/5) = 1/√5 = √5/5

    5. (1/2)[cos(5x) + cos(9x)]

    cos A cos B = (1/2)[cos(A - B) + cos(A + B)] A = 7x, B = 2x: A - B = 5x, A + B = 9x (1/2)[cos(5x) + cos(9x)]

    6. 2 cos(5x) sin(x)

    sin A - sin B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) sin((A - B)/2) A = 6x, B = 4x: (A + B)/2 = 5x, (A - B)/2 = x 2 cos(5x) sin(x)

    7. 2 sin(2x) cos(x) = 0. sin(2x) = 0 → x = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2; cos(x) = 0 → x = π/2, 3π/2. Combined: 0, π/2, π, 3π/2

    sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2) A = 3x, B = x → 2 sin(2x) cos(x) = 0 sin(2x) = 0: 2x in [0, 4π) → 2x = 0, π, 2π, 3π x = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 cos(x) = 0: x = π/2, 3π/2 Combined: 0, π/2, π, 3π/2

    Quick check — identities

    1. Simplify cot θ sec θ
    2. Simplify 1 - sin²θ
    3. sin(-θ)cos(-θ) in terms of positive angles
    4. cos²θ - sin²θ as a single function
    Answers

    1. (cos/sin)(1/cos) = 1/sin = csc θ

    cot θ sec θ = (cos θ/sin θ)(1/cos θ) = 1/sin θ = csc θ

    2. cos²θ

    sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 → 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ

    3. (-sin θ)(cos θ) = -sin θ cos θ

    sin(-θ) = -sin θ (odd), cos(-θ) = cos θ (even) (-sin θ)(cos θ) = -sin θ cos θ

    4. cos 2θ

    Double angle: cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ → cos 2θ

    Practice set — identities

    1. Verify tan θ cos θ = sin θ
    2. Verify (sec²θ - 1)/sec²θ = sin²θ
    3. Simplify csc θ tan θ
    4. Verify 1/(1 + cos θ) + 1/(1 - cos θ) = 2csc²θ
    5. Find sin 75° exactly
    6. If cos θ = -8/17 in QII, find sin 2θ
    Answers

    1. (sin/cos)(cos) = sin θ

    tan θ cos θ = (sin θ/cos θ) · cos θ = sin θ ✓

    2. sec² - 1 = tan²; tan²/sec² = (sin²/cos²)(cos²/1) = sin²θ

    sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ tan²θ/sec²θ = (sin²θ/cos²θ) ÷ (1/cos²θ) = (sin²θ/cos²θ)(cos²θ/1) = sin²θ ✓

    3. (1/sin)(sin/cos) = 1/cos = sec θ

    csc θ tan θ = (1/sin θ)(sin θ/cos θ) = 1/cos θ = sec θ

    4. Numerator 2, denominator 1 - cos² = sin² → 2/sin² = 2csc²θ

    Common denominator (1 + cos θ)(1 - cos θ) = 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ Top: (1 - cos θ) + (1 + cos θ) = 2 2/sin²θ = 2csc²θ ✓

    5. sin(45 + 30) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4

    sin(45° + 30°) = sin 45° cos 30° + cos 45° sin 30° = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = √6/4 + √2/4 = (√6 + √2)/4

    6. QII so sine positive: sin θ = 15/17. sin 2θ = 2(15/17)(-8/17) = -240/289

    cos θ = -8/17, QII → sine positive sin θ = √(1 - 64/289) = √(225/289) = 15/17 sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ = 2(15/17)(-8/17) = -240/289

    Quiz 3

    CoverageSections 9–10
    FocusFoundational trig identities, identity verification, sum/difference formulas, double-angle and half-angle formulas, and product-to-sum.
    Directions: Work without notes if you can. Show the identity or formula you use. Give exact answers unless a decimal approximation is specifically requested.

    Quiz 3 — 8 questions

    1. Simplify tan θ csc θ
    2. Simplify (1 - cos²θ) csc θ
    3. Verify (sec θ - cos θ)/sec θ = sin²θ
    4. Verify cos θ/(1 + sin θ) = (1 - sin θ)/cos θ
    5. Find cos 105° exactly.
    6. If sin θ = -5/13 with θ in Quadrant IV, find sin 2θ and cos 2θ.
    7. If cos θ = -1/8 with π < θ < 3π/2, find sin(θ/2) exactly.
    8. Write sin(4x) sin(2x) as a sum or difference.
    Quiz 3 answer key + worked solutions
    1. (sin θ/cos θ)(1/sin θ) = 1/cos θ = sec θ
      tan θ csc θ = (sin θ/cos θ)(1/sin θ) = 1/cos θ = sec θ
    2. sin²θ · (1/sin θ) = sin θ
      1 - cos²θ = sin²θ sin²θ · csc θ = sin²θ · (1/sin θ) = sin θ
    3. Split the fraction: sec θ/sec θ - cos θ/sec θ = 1 - cos θ · cos θ = 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ
      Split the fraction: sec θ/sec θ - cos θ/sec θ = 1 - cos θ · cos θ (÷ sec θ is × cos θ) = 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ ✓
    4. Multiply the left by (1 - sin θ)/(1 - sin θ): cos θ(1 - sin θ)/(1 - sin²θ) = cos θ(1 - sin θ)/cos²θ = (1 - sin θ)/cos θ
      Left × (1 - sin θ)/(1 - sin θ): cos θ(1 - sin θ)/[(1 + sin θ)(1 - sin θ)] = cos θ(1 - sin θ)/(1 - sin²θ) = cos θ(1 - sin θ)/cos²θ = (1 - sin θ)/cos θ ✓
    5. cos(60° + 45°) = cos 60° cos 45° - sin 60° sin 45° = √2/4 - √6/4 = (√2 - √6)/4
      105° = 60° + 45° cos(a + b) = cos a cos b - sin a sin b = (1/2)(√2/2) - (√3/2)(√2/2) = √2/4 - √6/4 = (√2 - √6)/4
    6. cos θ = 12/13 (positive in QIV). sin 2θ = 2(-5/13)(12/13) = -120/169; cos 2θ = 1 - 2(25/169) = 119/169
      sin θ = -5/13, QIV → cosine positive cos θ = √(1 - 25/169) = √(144/169) = 12/13 sin 2θ = 2(-5/13)(12/13) = -120/169 cos 2θ = 1 - 2sin²θ = 1 - 2(25/169) = 1 - 50/169 = 119/169
    7. π/2 < θ/2 < 3π/4, Quadrant II, sine positive. √[(1 - (-1/8))/2] = √[(9/8)/2] = √(9/16) = 3/4
      π < θ < 3π/2 → halve → π/2 < θ/2 < 3π/4 → QII → sine + sin(θ/2) = √[(1 - cos θ)/2] = √[(1 - (-1/8))/2] = √[(9/8)/2] = √(9/16) = 3/4
    8. sin A sin B = (1/2)[cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)] → (1/2)[cos(2x) - cos(6x)]
      sin A sin B = (1/2)[cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)] A = 4x, B = 2x: A - B = 2x, A + B = 6x (1/2)[cos(2x) - cos(6x)]

    Section 11 — Trig Equations

    Skills to know firstUnit circleInverse trigFactoringSections 9–10 identities

    Solving trig equations

    If sinx=12 on 0≤x<2π:

    1. reference angle is π/6
    2. sine is positive in Quadrants I and II
    3. solutions are π/6 and 5π/6
    Inverse trig on your calculator may return only one principal angle. You must use quadrants/unit circle to find all required solutions.
    Fast trig-equation recognition. Isolate one trig function first. If the equation looks quadratic in sin x, cos x, or tan x, temporarily set that trig function equal to u, factor/solve the quadratic, then substitute back. If the angle is 2x, 3x, etc., expand the target interval for the inside angle before finding solutions, then divide back at the end.

    Worked examples — trig equations

    Example 1 — a basic trig equation

    Solve 2 cos x + 1 = 0 on [0, 2π).

    Isolate the trig function first, exactly like a linear equation. 2 cos x = -1 cos x = -1/2 Reference angle: where does cosine equal +1/2? At π/3. Cosine is NEGATIVE in Quadrants II and III. QII: π - π/3 = 2π/3 QIII: π + π/3 = 4π/3 Answer: x = 2π/3, 4π/3
    Your calculator returns one angle. cos⁻¹(-0.5) gives 2π/3 and stops. The second solution has to come from the quadrant reasoning.
    Example 2 — a quadratic in disguise

    Solve 2sin²x - sin x - 1 = 0 on [0, 2π).

    Let u = sin x. The equation becomes 2u² - u - 1 = 0. ac = -2, add to -1 → -2 and 1 2u² - 2u + u - 1 2u(u - 1) + 1(u - 1) (2u + 1)(u - 1) = 0 u = -1/2 or u = 1 Substitute back: sin x = -1/2 reference π/6, sine negative in QIII and QIV QIII: π + π/6 = 7π/6 QIV: 2π - π/6 = 11π/6 sin x = 1 x = π/2 (only one place on [0, 2π)) Answer: x = π/2, 7π/6, 11π/6
    Example 3 — a multiple angle

    Solve sin(2x) = √3/2 on [0, 2π).

    Careful: if x runs over [0, 2π), then 2x runs over [0, 4π). You must find ALL solutions in the wider interval, then divide. sin(angle) = √3/2 → reference π/3, sine positive in QI and QII In [0, 2π): 2x = π/3, 2π/3 Add 2π for the second lap: In [2π, 4π): 2x = π/3 + 2π = 7π/3, 2π/3 + 2π = 8π/3 Now divide every one by 2: x = π/6, π/3, 7π/6, 4π/3
    Count your answers. A 2x problem on [0, 2π) usually has twice as many solutions as the same problem with plain x. If you only found two, you stopped early.
    Example 4 — general solution (all real numbers)

    Solve tan x = 1 for all x.

    Tangent equals 1 at π/4, and tangent repeats every π (not 2π). x = π/4 + πn, where n is any integer

    Sine and cosine problems use + 2πn. Tangent and cotangent use + πn, because their period is π.

    Equations that need factoring or an identity

    Never divide both sides by a trig function. Dividing by sin x throws away every solution where sin x = 0. Move everything to one side and factor instead.
    Example 5 — common factor

    Solve 2 sin x cos x = sin x on [0, 2π).

    Move everything left, then factor out sin x: 2 sin x cos x - sin x = 0 sin x (2cos x - 1) = 0 sin x = 0 sine is the y-coordinate; y = 0 on the x-axis → x = 0, π 2cos x - 1 = 0 2cos x = 1 → cos x = 1/2 reference π/3, cosine positive in QI and QIV QI: π/3 QIV: 2π - π/3 = 5π/3 Answer: x = 0, π/3, π, 5π/3

    Dividing by sin x at the start would have left only π/3 and 5π/3. Half the answer, gone.

    Example 6 — use a Pythagorean identity to get one function

    Solve 2cos²x + 3 sin x - 3 = 0 on [0, 2π).

    Two different functions. Trade cos²x for sine: cos²x = 1 - sin²x 2(1 - sin²x) + 3 sin x - 3 = 0 2 - 2sin²x + 3 sin x - 3 = 0 -2sin²x + 3 sin x - 1 = 0 2sin²x - 3 sin x + 1 = 0 (multiply by -1) Let u = sin x: 2u² - 3u + 1 = 0 ac = 2 · 1 = 2, add to -3 → -2 and -1 2u² - 2u - u + 1 2u(u - 1) - 1(u - 1) (2u - 1)(u - 1) = 0 (2 sin x - 1)(sin x - 1) = 0 2 sin x - 1 = 0 → sin x = 1/2 reference π/6, sine positive in QI and QII QI: π/6 QII: π - π/6 = 5π/6 sin x - 1 = 0 → sin x = 1 top of the circle → x = π/2 Answer: x = π/6, π/2, 5π/6
    Example 7 — use a double-angle identity

    Solve cos 2x + cos x = 0 on [0, 2π).

    Pick the cos 2x version that matches the other term: cos 2x = 2cos²x - 1 2cos²x - 1 + cos x = 0 2cos²x + cos x - 1 = 0 Let u = cos x: 2u² + u - 1 = 0 ac = 2 · (-1) = -2, add to 1 → 2 and -1 2u² + 2u - u - 1 2u(u + 1) - 1(u + 1) (2u - 1)(u + 1) = 0 (2cos x - 1)(cos x + 1) = 0 2cos x - 1 = 0 → cos x = 1/2 reference π/3, cosine positive in QI and QIV QI: π/3 QIV: 2π - π/3 = 5π/3 cos x + 1 = 0 → cos x = -1 far left of the circle → x = π Answer: x = π/3, π, 5π/3
    Example 8 — squaring both sides, then checking

    Solve sin x + cos x = 1 on [0, 2π).

    No single identity applies, so square both sides. (sin x + cos x)² = 1 sin²x + 2 sin x cos x + cos²x = 1 1 + 2 sin x cos x = 1 sin x cos x = 0 sin x = 0 → x = 0, π cos x = 0 → x = π/2, 3π/2 Squaring can create false solutions. CHECK every one in the original: x = 0: 0 + 1 = 1 ✓ x = π/2: 1 + 0 = 1 ✓ x = π: 0 + (-1) = -1 ✗ x = 3π/2: -1 + 0 = -1 ✗ Answer: x = 0, π/2

    Equations with non-special values

    When the value is not on the unit circle, the calculator supplies the reference angle and you supply the quadrants. Take the inverse of the positive value to get the reference angle, then place it.

    Example 9 — degrees, sine

    Solve 5 sin θ - 2 = 0 for 0° ≤ θ < 360°. Round to the nearest hundredth.

    sin θ = 2/5 = 0.4 Reference angle: sin⁻¹(0.4) ≈ 23.58° Sine is positive in QI and QII. QI: θ ≈ 23.58° QII: θ ≈ 180° - 23.58° = 156.42°
    TI-30XIIS (DEG). 2nd SIN .4 ) ENTER → 23.57817848 180 − 2nd ENTER ENTER → 156.4218215 2nd ENTER pastes the previous answer, so no digits are lost to retyping.
    Example 10 — radians, negative tangent

    Solve 3 tan x + 4 = 0 on [0, 2π). Round to four decimals.

    tan x = -4/3 Reference angle (use the POSITIVE value): tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 0.9273 Tangent is negative in QII and QIV. QII: x ≈ π - 0.9273 ≈ 2.2143 QIV: x ≈ 2π - 0.9273 ≈ 5.3559
    The calculator answer is not in the interval. In RAD mode, tan⁻¹(-4/3) returns -0.9273. That angle is coterminal with the QIV answer, but it is negative, so it is not in [0, 2π). Use the positive reference angle and place it yourself.
    Example 11 — every solution, written generally

    Find all solutions of sin x = -√2/2.

    Reference angle π/4. Sine is negative in QIII and QIV. QIII: π + π/4 = 5π/4 QIV: 2π - π/4 = 7π/4 Sine repeats every 2π: x = 5π/4 + 2πn or x = 7π/4 + 2πn, n any integer

    Quick check — trig equations

    1. Solve sin x = 0 on [0, 2π)
    2. Solve cos x = √2/2 on [0, 2π)
    3. Solve tan x = -1 on [0, 2π)
    4. How many solutions does sin 3x = 1/2 have on [0, 2π)?
    Answers

    1. x = 0, π

    sin x is the y-coordinate; y = 0 at (1, 0) and (-1, 0) x = 0, π

    2. x = π/4, 7π/4

    Reference π/4; cosine positive in QI and QIV QI: π/4 QIV: 2π - π/4 = 7π/4

    3. x = 3π/4, 7π/4

    Reference π/4; tangent negative in QII and QIV QII: π - π/4 = 3π/4 QIV: 2π - π/4 = 7π/4

    4. 3x runs over [0, 6π): three laps with two solutions each → 6

    x in [0, 2π) → 3x in [0, 6π): three laps sin = 1/2 twice per lap (QI and QII) 3 × 2 = 6 solutions

    Practice set — trig equations

    1. Solve 2 sin x - √3 = 0 on [0, 2π)
    2. Solve tan²x - 1 = 0 on [0, 2π)
    3. Solve cos(2x) = 0 on [0, 2π)
    4. Solve 2cos²x + cos x - 1 = 0 on [0, 2π)
    5. Solve sin²x - sin x = 0 on [0, 2π)
    6. Solve 2 sin²x = 1 + cos x on [0, 2π)
    7. Solve sin 2x = cos x on [0, 2π)
    8. Solve 4 cos θ + 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ θ < 360°, to the nearest hundredth
    9. All solutions of 2 cos x + 1 = 0
    10. Solve tan(x/2) = 1 on [0, 2π)
    Answers

    1. sin x = √3/2 → π/3, 2π/3

    2 sin x = √3 → sin x = √3/2 Reference π/3; sine positive in QI and QII π/3, π - π/3 = 2π/3

    2. tan x = ±1 → π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4

    tan²x = 1 → tan x = ±1 Reference π/4 in every quadrant π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4

    3. 2x covers [0, 4π); cosine is 0 at π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2 → x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4

    2x runs over [0, 4π) cos = 0 at π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2 ÷ 2: x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4

    4. (2cos x - 1)(cos x + 1) = 0 → cos x = 1/2 gives π/3, 5π/3; cos x = -1 gives π

    u = cos x: 2u² + u - 1 = 0 ac = -2, add 1 → 2 and -1 2u² + 2u - u - 1 = 2u(u + 1) - 1(u + 1) = (2u - 1)(u + 1) cos x = 1/2 → π/3, 5π/3 cos x = -1 → π

    5. sin x(sin x - 1) = 0 → 0, π/2, π

    Factor sin x: sin x(sin x - 1) = 0 sin x = 0 → 0, π sin x = 1 → π/2

    6. 2(1 - cos²x) = 1 + cos x → 2cos²x + cos x - 1 = 0 → π/3, π, 5π/3

    sin²x = 1 - cos²x: 2(1 - cos²x) = 1 + cos x 2 - 2cos²x = 1 + cos x 0 = 2cos²x + cos x - 1 (2cos x - 1)(cos x + 1) = 0 cos x = 1/2 → π/3, 5π/3; cos x = -1 → π

    7. cos x(2 sin x - 1) = 0 → π/6, π/2, 5π/6, 3π/2

    sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x: 2 sin x cos x - cos x = 0 cos x(2 sin x - 1) = 0 cos x = 0 → π/2, 3π/2 sin x = 1/2 → π/6, 5π/6

    8. cos θ = -0.25; cos⁻¹(-0.25) ≈ 104.48° (QII) and 360° - 104.48° = 255.52° (QIII)

    4cos θ = -1 → cos θ = -0.25 Reference: cos⁻¹(0.25) ≈ 75.52° Cosine negative in QII and QIII QII: 180° - 75.52° = 104.48° QIII: 180° + 75.52° = 255.52°

    9. cos x = -1/2 → x = 2π/3 + 2πn or x = 4π/3 + 2πn

    2cos x = -1 → cos x = -1/2 Reference π/3; QII and QIII QII: π - π/3 = 2π/3 QIII: π + π/3 = 4π/3 x = 2π/3 + 2πn or x = 4π/3 + 2πn

    10. x/2 runs over [0, π), so x/2 = π/4 only → x = π/2

    x in [0, 2π) → x/2 in [0, π) tan = 1 at π/4 (next one, 5π/4, is outside) x/2 = π/4 → x = π/2

    Section 12 — Law of Sines and Cosines

    Skills to know firstRight-triangle trigAnglesInverse trigAlgebra

    Law of Sines and Law of Cosines

    Law of Sines: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
    Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C
    Area: (1/2)ab sin C
    GivenUse
    AAS or ASALaw of Sines
    SSALaw of Sines — the ambiguous case, check for a second triangle
    SASLaw of Cosines
    SSSLaw of Cosines, solved for the angle
    Triangle-law shortcut. Look at the information pattern, not the picture: ASA/AAS → Law of Sines; SAS/SSS → Law of Cosines; SSA → Law of Sines plus the ambiguous-case check. If you already have one complete opposite side-angle pair, Law of Sines is usually the shortest route.
    Example 1 — Law of Sines (AAS)

    A = 40°, B = 75°, a = 12. Find b.

    a/sin A = b/sin B 12/sin 40° = b/sin 75° b = 12 sin 75° / sin 40° b ≈ 12(0.96593)/(0.64279) b ≈ 18.03
    Example 2 — Law of Cosines (SAS)

    a = 8, b = 11, C = 37°. Find c and the area.

    c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C = 64 + 121 - 2(8)(11)cos 37° = 185 - 176(0.79864) = 185 - 140.56 = 44.44 c ≈ 6.67 Area = (1/2)(8)(11) sin 37° = 44(0.60182) ≈ 26.48
    TI-30XIIS. Set DRG to DEG. 185 − 176 × COS 37 ) ENTER → 44.4396... 2nd x² 2nd ENTER ) ENTER Here 2nd ENTER inserts Ans, the most recently calculated result, inside the square-root function.

    The ambiguous case (SSA)

    Two sides and a non-included angle can describe zero, one, or two triangles. Every other configuration gives exactly one. This is the only setup where you must check for a second answer.
    1Use the Law of Sines to find the second angle, call it B.
    2If sin B > 1, no triangle exists. Stop.
    3Otherwise compute B₁ = sin⁻¹(...) and the supplement B₂ = 180° - B₁.
    4Test each: if A + B ≥ 180°, that option is impossible. Keep whichever survive.
    Example 1 — two triangles

    a = 8, b = 11, A = 40°. Solve the triangle.

    Law of Sines: sin B / b = sin A / a sin B = b sin A / a = 11 sin40° / 8 = 11(0.642788)/8 = 0.883833 B₁ = sin⁻¹(0.883833) ≈ 62.1° B₂ = 180 - 62.1 = 117.9° Test both against A = 40°: 40 + 62.1 = 102.1 < 180 ✓ valid 40 + 117.9 = 157.9 < 180 ✓ also valid TWO triangles. Triangle 1: C = 180 - 102.1 = 77.9° c = a sinC/sinA = 8(0.977736)/0.642788 ≈ 12.17 Triangle 2: C = 180 - 157.9 = 22.1° c = 8(0.376212)/0.642788 ≈ 4.68
    Your calculator only ever returns B₁. sin⁻¹ lives in [-90°, 90°], so the obtuse option never appears. You have to write down the supplement yourself and test it.
    Example 2 — no triangle

    a = 4, b = 15, A = 50°.

    sin B = 15 sin50° / 4 = 15(0.766044)/4 = 2.8727 Sine can never exceed 1. NO TRIANGLE EXISTS. Side a is too short to reach across.
    Count the triangles before you compute. With A acute and h = b sin A (the height from C): a < h → none; a = h → one right triangle; h < a < b → two; a ≥ b → one. If A is obtuse: a ≤ b → none; a > b → one.
    Example 3 — exactly one triangle

    a = 10, b = 6, A = 42°. Solve the triangle.

    Quick count: a = 10 ≥ b = 6, so exactly one triangle. Confirm anyway: sin B = 6 sin 42°/10 ≈ 6(0.669131)/10 ≈ 0.401478 B₁ ≈ 23.67° B₂ ≈ 180° - 23.67° = 156.33° but 42° + 156.33° > 180° ✗ One triangle: C = 180° - 42° - 23.67° = 114.33° c = a sin C/sin A ≈ 10(0.911)/0.669131 ≈ 13.62

    SSS: finding angles, and Heron's formula

    With three sides and no angles, solve the Law of Cosines for the cosine of an angle:

    cos C = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab)
    Find the largest angle first (it is opposite the longest side). If any angle is obtuse, that is the one. Once it is known, the other two must be acute, so nothing downstream can be ambiguous.
    Example 4 — solve an SSS triangle

    a = 7, b = 9, c = 12. Find all three angles.

    Largest side is c = 12, so find C first. cos C = (7² + 9² - 12²)/(2 · 7 · 9) = (49 + 81 - 144)/126 = -14/126 ≈ -0.111111 C ≈ 96.38° ← negative cosine, obtuse angle Next angle, Law of Cosines again (no ambiguity possible): cos A = (9² + 12² - 7²)/(2 · 9 · 12) = (81 + 144 - 49)/216 = 176/216 ≈ 0.814815 A ≈ 35.43° Last angle: B ≈ 180° - 96.38° - 35.43° = 48.19°
    TI-30XIIS (DEG). 2nd COS ( 7 x² + 9 x² − 12 x² ) ÷ ( 2 × 7 × 9 ) ) ENTER → 96.37937021 Wrap the whole numerator and the whole denominator in their own parentheses.

    Heron's formula gives the area straight from three sides. With the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c)/2:

    Area = √[s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)]
    Example 5 — Heron's formula, with a check

    Find the area of the triangle with sides 7, 9, and 12.

    s = (7 + 9 + 12)/2 = 14 Area = √[14(14 - 7)(14 - 9)(14 - 12)] = √[14 · 7 · 5 · 2] = √980 ← 14·7 = 98, 98·5 = 490, 490·2 = 980 = √(196 · 5) ← biggest perfect square in 980 is 196 = 14² = √196 · √5 = 14√5 ≈ 31.30 square units Check with the angle from Example 4: (1/2)ab sin C = (1/2)(7)(9) sin 96.38° ≈ 31.5(0.99381) ≈ 31.30 ✓

    Applications

    Example 6 — locating a fire (ASA)

    Two ranger towers are 18 miles apart. From tower A the angle between the line to tower B and the line to a fire is 47°; from tower B it is 62°. How far is the fire from tower A?

    Angles at A and B are known, so the angle at the fire F is F = 180° - 47° - 62° = 71° The side AB = 18 is opposite F. The side AF is opposite B = 62°. AF/sin 62° = 18/sin 71° AF = 18 sin 62°/sin 71° ≈ 18(0.882948)/0.945519 ≈ 16.81 miles
    Example 7 — distance between two boats (SAS)

    Two boats leave the same dock. One travels 14 miles and the other 20 miles, and the angle between their courses is 108°. How far apart are they?

    Two sides and the angle between them → Law of Cosines. d² = 14² + 20² - 2(14)(20)cos 108° = 196 + 400 - 560(-0.309017) = 596 + 173.05 = 769.05 d ≈ 27.73 miles

    An obtuse angle has a negative cosine, so the subtraction turns into addition. The third side comes out longer than either given side, as it should.

    Quick check — oblique triangles

    1. You know two sides and the angle between them. Which law?
    2. You know A, B, and a. Which law?
    3. a = 5, b = 8, A = 30°. How many triangles?
    4. Area of a triangle with a = 6, b = 10, C = 150°
    Answers

    1. Law of Cosines (SAS)

    Two sides and the included angle = SAS → Law of Cosines

    2. Law of Sines (AAS)

    Two angles and a side not between them = AAS → Law of Sines

    3. h = 8 sin 30° = 4, and 4 < 5 < 8 → two triangles

    SSA: height h = b sin A = 8 sin 30° = 8(1/2) = 4 Compare: h < a < b → 4 < 5 < 8 → two triangles

    4. (1/2)(6)(10) sin 150° = 30(1/2) = 15 square units

    K = (1/2)ab sin C = (1/2)(6)(10) sin 150° sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2 K = 30(1/2) = 15 square units

    Practice set — oblique triangles

    1. A = 35°, C = 80°, b = 15. Solve the triangle.
    2. a = 11, c = 15, B = 52°. Find b.
    3. a = 5, b = 7, c = 10. Find the largest angle.
    4. Area of the triangle with sides 8, 11, and 13 (Heron).
    5. a = 9, b = 12, A = 40°. How many triangles? Solve each.
    6. a = 3, b = 8, A = 25°. How many triangles?
    7. A parallelogram has sides 12 and 18 with a 65° angle. Find the length of the longer diagonal.
    Answers

    1. B = 65°; a = 15 sin 35°/sin 65° ≈ 9.49; c = 15 sin 80°/sin 65° ≈ 16.30

    B = 180° - 35° - 80° = 65° a/sin A = b/sin B: a = 15 sin 35°/sin 65° ≈ 15(0.573576)/0.906308 ≈ 9.49 c = 15 sin 80°/sin 65° ≈ 15(0.984808)/0.906308 ≈ 16.30

    2. b² = 121 + 225 - 330 cos 52° ≈ 142.83 → b ≈ 11.95

    b² = a² + c² - 2ac cos B = 121 + 225 - 2(11)(15)cos 52° = 346 - 330(0.615661) ≈ 346 - 203.17 = 142.83 b ≈ √142.83 ≈ 11.95

    3. cos C = (25 + 49 - 100)/70 ≈ -0.371429 → C ≈ 111.80°

    Largest angle is across from the longest side, c = 10 cos C = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab) = (25 + 49 - 100)/(2·5·7) = -26/70 ≈ -0.371429 C ≈ 111.80°

    4. s = 16; √[16 · 8 · 5 · 3] = √1920 = 8√30 ≈ 43.82 square units

    s = (8 + 11 + 13)/2 = 16 Area = √[16(16 - 8)(16 - 11)(16 - 13)] = √(16 · 8 · 5 · 3) = √1920 = √(64 · 30) = 8√30 ≈ 43.82 square units

    5. h = 12 sin 40° ≈ 7.71 < 9 < 12 → two. sin B ≈ 0.857050. Triangle 1: B ≈ 58.99°, C ≈ 81.01°, c ≈ 13.83. Triangle 2: B ≈ 121.01°, C ≈ 18.99°, c ≈ 4.56

    h = 12 sin 40° ≈ 7.71; 7.71 < 9 < 12 → two triangles sin B = 12 sin 40°/9 ≈ 0.857050 Triangle 1: B ≈ 58.99° C = 180° - 40° - 58.99° = 81.01° c = 9 sin 81.01°/sin 40° ≈ 13.83 Triangle 2: B ≈ 180° - 58.99° = 121.01° C = 180° - 40° - 121.01° = 18.99° c = 9 sin 18.99°/sin 40° ≈ 4.56

    6. h = 8 sin 25° ≈ 3.38 > 3 → no triangle

    h = 8 sin 25° ≈ 8(0.422618) ≈ 3.38 a = 3 < h → side a cannot reach → no triangle (check: sin B = 8 sin 25°/3 ≈ 1.13 > 1)

    7. The longer diagonal is opposite the 115° angle: d² = 144 + 324 - 432 cos 115° ≈ 650.57 → d ≈ 25.51

    Adjacent angles in a parallelogram add to 180°: 180° - 65° = 115° The longer diagonal sits across from the 115° angle d² = 12² + 18² - 2(12)(18)cos 115° = 144 + 324 - 432(-0.422618) = 468 + 182.57 = 650.57 d ≈ 25.51

    Test 3 Study Guide

    CoverageSections 9–12
    GoalRecognize whether the problem calls for an identity, an identity formula, a trig-equation strategy, or a triangle law.

    Know how to

    Section 9 — Trig Identities — Part 1




    Section 10 — Trig Identities — Part 2





    Section 11 — Trig Equations




    Section 12 — Law of Sines and Cosines





    Must-know formulas and rules

    Core identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ; tanθ = sinθ/cosθ
    Sum/difference: sin(A±B)=sinA cosB ± cosA sinB; cos(A±B)=cosA cosB ∓ sinA sinB
    Double angle: sin2θ=2sinθcosθ; cos2θ=cos²θ-sin²θ=2cos²θ-1=1-2sin²θ
    Half angle: sin(θ/2)=±√((1-cosθ)/2); cos(θ/2)=±√((1+cosθ)/2)
    Law of Sines: a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC
    Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cosC;   Area: K=(1/2)ab sinC

    Common mistakes

    Do not work both sides of an identity at once. Usually simplify one side until it matches the other.
    Watch the cosine sign. In cos(A±B), the middle sign flips.
    Half-angle signs come from the quadrant of θ/2. The radical itself does not decide the sign.
    Inverse trig gives one principal angle, not every equation solution. Use the interval and quadrant signs to finish.
    For cos(2x) and similar equations, solve for the inside angle first and account for the full required interval.
    SSA is not finished after the calculator returns one angle. Test 180° - B₁ when it is possible.

    Calculator reminders

    • Identity and exact-value work should stay exact unless a decimal is requested.
    • For triangle laws, confirm DEG mode before using SIN, COS, or inverse trig with degree angles.
    • Inverse trig returns only a principal angle; write the supplement yourself for SSA and use quadrant reasoning for trig equations.
    • Carry several decimal places through triangle calculations and round only the final requested result.

    Test 3 answer key + worked solutions
    1. tan²θ cos²θ = (sin²θ/cos²θ)cos²θ = sin²θ
      sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ tan²θ cos²θ = (sin²θ/cos²θ)cos²θ = sin²θ
    2. sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
      ÷ csc θ is × sin θ; ÷ sec θ is × cos θ sin θ · sin θ + cos θ · cos θ = sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
    3. sec²θ/tan²θ = (1/cos²θ)(cos²θ/sin²θ) = 1/sin²θ = csc²θ
      1 + tan²θ = sec²θ sec²θ/tan²θ = (1/cos²θ) ÷ (sin²θ/cos²θ) = (1/cos²θ)(cos²θ/sin²θ) = 1/sin²θ = csc²θ ✓
    4. Common denominator: [(1 - sin θ)² + cos²θ]/[cos θ(1 - sin θ)] = (2 - 2 sin θ)/[cos θ(1 - sin θ)] = 2/cos θ = 2 sec θ
      Common denominator cos θ(1 - sin θ): [(1 - sin θ)² + cos²θ] / [cos θ(1 - sin θ)] Top: 1 - 2sin θ + sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 - 2sin θ + 1 = 2(1 - sin θ) 2(1 - sin θ)/[cos θ(1 - sin θ)] = 2/cos θ = 2 sec θ ✓
    5. cos θ · (-tan θ) = -cos θ · sin θ/cos θ = -sin θ
      cos(-θ) = cos θ, tan(-θ) = -tan θ cos θ(-tan θ) = -cos θ · sin θ/cos θ = -sin θ ✓
    6. sin(45° - 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) - (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 - √2)/4
      15° = 45° - 30° sin(a - b) = sin a cos b - cos a sin b = (√2/2)(√3/2) - (√2/2)(1/2) = √6/4 - √2/4 = (√6 - √2)/4
    7. tan(45° + 30°) = (1 + √3/3)/(1 - √3/3) = (3 + √3)/(3 - √3) = (12 + 6√3)/6 = 2 + √3
      75° = 45° + 30° tan(a + b) = (tan a + tan b)/(1 - tan a tan b) = (1 + √3/3)/(1 - √3/3) × 3/3: (3 + √3)/(3 - √3) × (3 + √3)/(3 + √3): top (3 + √3)² = 9 + 6√3 + 3 = 12 + 6√3 bottom 9 - 3 = 6 (12 + 6√3)/6 = 2 + √3
    8. cos α = -3/5, sin β = 12/13. (-3/5)(5/13) + (4/5)(12/13) = -15/65 + 48/65 = 33/65
      α in QII, sin α = 4/5 → cos α = -3/5 β in QI, cos β = 5/13 → sin β = 12/13 cos(α - β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β = (-3/5)(5/13) + (4/5)(12/13) = -15/65 + 48/65 = 33/65
    9. sin θ = -3/5, cos θ = -4/5. sin 2θ = 24/25; cos 2θ = 16/25 - 9/25 = 7/25; tan 2θ = 24/7
      tan θ = 3/4 in QIII → x = -4, y = -3, r = 5 sin θ = -3/5, cos θ = -4/5 sin 2θ = 2(-3/5)(-4/5) = 24/25 cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ = 16/25 - 9/25 = 7/25 tan 2θ = (24/25)/(7/25) = 24/7
    10. (1 - cos(π/4))/sin(π/4) = (1 - √2/2)/(√2/2) = √2 - 1
      π/8 = (π/4)/2 tan(θ/2) = (1 - cos θ)/sin θ = (1 - √2/2)/(√2/2) × 2/2: (2 - √2)/√2 = 2/√2 - 1 = √2 - 1
    11. -2 sin(4x) sin(x)
      cos A - cos B = -2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((A - B)/2) A = 5x, B = 3x: (A + B)/2 = 4x, (A - B)/2 = x -2 sin(4x) sin(x)
    12. cos x = √2/2 → π/4, 7π/4
      2cos x = √2 → cos x = √2/2 Reference π/4; QI and QIV → π/4, 7π/4
    13. sin x = ±√3/2 → π/3, 2π/3, 4π/3, 5π/3
      4sin²x = 3 → sin²x = 3/4 → sin x = ±√3/2 Reference π/3 in all four quadrants π/3, 2π/3, 4π/3, 5π/3
    14. (2cos x - 1)(cos x - 1) = 0 → 0, π/3, 5π/3
      u = cos x: 2u² - 3u + 1 = 0 ac = 2, add -3 → -2 and -1 (2u - 1)(u - 1) = 0 cos x = 1/2 → π/3, 5π/3 cos x = 1 → 0 x = 0, π/3, 5π/3
    15. 2x runs over [0, 4π): 2x = π/4, 5π/4, 9π/4, 13π/4 → x = π/8, 5π/8, 9π/8, 13π/8
      x in [0, 2π) → 2x in [0, 4π) tan = 1 every π starting at π/4: 2x = π/4, 5π/4, 9π/4, 13π/4 x = π/8, 5π/8, 9π/8, 13π/8
    16. 1 - 2sin²x = sin x → (2 sin x - 1)(sin x + 1) = 0 → π/6, 5π/6, 3π/2
      cos 2x = 1 - 2sin²x: 1 - 2sin²x = sin x 0 = 2sin²x + sin x - 1 (2 sin x - 1)(sin x + 1) = 0 sin x = 1/2 → π/6, 5π/6 sin x = -1 → 3π/2
    17. cos θ = -1/3: cos⁻¹(-1/3) ≈ 109.47° and 360° - 109.47° = 250.53°
      cos θ = -1/3 Reference cos⁻¹(1/3) ≈ 70.53° QII: 180° - 70.53° = 109.47° QIII: 180° + 70.53° = 250.53°
    18. C = 65°; a = 20 sin 48°/sin 65° ≈ 16.40; b = 20 sin 67°/sin 65° ≈ 20.31
      C = 180° - 48° - 67° = 65° a = 20 sin 48°/sin 65° ≈ 20(0.743145)/0.906308 ≈ 16.40 b = 20 sin 67°/sin 65° ≈ 20(0.920505)/0.906308 ≈ 20.31
    19. cos C = (64 + 169 - 289)/208 ≈ -0.269231 → C ≈ 105.62°. Heron: s = 19, area √(19 · 11 · 6 · 2) = √2508 ≈ 50.08
      Largest angle across from c = 17 cos C = (64 + 169 - 289)/(2·8·13) = -56/208 ≈ -0.269231 C ≈ 105.62° Heron: s = (8 + 13 + 17)/2 = 19 Area = √[19(11)(6)(2)] = √2508 ≈ 50.08
    20. h = 18 sin 38° ≈ 11.08 < 14 < 18 → two. sin B ≈ 0.791565. Triangle 1: B ≈ 52.33°, C ≈ 89.67°, c ≈ 22.74. Triangle 2: B ≈ 127.67°, C ≈ 14.33°, c ≈ 5.63
      h = 18 sin 38° ≈ 11.08; 11.08 < 14 < 18 → two triangles sin B = 18 sin 38°/14 ≈ 0.791565 Triangle 1: B ≈ 52.33°, C = 180 - 38 - 52.33 = 89.67° c = 14 sin 89.67°/sin 38° ≈ 22.74 Triangle 2: B ≈ 180 - 52.33 = 127.67°, C = 180 - 38 - 127.67 = 14.33° c = 14 sin 14.33°/sin 38° ≈ 5.63

    Essential formulas

    Functions: average rate of change = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a);   composition (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x))
    Exponentials/logs: A=P(1+r/n)nt; A=Pert; log(MN)=logM+logN; log(M/N)=logM-logN; log(Mp)=p logM
    Right-triangle trig: sinθ=opp/hyp; cosθ=adj/hyp; tanθ=opp/adj
    Angles/circular measure: 180°=π rad; s=rθ; A=(1/2)r²θ; v=rω   (circular formulas use radians)
    Unit circle: (x,y)=(cosθ,sinθ); tanθ=sinθ/cosθ
    Trig graphs: y=A sin(B(x-C))+D or cosine; amplitude |A|; period 2π/|B|; tangent/cotangent period π/|B|
    Inverse-trig principal ranges: arcsin [-π/2,π/2]; arccos [0,π]; arctan (-π/2,π/2)
    Core identities: sin²θ+cos²θ=1; 1+tan²θ=sec²θ; 1+cot²θ=csc²θ; tanθ=sinθ/cosθ
    Advanced identities: know the sine/cosine sum-difference, double-angle, half-angle, and product/sum formulas from Sections 9–10.
    Triangle laws: a/sinA=b/sinB=c/sinC; c²=a²+b²-2ab cosC; area K=(1/2)ab sinC

    Common mistakes

    Domain restrictions survive the whole problem. Denominators cannot be zero, radical inputs must fit the problem, and logarithm inputs must be positive.
    Inverse is not reciprocal. f⁻¹ reverses a function; sin⁻¹ is arcsine; csc is the reciprocal of sine.
    Factor before classifying rational-function discontinuities. Canceled denominator factors create holes; uncanceled zeros create vertical asymptotes.
    Check DEG/RAD before trig calculations. Use radians in circular-measure formulas and when a graph/equation is stated in radians.
    Reference angles do not determine the sign. Use the quadrant after finding the reference angle.
    Do not decimalize exact trig values early. Keep values such as √3/2 exact unless a decimal is requested.
    For identities, transform one side. For equations, an inverse-trig result is only a starting angle—finish the interval and quadrant work.
    SSA needs a second-angle check. One inverse-sine result does not automatically mean there is only one triangle.

    Calculator reminders

    • Use full parentheses around numerators, denominators, exponents, and inverse-trig inputs.
    • Use log or ln consistently for exponential equations; with e-based models, ln is usually the cleanest choice.
    • Check DEG or RAD before every trig block of work.
    • Use inverse SIN/COS/TAN to get an angle, then use quadrant/interval reasoning when more than one solution is possible.
    • Keep extra calculator digits until the final rounding step.

    29. 7-24-25 triangle, Q1 → 24/25
      θ = sin⁻¹(7/25): sin θ = 7/25, positive → QI opp 7, hyp 25, adj = √(625 - 49) = √576 = 24 cos θ = 24/25
    30. (x-5)(x+5)/[(x-5)(x+2)] = (x+5)/(x+2), x ≠ 5. Hole at (5, 10/7); VA x = -2; HA y = 1; x-int (-5, 0); y-int (0, 5/2)
      Top (x - 5)(x + 5); bottom (x - 5)(x + 2) Cancel (x - 5): (x + 5)/(x + 2), x ≠ 5 Hole: (5 + 5)/(5 + 2) = 10/7 → (5, 10/7) VA x = -2 Degrees equal 1/1 → HA y = 1 x-int: x + 5 = 0 → (-5, 0) y-int: 5/2 → (0, 5/2)
    31. QII so sine positive: sin θ = 15/17. sin 2θ = 2(15/17)(-8/17) = -240/289
      cos θ = -8/17, QII → sine positive sin θ = √(1 - 64/289) = √(225/289) = 15/17 sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ = 2(15/17)(-8/17) = -240/289

      2x runs over [0, 4π) cos = 0 at π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2 ÷ 2: x = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4
