    How the columns connect: csc = 1/sin • sec = 1/cos • cot = 1/tan = cos/sin.

    Rationalize, e.g. csc 60° = 1/sin 60°: 1/(√3/2) = 1 · 2/√3 dividing by a fraction → multiply by its flip = 2/√3 = 2/√3 · √3/√3 multiply top and bottom by √3 = 2√3/(√3·√3) = 2√3/3 √3·√3 = 3

    "undefined" appears wherever the denominator is 0. tan and sec are undefined where cos θ = 0 (90°, 270°). cot and csc are undefined where sin θ = 0 (0°, 180°, 360°).

    Signs: each row is the Quadrant I row with the ASTC signs applied. 150° uses the 30° values, and only sin and csc stay positive.

    6. Trig on the xy-plane

    For a point (x, y) at distance r = √(x² + y²) from the origin:

    FunctionUnit circle (r = 1)x / y / rUndefined
    sin θyy/r
    cos θxx/r
    tan θy/xy/xπ/2, 3π/2
    sec θ1/xr/xπ/2, 3π/2
    cot θx/yx/yπ, 2π
    csc θ1/yr/yπ, 2π
    • Why undefined: tan and sec divide by x, and x = 0 at π/2 and 3π/2 (the top and bottom of the circle). cot and csc divide by y, and y = 0 at π and 2π (2π is the same point as 0).
    • r is always positive. The signs of x and y set the quadrant.

    Typical problem: given sin θ = 3/5 with θ in QII, find the rest.

    Step 1 Read y and r. sin θ = y/r = 3/5 y = 3, r = 5 Step 2 Find x: x² + y² = r² x² + 3² = 5² x² + 9 = 25 x² = 16 x = ±4 Step 3 QII → x is negative. x = −4 Step 4 Write every ratio. cos θ = x/r = −4/5 tan θ = y/x = 3/(−4) = −3/4 csc θ = r/y = 5/3 sec θ = r/x = −5/4 cot θ = x/y = −4/3

    7. Graphs of sine and cosine

    Form: y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D, same for cosine.

    • Amplitude = |A|. Negative A flips the graph vertically.
    • Period = 2π/|B|.
    • Phase shift = C, right if positive, left if negative.
    • Midline y = D. Range = [D − |A|, D + |A|].
    • Five key points spaced one quarter period apart.
    • Sine starts at the midline going up. Cosine starts at the maximum.

    Factor B out first. On paper, before you read the shift:

    y = sin(2x − π) Step 1 Copy just the inside. 2x − π Step 2 Write B = 2 in front of an empty parenthesis. 2( ) Step 3 Divide EACH term by 2 and write the results inside. 2x ÷ 2 = x π ÷ 2 = π/2 2(x − π/2) Step 4 Check: distribute the 2 back. 2·x − 2·(π/2) = 2x − π ✓ Step 5 Put it back in the function. y = sin(2(x − π/2)) Step 6 Match to y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D. B = 2, C = π/2 C positive → shift π/2 RIGHT (not π)

    Plus sign inside: same steps, then rewrite the plus as minus a negative.

    y = sin(3x + π) 3x ÷ 3 = x, π ÷ 3 = π/3 y = sin(3(x + π/3)) x + π/3 = x − (−π/3) C = −π/3 → shift π/3 LEFT

    Quick check: set the inside equal to 0 and solve. 2x − π = 0 → 2x = π → x = π/2. That x is the shift.

    From a graph or data: amplitude = (max − min)/2 • midline = (max + min)/2 • measure one full cycle for the period, then B = 2π/period.

    8. Graphing with an old → new table

    Example: graph y = −(3/2) cos((1/2)x) − 2 for one full cycle.

    • A = −3/2 → amplitude 3/2, and the minus reflects the graph over the midline.
    • B = 1/2 → period 2π ÷ (1/2) = 4π.
    • C = 0 → no phase shift. D = −2 → midline y = −2.
    • Range: [−2 − 3/2, −2 + 3/2] = [−7/2, −1/2].

    Rules for the table:

    • new x = parent x ÷ B = parent x ÷ (1/2) = 2 · parent x
    • new y = A · parent y + D = −(3/2) · parent y − 2
    parent x (θ)parent ynew xnew y
    010−7/2  minimum
    π/20π−2  midline
    π−12π−1/2  maximum
    3π/203π−2  midline
    2π14π−7/2  minimum

    The parent columns are the five key points of y = cos θ. The new columns are where those points land: the minima, the maximum and the midline crossings for one cycle, 0 ≤ x ≤ 4π.

    x-intercepts: none. The whole graph stays between −7/2 and −1/2, so it never reaches y = 0. The parent's zeros (π/2 and 3π/2) become the midline crossings (π, −2) and (3π, −2). Always check the range before listing x-intercepts.
    Trap: (1/2)x stretches the graph horizontally. Multiply the parent x-values by 2. Do not divide them. And the negative A turns the parent's maximum at x = 0 into a minimum.

    9. Graphs of tangent, cotangent, secant, cosecant

    FunctionPeriodAsymptotes
    y = A tan(Bx)π/|B|where cos = 0
    y = A cot(Bx)π/|B|where sin = 0
    y = A sec(Bx)2π/|B|where cos = 0
    y = A csc(Bx)2π/|B|where sin = 0
    • Tangent has no amplitude. A is just a stretch.
    • Tangent rises through its center point, cotangent falls.
    • Sec and csc: graph the matching cos or sin first, then draw U shapes touching each peak and valley, with asymptotes at every zero.

    10. Inverse trig functions

    FunctionDomain (inputs)Range (outputs)QuadrantsNegative input lands in
    arcsin x = sin⁻¹x[−1, 1][−π/2, π/2] = [−90°, 90°]QI and QIVQIV, a negative angle
    arccos x = cos⁻¹x[−1, 1][0, π] = [0°, 180°]QI and QIIQII, an obtuse angle
    arctan x = tan⁻¹xall real numbers(−π/2, π/2) = (−90°, 90°)QI and QIVQIV, a negative angle
    • Ask: which angle inside the range has this value? sin⁻¹(−1/2) = −π/6, not 7π/6 or 11π/6.
    • arccos never gives a negative angle: cos⁻¹(−1/2) = 2π/3.
    • sin(sin⁻¹x) = x for x in [−1, 1], but sin⁻¹(sin θ) folds θ back into the range: sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6) = π/6.
      Step 1 Do the inside first. 5π/6 is in QII, reference angle π/6, sine is + in QII sin(5π/6) = 1/2 Step 2 sin⁻¹(1/2): which angle in [−π/2, π/2] has sine 1/2? π/6 Answer: π/6. Not 5π/6, because 5π/6 is outside the range.
    • Compositions like cos(sin⁻¹(3/5)): draw the triangle in the quadrant the range allows, then read the other ratio, here 4/5.
      Step 1 Name the inside angle. θ = sin⁻¹(3/5), so sin θ = 3/5 = O/H Step 2 3/5 is positive → θ is in QI. Step 3 Triangle: O = 3, H = 5. Find A. A² + 3² = 5² A² + 9 = 25 A² = 16 A = 4 Step 4 Read cos θ = A/H. cos(sin⁻¹(3/5)) = 4/5
    • Less common: arccot (0, π) • arcsec [0, π] except π/2 • arccsc [−π/2, π/2] except 0.
    Trap: sin⁻¹x means the inverse function, not 1/sin x. 1/sin x is csc x.

    11. Fundamental identities

    Reciprocal: csc θ = 1/sin θ • sec θ = 1/cos θ • cot θ = 1/tan θ.

    Quotient: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ • cot θ = cos θ/sin θ.

    Pythagorean: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 • 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ • 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

    Rearranged forms worth knowing: sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ • cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ • tan²θ = sec²θ − 1 • cot²θ = csc²θ − 1.

    Even and odd: cos(−θ) = cos θ and sec(−θ) = sec θ. All four others are odd: sin(−θ) = −sin θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ, csc and cot follow.

    Cofunction: sin θ = cos(90° − θ) • tan θ = cot(90° − θ) • sec θ = csc(90° − θ). In radians use π/2 − θ.

    Periodicity: sin and cos repeat every 2π. tan and cot repeat every π.

    12. Sum and difference identities

    • sin(a ± b) = sin a cos b ± cos a sin b
    • cos(a ± b) = cos a cos b ∓ sin a sin b
    • tan(a ± b) = (tan a ± tan b) / (1 ∓ tan a tan b)

    Sign memory: sine keeps the sign (+ stays +). Cosine flips it (a + b gives a minus). Tangent keeps it on top and flips it on the bottom.

    Angles to split: 15° = 45° − 30° • 75° = 45° + 30° • 105° = 60° + 45° • 165° = 120° + 45° • π/12 = π/3 − π/4 • 5π/12 = π/4 + π/6 • 7π/12 = π/3 + π/4.

    Worked: sin 75°

    Step 1 Split into special angles. 75° = 45° + 30° Step 2 sin(a + b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b sin 45° cos 30° + cos 45° sin 30° Step 3 Substitute the exact values. (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) Step 4 Multiply each pair: top × top, bottom × bottom. (√2/2)(√3/2) = (√2·√3)/(2·2) = √6/4 (√2/2)(1/2) = (√2·1)/(2·2) = √2/4 Step 5 Same denominator → add the tops. √6/4 + √2/4 = (√6 + √2)/4

    Worked: cos 15°

    Step 1 15° = 45° − 30° Step 2 cos(a − b) = cos a cos b + sin a sin b (minus inside → plus between) cos 45° cos 30° + sin 45° sin 30° Step 3 (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) Step 4 √6/4 + √2/4 Step 5 (√6 + √2)/4

    Same value as sin 75°, because they are cofunctions.

    Values worth knowing: sin 15° = cos 75° = (√6 − √2)/4 • sin 75° = cos 15° = (√6 + √2)/4 • tan 15° = 2 − √3 • tan 75° = 2 + √3.

    Given-ratio problems (sin a = 3/5 in QII, cos b = 5/13 in QI): draw a triangle for each angle, find the missing sides with the Pythagorean theorem, attach the quadrant signs, then substitute.

    Trap: sin(a + b) is not sin a + sin b. sin(45° + 30°) ≈ 0.966, but sin 45° + sin 30° ≈ 1.207.

    13. Half-angle identities

    • sin(θ/2) = ± √( (1 − cos θ) / 2 )
    • cos(θ/2) = ± √( (1 + cos θ) / 2 )
    • tan(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ) / sin θ = sin θ / (1 + cos θ), and the tangent forms need no ± sign.

    Memory: sine goes with minus, cosine goes with plus. Every form needs only cos θ, plus sin θ for tangent.

    1. Find the quadrant of θ/2 by dividing the interval for θ by 2.
    2. Find cos θ, drawing a triangle if you are given a different ratio.
    3. Substitute, simplify the fraction inside the root, then pick the sign from step 1.

    Worked: sin 22.5°

    Step 1 22.5° = 45°/2, so θ = 45°. Step 2 22.5° is in QI → the sign is +. Step 3 Substitute cos 45° = √2/2. sin 22.5° = +√((1 − √2/2)/2) Step 4 Clean up the top: write 1 as 2/2. 1 − √2/2 = 2/2 − √2/2 = (2 − √2)/2 Step 5 Dividing by 2 multiplies the bottom by 2. ((2 − √2)/2) ÷ 2 = (2 − √2)/4 Step 6 Root of the top over root of the bottom. √((2 − √2)/4) = √(2 − √2)/√4 = √(2 − √2)/2

    Worked: cos 112.5°

    Step 1 112.5° = 225°/2, so θ = 225°. Step 2 112.5° is in QII → cosine is negative, use −. Step 3 cos 225° = −√2/2 (QIII, reference angle 45°) cos 112.5° = −√((1 + cos 225°)/2) = −√((1 + (−√2/2))/2) = −√((1 − √2/2)/2) Step 4 Same cleanup as sin 22.5°. 1 − √2/2 = (2 − √2)/2 ÷ 2 → (2 − √2)/4 −√((2 − √2)/4) = −√(2 − √2)/2

    Worked: tan 15°

    Step 1 15° = 30°/2, so θ = 30°. Step 2 tan(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/sin θ (1 − √3/2)/(1/2) Step 3 Clean up the top: write 1 as 2/2. 1 − √3/2 = (2 − √3)/2 Step 4 Dividing by 1/2 means multiplying by 2. (2 − √3)/2 · 2 = 2 − √3
    Trap: with π < θ < 3π/2, θ/2 is between π/2 and 3π/4, which is QII. Divide the whole interval by 2 before you pick the sign.

    14. Double-angle, power-reducing and product-sum formulas

    Double angle

    • sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ
    • cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1
    • tan 2θ = 2tan θ/(1 − tan²θ)

    Power reducing

    • sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2 • cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 • tan²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/(1 + cos 2θ)

    Product to sum

    • sin a cos b = ½[sin(a+b) + sin(a−b)]
    • cos a cos b = ½[cos(a−b) + cos(a+b)]
    • sin a sin b = ½[cos(a−b) − cos(a+b)]

    Sum to product

    • sin a + sin b = 2 sin((a+b)/2) cos((a−b)/2)
    • cos a + cos b = 2 cos((a+b)/2) cos((a−b)/2)
    • cos a − cos b = −2 sin((a+b)/2) sin((a−b)/2)

    15. Verifying identities

    1. Work on one side only, the more complicated one.
    2. Look for algebra first: common denominator, factor, distribute, split a fraction.
    3. Apply Pythagorean identities when you see a squared trig function.
    4. Convert everything to sine and cosine when you are stuck.
    5. Multiply by a conjugate when you see 1 ± sin or 1 ± cos in a denominator.
    6. Stop when the side matches the other side exactly.
    Trap: do not move terms across the equals sign. You are proving it, not solving it.

    16. Trig equations

    • Basic: isolate the trig function, find the reference angle, place it in every quadrant that matches the sign, list all solutions in the interval.
    • All solutions: add 2πn for sine and cosine, πn for tangent.
    • Quadratic form: substitute u for the repeated trig function, factor or use the quadratic formula, then solve each piece.
    • Mixed functions: use identities to get everything into one function first.
    • Multiple angle: for sin 2x on [0, 2π), solve over [0, 4π) for the inner angle, then divide the answers by 2.
    • Factoring: never divide both sides by a trig function, you will lose solutions. Move everything to one side and factor.
    • Check for extraneous answers if you squared both sides.

    17. Non-right triangles

    Law of Sines: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use for ASA, AAS and SSA.

    Law of Cosines: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use for SAS and SSS.

    Finding an angle from SSS: cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc).

    Area

    • Two sides and the included angle: K = ½ab sin C.
    • Three sides, Heron: s = (a+b+c)/2, then K = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)).

    SSA ambiguous case: after finding an angle with the Law of Sines, also test 180° minus that angle. If the remaining angles still total under 180°, a second triangle exists. Zero, one or two triangles are all possible.

    Trap: pair each side with the angle opposite it, not the one next to it.

    18. Law of Cosines

    Side c is always across from angle C.

    Find a side (two sides and the angle between them):

    • c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C
    • a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A
    • b² = a² + c² − 2ac cos B

    Find an angle (all three sides):

    • cos C = (a² + b² − c²) / (2ab)
    • cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc)
    • cos B = (a² + c² − b²) / (2ac)
    You knowUseFirst step
    SAS: two sides and the angle between themLaw of CosinesFind the side across from the known angle
    SSS: all three sidesLaw of CosinesFind the largest angle first (across from the longest side)
    ASA, AAS, SSALaw of Sinesa/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C

    Worked (SAS): a = 7, b = 10, C = 50°. Find c.

    Step 1 Write the formula for the side across from C. c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C c² = 7² + 10² − 2(7)(10) cos 50° Step 2 Squares and the product. 7² = 49, 10² = 100, 2·7·10 = 140 c² = 49 + 100 − 140 cos 50° Step 3 Multiply BEFORE subtracting (DEG mode). cos 50° ≈ 0.6428 140 × 0.6428 ≈ 89.99 Step 4 Now subtract. c² ≈ 149 − 89.99 = 59.01 Step 5 Square root. c ≈ √59.01 ≈ 7.68

    Then switch to the Law of Sines for another angle.

    Check: if C = 90°, cos C = 0 and the law becomes c² = a² + b². If cos C comes out negative, the angle is obtuse, which is fine.

    Trap: do the multiplication 2ab cos C before subtracting. 149 − 140 cos 50° is not 9 cos 50°. On the TI-30XIIS, type it in one line: 49 + 100 − 140 × COS 50 ) ENTER.

    19. Vectors

    • Component form ⟨a, b⟩. Magnitude ||v|| = √(a² + b²).
    • Direction angle θ = tan⁻¹(b/a), adjusted for the correct quadrant.
    • From magnitude and angle: ⟨||v||cos θ, ||v||sin θ⟩.
    • Add and subtract componentwise. Scalar multiply each component.
    • Unit vector: divide the vector by its magnitude.
    • Dot product v·w = a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = ||v|| ||w|| cos θ.
    • Perpendicular vectors have a dot product of 0.

    20. Polar and complex form

    • Polar to rectangular: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.
    • Rectangular to polar: r = √(x² + y²), θ = tan⁻¹(y/x) with a quadrant check.
    • Complex number a + bi in polar form: r(cos θ + i sin θ), with r = √(a² + b²).
    • Multiply: multiply the r values, add the angles. Divide: divide r values, subtract angles.
    • De Moivre: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).
    • nth roots: take the nth root of r, and use angles (θ + 2πk)/n for k = 0 to n−1.

    21. Trig errors that cost the most points

    • Calculator in the wrong angle mode.
    • Giving one solution when the interval holds several.
    • Forgetting the quadrant sign after finding a reference angle.
    • Dividing an equation by sin x or cos x and losing solutions.
    • Not factoring B out before reading the phase shift.
    • Using the wrong half-angle sign, which depends on θ/2.
    • Pairing a side with the wrong angle in the Law of Sines.
    • Skipping the second-angle check in an SSA problem.
    • Treating sin²x as sin(x²). They are different.
    • Writing sin⁻¹x when you mean 1/sin x. That is csc x.
    • Rounding an intermediate angle and then using it in the next step.

    22. The memorize-first list

    1. SOH CAH TOA and the three reciprocals.
    2. The two special triangles, 45-45-90 and 30-60-90.
    3. QI unit-circle values and the ASTC sign rule.
    4. Reference angle rules for all four quadrants.
    5. Degree and radian conversions plus the common angles.
    6. Amplitude, period, phase shift and midline from A, B, C, D.
    7. The three Pythagorean identities.
    8. Sum, difference, double-angle and half-angle formulas.
    9. Inverse trig ranges.
    10. Inverse trig quadrants: arcsin and arctan in QI/QIV, arccos in QI/QII.
    11. When to use the Law of Sines versus the Law of Cosines.

    Study method: dump this list onto blank paper from memory before you open the book. Whatever you cannot rebuild is what to study.

    Domain & Range — Master Cheat Sheet

    Everything that can restrict a domain, every standard range, and how to write the answer in interval notation. Print the whole sheet, or tick only the cards you need for a specific test.

    1. Interval notation — how to write the answer

    InequalityIntervalMeaning
    x > a(a, ∞)a not included
    x ≥ a[a, ∞)a included
    x < b(−∞, b)b not included
    x ≤ b(−∞, b]b included
    a < x ≤ b(a, b]mixed ends are normal
    all real numbers(−∞, ∞)no restrictions
    x ≠ 4(−∞, 4) ∪ (4, ∞)one point punched out
    x ≠ −1 and x ≠ 3(−∞,−1) ∪ (−1,3) ∪ (3,∞)two points punched out
    no solution∅ or { }empty set

    Rules: smaller number on the left • ∞ and −∞ always get a parenthesis • use ∪ to join separated pieces, never a comma • a single point is written {5} in set notation, not [5,5].

    Set-builder version: {x | x ≥ 2} reads "all x such that x is at least 2".

    Trap: writing (−∞, 4) ∪ (4, ∞) as (−∞, ∞) loses the hole. Writing [∞) is always wrong.

    2. The master restriction checklist (run this on every function)

    Start with all real numbers, then take away what breaks the math. Only five things break it.

    #If the function containsRequirementSet up and solve
    1a denominatordenominator ≠ 0set denominator = 0, solve, exclude those x
    2an even root (√, ⁴√, any even index)radicand ≥ 0solve the inequality
    3an even root in a denominatorradicand > 0strict, zero is not allowed
    4a log (log, ln, log_b)argument > 0solve the inequality, strict
    5a rational exponent x^(m/n) with n evenbase ≥ 0same as an even root

    Bonus restrictions: tan and sec break where cos = 0 • cot and csc break where sin = 0 • arcsin and arccos need input in [−1, 1] • a negative exponent means that base ≠ 0 • applied problems add physical limits.

    More than one restriction? Intersect them. The domain is what satisfies all conditions at once, not the union.

    3. Domain by function type

    FunctionDomain
    Linear, constant(−∞, ∞)
    Quadratic, any polynomial(−∞, ∞)
    Absolute value(−∞, ∞)
    Rational p(x)/q(x)all real x with q(x) ≠ 0
    Even root √(u)u ≥ 0
    Odd root ³√(u)(−∞, ∞)
    Exponential b^x(−∞, ∞)
    Logarithm log_b(u)u > 0
    sin x, cos x(−∞, ∞)
    tan x, sec xx ≠ π/2 + πn
    cot x, csc xx ≠ πn
    arcsin x, arccos x[−1, 1]
    arctan x(−∞, ∞)

    4. Range by function type

    FunctionRange
    Linear mx+b, m ≠ 0(−∞, ∞)
    Constant y = c{c}
    Quadratic, vertex (h,k)[k,∞) if a > 0 • (−∞,k] if a < 0
    Odd-degree polynomial(−∞, ∞)
    Even-degree polynomialbounded on one side, read the graph
    |x| type, a|x−h|+k[k,∞) if a > 0 • (−∞,k] if a < 0
    √x type, a√(x−h)+k[k,∞) if a > 0 • (−∞,k] if a < 0
    Odd root ³√(−∞, ∞)
    Exponential ab^x + k(k,∞) if a > 0 • (−∞,k) if a < 0
    Logarithm(−∞, ∞)
    sin, cos with amplitude |A|, midline D[D−|A|, D+|A|]
    tan, cot(−∞, ∞)
    sec, csc (basic)(−∞,−1] ∪ [1,∞)
    Rational (simple)usually all reals except the horizontal asymptote value
    Exponential trap: the horizontal asymptote value is never reached, so the range end is a parenthesis, not a bracket.

    5. Roots and radicals

    Even index (√, ⁴√, ⁶√): radicand ≥ 0. Set the inside ≥ 0 and solve.

    Odd index (³√, ⁵√): no restriction. Negative inputs are fine. Domain and range are both all reals.

    Even root in a denominator: the inside must be strictly > 0.

    Examples

    • √(3 − x): 3 − x ≥ 0 → x ≤ 3 → (−∞, 3]
    • 5/√(3 − x): 3 − x > 0 → x < 3 → (−∞, 3)
    • √(2x + 8): x ≥ −4 → [−4, ∞)
    • √(x² − 9): sign chart → (−∞,−3] ∪ [3,∞)
    • ³√(x − 7): (−∞, ∞)
    √(3 − x) 3 − x ≥ 0 −x ≥ −3 subtract 3 x ≤ 3 ÷ (−1), FLIP (−∞, 3] 5/√(3 − x) root on the bottom → > 3 − x > 0 −x > −3 x < 3 FLIP (−∞, 3) √(2x + 8) 2x + 8 ≥ 0 2x ≥ −8 subtract 8 x ≥ −4 ÷ 2 [−4, ∞) √(x² − 9) x² − 9 ≥ 0 (x − 3)(x + 3) ≥ 0 zeros: 3, −3 (closed, ≥) x = −4: (−7)(−1) = 7 + x = 0: (−3)(3) = −9 − x = 4: (1)(7) = 7 + keep +: (−∞, −3] ∪ [3, ∞) ³√(x − 7) odd root → no rule (−∞, ∞)

    Range of a√(x−h)+k: the root itself gives [0,∞), so the output starts at k and goes up when a > 0, down when a < 0.

    Trap: dividing an inequality by a negative flips the sign. 3 − x ≥ 0 → −x ≥ −3 → x ≤ 3.

    6. Rational functions

    Domain: factor the denominator, set each factor = 0, exclude those x. Do this on the original function.

    Holes vs asymptotes: a factor that cancels gives a hole at that x, a factor that survives gives a vertical asymptote. Either way that x is out of the domain.

    Range, three tools

    • Horizontal asymptote y = L is usually excluded, so range = all reals except L.
    • Solve for x: set y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, any y that breaks that equation is out of the range.
    • If the graph has a hole at (a, b), then b is out of the range too.

    Horizontal asymptote rules: deg top < deg bottom → y = 0 • degrees equal → y = ratio of leading coefficients • deg top one higher → slant asymptote, no horizontal one.

    Example: f(x) = (2x+1)/(x−3)

    Domain x − 3 = 0 → x = 3, exclude it (−∞, 3) ∪ (3, ∞) Horizontal asymptote top degree 1, bottom degree 1 equal → ratio of leaders 2x/x → y = 2/1 = 2 Range: everything except 2 (−∞, 2) ∪ (2, ∞)
    Trap: simplifying first and then finding the domain. (x²−4)/(x−2) simplifies to x+2, but x = 2 is still excluded.

    7. Quadratics and parabolas

    Domain: always (−∞, ∞).

    Range: find the vertex, then go one direction only.

    • Standard form y = ax²+bx+c: x = −b/(2a), then plug back in for k.
    • Vertex form y = a(x−h)²+k: vertex is (h, k) directly.
    • a > 0 opens up → range [k, ∞)
    • a < 0 opens down → range (−∞, k]

    Example: f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 1

    Step 1 a = 2, b = −8, c = 1 Step 2 x = −b/(2a) = −(−8)/(2·2) = 8/4 = 2 Step 3 Plug x = 2 back in. f(2) = 2(2)² − 8(2) + 1 = 2(4) − 16 + 1 = 8 − 16 + 1 = −7 Step 4 a = 2 > 0 → opens up range [−7, ∞)

    Restricted domain version: if the problem says x ≥ 0 or 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, the range is only the outputs over that piece. Check the vertex and both endpoints, then take the min and max.

    Trap: the vertex y-value is included, so the range end uses a bracket.

    8. Polynomials and power functions

    Domain of any polynomial: (−∞, ∞). There is nothing to exclude.

    Range by degree

    • Odd degree → (−∞, ∞), the ends go opposite directions.
    • Even degree, positive lead → [min, ∞).
    • Even degree, negative lead → (−∞, max].

    Power functions x^n

    • n a positive even integer: D all reals, R [0, ∞).
    • n a positive odd integer: D and R all reals.
    • n negative: x ≠ 0.
    • x^(m/n) with n even: base ≥ 0. With n odd: all reals.
    • x^(−m/n) with n even: base > 0.

    Examples: (x−1)^(3/2) needs x ≥ 1 • (x−1)^(−1/2) needs x > 1 • x^(2/3) is all reals.

    (x−1)^(3/2) = (√(x−1))³ bottom of 3/2 is 2, even x − 1 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 1 (x−1)^(−1/2) = 1/√(x−1) even root on the bottom x − 1 > 0 → x > 1 x^(2/3) = (³√x)² bottom of 2/3 is 3, odd no rule → all reals

    9. Absolute value

    Domain: always (−∞, ∞). Absolute value never breaks.

    Range of a|x−h| + k: [k, ∞) if a > 0, (−∞, k] if a < 0. The vertex is (h, k).

    Example: f(x) = −2|x+1| + 7

    Step 1 Match a|x − h| + k. x + 1 = x − (−1) → h = −1 k = 7, a = −2 Step 2 Vertex (h, k) = (−1, 7) Step 3 a = −2 < 0 → opens down, 7 is the top. range (−∞, 7]

    Where it matters most: absolute value inside a fraction or a root changes the answer.

    • 6/(|x|+4): |x| ≥ 0 so the denominator is at least 4 and never zero → domain (−∞, ∞).
    • Range of 6/(|x|+4): denominator runs over [4, ∞) so the output runs over (0, 1.5].
    • 1/(|x|−3): excluded where |x| = 3 → x ≠ 3 and x ≠ −3.
    • √(|x| − 2): |x| ≥ 2 → (−∞,−2] ∪ [2, ∞).

    10. Exponential functions

    Form: f(x) = a·b^(x−h) + k with b > 0 and b ≠ 1.

    Domain: (−∞, ∞). An exponent never restricts anything.

    Range: b^x is always positive, so the graph hugs the horizontal asymptote y = k but never touches it.

    • a > 0 → range (k, ∞)
    • a < 0 → range (−∞, k)
    • Base case y = b^x → range (0, ∞)

    Examples: 3·2^x − 5 → (−5, ∞) • −4e^x + 2 → (−∞, 2) • 2^x → (0, ∞).

    3·2^x − 5 k = −5 → asymptote y = −5 a = 3 > 0 → above it (−5, ∞) −4e^x + 2 k = 2 → asymptote y = 2 a = −4 < 0 → below it (−∞, 2) 2^x k = 0, a = 1 > 0 (0, ∞)

    Applied models A = A₀(1+r)^t usually get t ≥ 0, so the domain is [0, ∞) and the range starts at A₀.

    Trap: the asymptote is never included. Parenthesis, not bracket.

    11. Logarithmic functions

    Rule: the argument must be strictly greater than zero. Set inside > 0 and solve the inequality.

    Range: all reals, (−∞, ∞), for every log function. Transformations do not change that.

    Examples

    • log(x − 5) → x > 5 → (5, ∞)
    • ln(3 − x) → x < 3 → (−∞, 3)
    • log(2x + 8) → x > −4 → (−4, ∞)
    • log(x² − 9) → sign chart → (−∞,−3) ∪ (3, ∞)
    • ln((x−1)/(x+2)) → sign chart → (−∞,−2) ∪ (1, ∞)
    • log(x²) → everything except x = 0 → (−∞,0) ∪ (0,∞)
    log(x − 5) x − 5 > 0 x > 5 add 5 (5, ∞) ln(3 − x) 3 − x > 0 −x > −3 subtract 3 x < 3 ÷ (−1), FLIP (−∞, 3) log(2x + 8) 2x + 8 > 0 2x > −8 x > −4 (−4, ∞) log(x² − 9) (x − 3)(x + 3) > 0 zeros 3, −3 (open, >) x = −4: (−7)(−1) = 7 + x = 0: (−3)(3) = −9 − x = 4: (1)(7) = 7 + (−∞, −3) ∪ (3, ∞) ln((x−1)/(x+2)) top 0: x = 1 bottom 0: x = −2 x = −3: (−4)/(−1) = 4 + x = 0: (−1)/(2) = −1/2 − x = 2: (1)/(4) = 1/4 + (−∞, −2) ∪ (1, ∞) log(x²) x² > 0 for every x but 0 (−∞, 0) ∪ (0, ∞)

    Vertical asymptote: at whatever x makes the argument zero. It is the domain boundary and it is never included.

    Trap: a minus sign outside, like −log(x−2), does not change the domain. Only the argument matters.
    Solving log equations: always test your answers back in the original argument. Any answer making an argument ≤ 0 is extraneous and gets thrown out.

    12. Trig functions

    FunctionDomainRange
    sin xall reals[−1, 1]
    cos xall reals[−1, 1]
    tan xx ≠ π/2 + πnall reals
    cot xx ≠ πnall reals
    sec xx ≠ π/2 + πn(−∞,−1] ∪ [1,∞)
    csc xx ≠ πn(−∞,−1] ∪ [1,∞)

    Why: tan and sec have cos in the denominator, cot and csc have sin in the denominator. The domain gaps are wherever that denominator is zero.

    Transformed sine and cosine y = A sin(B(x−C)) + D: range is [D − |A|, D + |A|]. Domain stays all reals.

    Examples: 3sin(2x) − 1 → range [−4, 2] • −5cos x + 2 → range [−3, 7] • 2sec x → range (−∞,−2] ∪ [2,∞).

    3sin(2x) − 1 |A| = 3, D = −1 [D − |A|, D + |A|] [−1 − 3, −1 + 3] = [−4, 2] −5cos x + 2 |A| = |−5| = 5, D = 2 [2 − 5, 2 + 5] = [−3, 7] 2sec x sec x: (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞) × 2: (−∞, −2] ∪ [2, ∞)

    Transformed tangent y = tan(Bx): asymptotes where Bx = π/2 + πn, so solve for x to list the excluded values.

    13. Inverse trig functions

    FunctionDomainRange (principal)
    arcsin x[−1, 1][−π/2, π/2]
    arccos x[−1, 1][0, π]
    arctan x(−∞, ∞)(−π/2, π/2)
    arccot x(−∞, ∞)(0, π)
    arcsec x(−∞,−1] ∪ [1,∞)[0, π], x ≠ π/2
    arccsc x(−∞,−1] ∪ [1,∞)[−π/2, π/2], x ≠ 0

    Memory hook: inverse domain = original range, inverse range = original restricted domain.

    Domain of arcsin(u): solve −1 ≤ u ≤ 1. For arcsin(2x−1) that gives 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

    −1 ≤ 2x − 1 ≤ 1 0 ≤ 2x ≤ 2 add 1 to all three 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 ÷ 2 all three [0, 1]
    Trap: arcsin(sin θ) does not always return θ. It returns the angle in [−π/2, π/2] with the same sine.

    14. Piecewise functions

    Domain: the union of the intervals listed next to the pieces. If some x is never covered, it is not in the domain.

    Range: find the range of each piece over its own interval, then union them.

    Method

    • Evaluate each piece at its endpoints.
    • Check for a vertex, asymptote or turn inside the interval.
    • Open circle at an endpoint → parenthesis. Closed circle → bracket.
    • Overlapping output values collapse into one interval.

    Example: f(x) = x² for x < 0, and 2x + 1 for x ≥ 0.

    Domain x < 0 and x ≥ 0 cover everything → (−∞, ∞) Piece 1: x² on x < 0 endpoint x = 0 → 0² = 0, open (x < 0) x = −1 → 1, x = −3 → 9 outputs (0, ∞) Piece 2: 2x + 1 on x ≥ 0 endpoint x = 0 → 1, closed slope 2, keeps rising outputs [1, ∞) Union (0, ∞) ∪ [1, ∞) = (0, ∞)
    Trap: gaps in the range are common even when the domain is all reals. Graph it if you are unsure.

    15. Combining functions

    OperationDomain
    (f+g), (f−g), (fg)domain of f ∩ domain of g
    (f/g)domain of f ∩ domain of g, and g(x) ≠ 0
    (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x))x must be in the domain of g and g(x) must be in the domain of f

    Composition method

    • Write down the restrictions from the inside function first.
    • Build the composed formula and find its own restrictions.
    • Keep both sets. Never drop the inside restriction.

    Examples

    • f(x)=√x, g(x)=x−5 → (f∘g)=√(x−5), domain [5, ∞).
    • f(x)=x², g(x)=√x → (f∘g)=x but the domain is still [0, ∞).
    • f(x)=1/x, g(x)=x−2 → (g∘f)=1/x − 2, domain x ≠ 0.
    Trap: simplifying the composed formula can hide a restriction. Check the inside function before you simplify.

    16. Inverse functions

    Core fact: domain and range swap. Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f. Range of f⁻¹ = domain of f.

    Exists only if f is one to one. Use the horizontal line test. If it fails, restrict the domain first, and that restriction becomes the range of the inverse.

    Example: f(x) = x² on [0, ∞) has range [0, ∞), so f⁻¹(x) = √x with domain [0, ∞) and range [0, ∞).

    Example: f(x) = 2^x has domain all reals and range (0, ∞). Its inverse log₂x has domain (0, ∞) and range all reals.

    Use this as a shortcut: when a range is hard to find, find the inverse and take its domain instead.

    17. What transformations do to domain and range

    For y = a·f(b(x − h)) + k:

    ChangeDomain effectRange effect
    +k vertical shiftnoneshift range by k
    −h horizontal shiftshift domain by hnone
    a vertical stretchnonemultiply range by |a|
    a < 0 reflect over x-axisnoneflip range around the shift value
    b horizontal compressdivide domain bounds by |b|none
    b < 0 reflect over y-axisflip domain around hnone

    Order that works: start from the parent function's domain and range, apply horizontal changes to the domain, apply vertical changes to the range.

    Example: parent √x has D [0,∞), R [0,∞). For y = −3√(x−2)+5:

    Domain (horizontal: h = 2) x − 2 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 2 [2, ∞) Range (vertical: a = −3, k = 5) √(x − 2) gives [0, ∞) × (−3) flips: (−∞, 0] + 5 shifts up: (−∞, 5]

    18. Sign chart method (for compound restrictions)

    Use it whenever the inside of a root or a log is a quadratic, a product or a fraction.

    1. Set the expression = 0 and solve. Those are your boundary points.
    2. Add any x that makes a denominator zero. Those are always open.
    3. Put all boundary points on a number line, splitting it into intervals.
    4. Test one easy number in each interval, record + or −.
    5. Keep the intervals matching the requirement (≥ 0 keeps positive plus the zeros, > 0 keeps positive only).

    Example: domain of √((x−2)/(x+1)). Boundaries x = 2 (zero, allowed) and x = −1 (denominator, never allowed). Testing gives + on (−∞,−1), − on (−1,2), + on (2,∞). Domain (−∞,−1) ∪ [2, ∞).

    (x − 2)/(x + 1) ≥ 0 top 0: x = 2 closed bottom 0: x = −1 open x = −2: (−4)/(−1) = 4 + x = 0: (−2)/(1) = −2 − x = 3: (1)/(4) = 1/4 + (−∞, −1) ∪ [2, ∞)

    Example: domain of √(x² − 4x + 3)

    Step 1 Inside ≥ 0. x² − 4x + 3 ≥ 0 Step 2 Factor: multiply to 3, add to −4 → −1 and −3. (x − 1)(x − 3) ≥ 0 Step 3 Zeros 1 and 3, closed (≥). Step 4 Test each interval. x = 0: (−1)(−3) = 3 + x = 2: (1)(−1) = −1 − x = 4: (3)(1) = 3 + Step 5 Keep +. (−∞, 1] ∪ [3, ∞)

    19. Range-finding toolbox

    Range is harder than domain because the rules are about output. Pick a tool.

    • Know the parent: use the range table, then apply the transformations.
    • Vertex or turning point: quadratics and absolute values. The vertex y-value is the boundary.
    • Asymptote: exponentials and rationals. The asymptote value is usually excluded.
    • Solve for x: set y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, exclude any y that makes that solution impossible.
    • Endpoints: on a restricted domain, test both endpoints and any interior turn, then take the smallest and largest.
    • Graph it: sweep the graph with a horizontal line. Every height the line touches is in the range.

    Solve-for-x example: y = (3x)/(x−1)

    Step 1 Multiply both sides by (x − 1). y(x − 1) = 3x Step 2 Distribute the y. xy − y = 3x Step 3 x terms left, the rest right. xy − 3x = y (−3x, +y) Step 4 Factor out x. x(y − 3) = y Step 5 Divide by (y − 3). x = y/(y − 3) Step 6 Which y breaks it? y − 3 = 0 → y = 3 range (−∞, 3) ∪ (3, ∞)

    20. Applied and real-world domains

    Word problems add restrictions the algebra does not show.

    • Time t usually starts at 0 → t ≥ 0.
    • Counts of people, items or trips must be whole numbers → domain is a set of integers, not an interval.
    • Lengths, widths, radii and prices must be positive.
    • Percentages and probabilities live in [0, 1] or [0, 100].
    • A model can stop being valid (a projectile stops at ground level, a box stops when a side hits zero).

    Example: a box folded from a 10 by 16 sheet with corner cut x has volume x(10−2x)(16−2x). Algebraically all reals, physically 0 < x < 5.

    Every length must be positive: height x > 0 width 10 − 2x > 0 −2x > −10 x < 5 FLIP length 16 − 2x > 0 −2x > −16 x < 8 FLIP All three at once (intersect): 0 < x < 5
    On a test: if the problem has units, ask what values make physical sense before writing the answer.

    21. Circles, conics and relations

    These are relations, not functions, but tests still ask for domain and range.

    • Circle (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r² → domain [h−r, h+r], range [k−r, k+r].
    • Ellipse with horizontal radius a and vertical radius b → domain [h−a, h+a], range [k−b, k+b].
    • Horizontal hyperbola → domain (−∞, h−a] ∪ [h+a, ∞), range all reals.
    • Vertical hyperbola → domain all reals, range (−∞, k−b] ∪ [k+b, ∞).
    • Half circle y = √(r²−x²) → domain [−r, r], range [0, r].

    Vertical line test: if a vertical line hits the graph twice it is not a function, though the domain question still has an answer.

    22. Worked examples, the exact style tests use

    ProblemWorkAnswer
    f(x) = (x−3)/(x−4)x − 4 = 0 → x = 4, avoid it(−∞,4) ∪ (4,∞)
    m(x) = 6/(|x|+4)|x| ≥ 0 so |x|+4 ≥ 4, never zero(−∞, ∞)
    s(x) = 5/√(3−x)root in the denominator → 3−x > 0 → x < 3(−∞, 3)
    f(x) = √(2x−6)2x − 6 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 3[3, ∞)
    g(x) = (x+1)/(x²−9)x² − 9 = 0 → x = ±3(−∞,−3) ∪ (−3,3) ∪ (3,∞)
    h(x) = ln(4 − 2x)4 − 2x > 0 → x < 2(−∞, 2)
    Range of f(x) = −x²+6x−5x = 3, f(3) = 4, opens down(−∞, 4]
    Range of f(x) = 4·3^x − 2asymptote y = −2, a > 0(−2, ∞)
    Range of f(x) = 2√(x+1) − 3root gives [0,∞), stretch, shift down 3[−3, ∞)
    Range of f(x) = 5 − 3|x−2|vertex (2, 5), opens down(−∞, 5]
    Domain of √(x²−16)(x−4)(x+4) ≥ 0, sign chart(−∞,−4] ∪ [4,∞)
    Domain of (f∘g) with f=√x, g=x²−4x²−4 ≥ 0(−∞,−2] ∪ [2,∞)

    Every row, on paper:

    1. f(x) = (x−3)/(x−4) Bottom = 0: x − 4 = 0 x = 4 add 4 Exclude 4: (−∞, 4) ∪ (4, ∞)
    2. m(x) = 6/(|x|+4) Smallest |x| can be is 0: |x| ≥ 0 |x| + 4 ≥ 4 add 4 Bottom is at least 4, never 0. Nothing to exclude: (−∞, ∞)
    3. s(x) = 5/√(3−x) Root on the bottom → strict > 3 − x > 0 −x > −3 subtract 3 x < 3 ÷ (−1), FLIP (−∞, 3)
    4. f(x) = √(2x−6) Even root → inside ≥ 0 2x − 6 ≥ 0 2x ≥ 6 add 6 x ≥ 3 ÷ 2 [3, ∞)
    5. g(x) = (x+1)/(x²−9) Bottom = 0: x² − 9 = 0 (x − 3)(x + 3) = 0 x = 3 or x = −3 Exclude both, three pieces: (−∞, −3) ∪ (−3, 3) ∪ (3, ∞)
    6. h(x) = ln(4 − 2x) Log → argument > 0 4 − 2x > 0 −2x > −4 subtract 4 x < 2 ÷ (−2), FLIP (−∞, 2)
    7. Range of f(x) = −x² + 6x − 5 a = −1, b = 6 Vertex x: x = −b/(2a) = −6/(2·(−1)) = −6/(−2) = 3 Vertex y: f(3) = −(3)² + 6(3) − 5 = −9 + 18 − 5 = 4 a < 0 → opens down, 4 is the top (−∞, 4]
    8. Range of f(x) = 4·3^x − 2 Match a·b^x + k: a = 4, k = −2 Asymptote y = −2 (never reached) a > 0 → graph sits above it (−2, ∞)
    9. Range of f(x) = 2√(x+1) − 3 Start with the root: √(x+1) gives [0, ∞) × 2 (stretch): [0, ∞) − 3 (down 3): [−3, ∞)
    10. Range of f(x) = 5 − 3|x−2| Reorder to a|x − h| + k: −3|x − 2| + 5 a = −3, h = 2, k = 5 Vertex (2, 5) a < 0 → opens down, 5 is the top (−∞, 5]
    11. Domain of √(x² − 16) Inside ≥ 0, then factor: x² − 16 ≥ 0 (x − 4)(x + 4) ≥ 0 Zeros 4 and −4, closed (≥) x = −5: (−9)(−1) = 9 + x = 0: (−4)(4) = −16 − x = 5: (1)(9) = 9 + Keep +: (−∞, −4] ∪ [4, ∞)
    12. Domain of f∘g, f = √x, g = x² − 4 Inside function g: all reals, no restriction to carry. Build it: f(g(x)) = √(x² − 4) Inside ≥ 0, then factor: (x − 2)(x + 2) ≥ 0 x = −3: (−5)(−1) = 5 + x = 0: (−2)(2) = −4 − x = 3: (1)(5) = 5 + (−∞, −2] ∪ [2, ∞)

    23. Point-losing traps

    • Simplifying a rational function before finding the domain. The excluded value stays excluded.
    • Using ≥ instead of > for a root that sits in a denominator.
    • Using ≥ for a log argument. Logs are always strict.
    • Forgetting to flip the inequality when dividing by a negative.
    • Writing a bracket next to ∞.
    • Using a comma instead of ∪ between separated intervals.
    • Treating an odd root like an even root. ³√ has no restriction.
    • Dropping the inside function's restriction after composing.
    • Including the horizontal asymptote in an exponential range.
    • Giving the domain when the question asked for the range.
    • Ignoring a restricted domain stated in the problem, like x ≥ 0.
    • Keeping an extraneous solution that makes a log argument or a denominator zero.

    24. Test-day routine

    1. Name the function type. Polynomial, rational, radical, log, exponential, trig, piecewise, composition.
    2. Scan for the five restrictions. Denominator, even root, even root in a denominator, log, even rational exponent.
    3. Write each restriction as an equation or inequality and solve it.
    4. Intersect every restriction, not union.
    5. Add any restriction the problem states in words.
    6. Write the answer in interval notation, smallest to largest, ∪ between pieces.
    7. For range: identify the parent, apply transformations, then double check the boundary is open or closed.
    8. Sanity check by plugging in a number just inside and just outside a boundary.

    Printing: the buttons above build a clean packet with no navigation or sidebar. For a regular browser print of just this page area, use Letter portrait with background graphics off.

    Rule Cheat Sheets — What to Recognize, What Rule to Use

    Use these as memory sheets: identify the problem type, apply the rule, then check the common trap. Print this section by itself from your browser if you want a compact rules packet.

    Factoring — decision tree

    See thisDo this
    Every term shares somethingGCF first. Always.
    a²−b²(a−b)(a+b)
    a³+b³(a+b)(a²−ab+b²)
    a³−b³(a−b)(a²+ab+b²)
    x²+bx+cFind m,n with mn=c and m+n=b → (x+m)(x+n).
    ax²+bx+c, a≠1AC method: multiply ac → split b → group.
    4 termsTry grouping in pairs.
    Quadratic in disguiseLet u=x², x³, sin x, etc.; factor in u; substitute back.

    Finish check: expand your factors mentally. If the middle/signs do not return, fix them.

    Quadratics & Parabolas

    Standard: y=ax²+bx+c. Opens up if a>0, down if a<0. y-intercept=(0,c).

    Vertex: x=−b/(2a), then plug in for y. Axis: x=−b/(2a).

    Vertex form: y=a(x−h)²+k → vertex (h,k).

    Zeros: factor if easy; otherwise quadratic formula. Discriminant D=b²−4ac: D>0 two real, D=0 one repeated, D<0 no real.

    Graph fast: vertex → axis → y-intercept → reflect a point → zeros if available.

    Functions, Composition & Inverses

    Function: each x gets one y; graph → vertical-line test.

    Evaluate: replace every x with the input, using parentheses.

    Composition: (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)): do the inside function first, then substitute the whole result into the outside.

    Inverse: y=f(x) → swap x,y → solve for y → rename f⁻¹(x). One-to-one graph → horizontal-line test.

    Check inverse: f(f⁻¹(x))=x and f⁻¹(f(x))=x on the allowed domains.

    Domain & Range

    Polynomial: domain all real.

    Fraction: denominator ≠0.

    Even root: radicand ≥0.

    Log: argument >0.

    Composition: x must be allowed by the inside function and its output must be allowed by the outside function.

    Inverse: domain and range swap.

    Rational Functions & Asymptotes

    Factor before anything else. Canceled denominator zero → hole. Uncanceled denominator zero → vertical asymptote.

    Horizontal: degree top < bottom → y=0; equal → ratio of leading coefficients; top > bottom → no horizontal asymptote.

    Slant: numerator degree exactly one more → polynomial long/synthetic division; quotient is the slant line.

    Intercepts: x-intercepts from uncanceled numerator zeros; y-intercept plug x=0 if defined.

    Exponents & Radicals

    xᵐxⁿ=xᵐ⁺ⁿ • xᵐ/xⁿ=xᵐ⁻ⁿ • (xᵐ)ⁿ=xᵐⁿ • (xy)ⁿ=xⁿyⁿ.

    x⁰=1 (x≠0) • x⁻ⁿ=1/xⁿ • x^(m/n)=ⁿ√(xᵐ).

    Radicals: pull perfect powers out; combine only like radicals.

    Trap: (a+b)² ≠ a²+b². Expand: a²+2ab+b².

    Exponential Functions

    y=abˣ: a=initial value; b>1 growth; 0<b<1 decay.

    Solve: make bases match first. If they cannot, isolate exponential → take ln/log → use power rule → solve.

    Models: A=A₀(1+r)ᵗ growth; A=A₀(1−r)ᵗ decay. Continuous: A=A₀e^(kt).

    Do not round k early.

    Logs — rules & solving

    log_b x=y ⇔ bʸ=x. Domain: x>0.

    Product: log(MN)=logM+logN. Quotient: log(M/N)=logM−logN. Power: log(Mᵖ)=p logM.

    Change base: log_b a=ln(a)/ln(b).

    Solve log equations: condense if useful → rewrite exponential or exponentiate → solve → check every log argument >0.

    Trap: log(M+N) cannot be split.

    Lines & Coordinate Rules

    Slope m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁). Point-slope: y−y₁=m(x−x₁). Slope-intercept: y=mx+b.

    Parallel → same slope. Perpendicular → negative reciprocal (when slopes are defined).

    Midpoint=((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2). Distance=√((x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²).

    Angles, Radians & Circular Measure

    deg→rad: ×π/180. rad→deg: ×180/π.

    Coterminal: ±360° or ±2π. Arc length s=rθ. Sector area A=½r²θ; θ must be radians.

    Reference angle: QI θ; QII π−θ; QIII θ−π; QIV 2π−θ. Then apply quadrant sign.

    Right-Triangle Trig

    SOH CAH TOA: sin=O/H, cos=A/H, tan=O/A.

    Missing side → choose ratio containing known side + unknown side. Missing angle → inverse trig.

    a²+b²=c². Hypotenuse is opposite 90°.

    Calculator trap: confirm DEG or RAD before calculating.

    Unit Circle & Exact Trig

    Point=(cosθ,sinθ). tanθ=sinθ/cosθ.

    QI sine at 0°,30°,45°,60°,90°: √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. Cosine reverses.

    Signs by quadrant: I all +; II sin +; III tan +; IV cos +.

    45-45-90: 1:1:√2. 30-60-90: 1:√3:2.

    Trig Graphs

    y=A sin(B(x−C))+D or cos: amplitude |A|; period 2π/|B|; phase shift C; midline y=D.

    Fast graph: start at x=C and mark 5 points separated by period/4.

    Tangent: period π/|B|; center x=C; asymptotes half a period from center.

    From max/min: amplitude=(max−min)/2; midline=(max+min)/2.

    Inverse Trig

    arcsin range [−π/2,π/2]; arccos [0,π]; arctan (−π/2,π/2).

    Ask: “Which angle in the principal range has this trig value?”

    sin(arcsin x)=x for −1≤x≤1. But arcsin(sinθ) may return a different coterminal/reference-related angle in its principal range.

    Trig Identities — core

    Reciprocal: csc=1/sin, sec=1/cos, cot=1/tan.

    Quotient: tan=sin/cos, cot=cos/sin.

    Pythagorean: sin²+cos²=1; 1+tan²=sec²; 1+cot²=csc².

    Verify: work on the more complicated side only → algebra/factor/common denominator → identities → convert to sin/cos if stuck.

    Trig Identities — angle formulas

    sin(a±b)=sin a cos b ± cos a sin b.

    cos(a±b)=cos a cos b ∓ sin a sin b.

    sin2x=2sinxcosx.

    cos2x=cos²x−sin²x=1−2sin²x=2cos²x−1.

    sin(x/2)=±√((1−cosx)/2); cos(x/2)=±√((1+cosx)/2). Choose sign from quadrant of x/2.

    Trig Equations

    Workflow: isolate trig → get reference/principal angle → find correct quadrants → list every answer in interval.

    Quadratic form: let u=sinx/cosx/etc. → factor/quad formula → solve each resulting trig equation.

    Multiple angle: expand interval for 2x/3x first → solve → divide back.

    Non-right Triangles

    ASA/AAS: Law of Sines. SAS/SSS: Law of Cosines. SSA: Law of Sines + ambiguous-case check.

    Law of Sines: a/sinA=b/sinB=c/sinC. Match opposite pairs.

    Law of Cosines: a²=b²+c²−2bc cosA.

    Area with SAS: K=½bc sinA.

    Polynomial Division & Remainders

    Use synthetic division only for divisor x−c. Otherwise use long division.

    Remainder theorem: remainder when f(x) is divided by x−c is f(c).

    Factor theorem: x−c is a factor exactly when f(c)=0.

    Fractions & Algebra Survival Rules

    Fractions: add/subtract only after common denominator; multiply straight across; divide by multiplying reciprocal.

    Equations: distribute → combine like terms → move variable terms → constants → divide.

    Rational equations: state restrictions first, multiply by LCD, solve, reject restricted values.

    Absolute value |u|=a (a≥0) → u=a or u=−a.

    Test-Day “What do I try first?”

    Quadratic? factor → quadratic formula if needed.

    Rational? factor before graphing/solving.

    Exponential? matching bases before logs.

    Log? combine/rewrite, then domain check.

    Trig exact value? unit circle/reference angle before calculator.

    Identity? simplify complicated side.

    Triangle? identify ASA/AAS, SAS/SSS, or SSA before choosing law.

    Print tip: These cards are kept intact in print so a rule box will move to the next page instead of splitting in half.

    Additional Topics

    Polynomial and rational inequalities

    Sign-chart method. Get everything on one side against zero. Factor. Mark every zero of the numerator and denominator on a number line. Test one point in each interval. Include numerator zeros for ≤ and ≥; never include denominator zeros.
    Example 1 — polynomial

    Solve x² - x - 6 > 0.

    Factor: (x - 3)(x + 2) > 0 Critical values: x = 3, x = -2 Number line: -----(-2)-----(3)----- Test x = -3: (-6)(-1) = +6 positive ✓ Test x = 0: (-3)(2) = -6 negative Test x = 4: (1)(6) = +6 positive ✓ Strictly greater than, so the endpoints are excluded. Answer: (-∞, -2) ∪ (3, ∞)
    Example 2 — rational

    Solve (x - 1)/(x + 4) ≤ 0.

    Already one fraction against zero. Do NOT multiply by (x + 4) — you do not know its sign. Critical values: numerator zero x = 1, denominator zero x = -4 Test x = -5: (-6)/(-1) = +6 positive Test x = 0: (-1)/(4) = -.25 negative ✓ Test x = 2: (1)/(6) = +.17 positive x = 1 makes it zero, and ≤ allows zero → INCLUDE x = -4 makes it undefined → EXCLUDE always Answer: (-4, 1]

    Piecewise functions

    Example

    f(x) = 2x + 1 if x < 0; x² if 0 ≤ x ≤ 3; 5 if x > 3. Find f(-2), f(0), f(3), f(10).

    Pick the rule by checking which condition the INPUT satisfies. f(-2): -2 < 0 → use 2x + 1 → -3 f(0): 0 is in [0,3] → use x² → 0 f(3): 3 is in [0,3] → use x² → 9 f(10): 10 > 3 → use 5 → 5

    Check continuity by comparing the two rules at each boundary. At x = 0: left rule gives 1, right rule gives 0. They disagree, so there is a jump at x = 0.

    Systems of equations

    Example 1 — elimination

    Solve 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x - 2y = 8.

    The y terms are already opposites. Add the equations. 3x + 2y = 16 + 5x - 2y = 8 ---------------- 8x = 24 x = 3 Substitute back into either original: 3(3) + 2y = 16 9 + 2y = 16 2y = 7 ← subtract 9 y = 7/2 ← divide by 2 Answer: (3, 7/2)
    Example 2 — nonlinear system by substitution

    Solve y = x² - 3 and y = 2x.

    Both equal y, so set them equal. x² - 3 = 2x x² - 2x - 3 = 0 (x - 3)(x + 1) = 0 x = 3 or x = -1 Find each y with the simpler equation, y = 2x: x = 3 → y = 6 x = -1 → y = -2 Answer: (3, 6) and (-1, -2)
    A nonlinear system can have 0, 1, 2, or more solutions. Getting two answers is normal here, unlike a pair of lines.

    Sequences and series

    ArithmeticGeometric
    nth termaₙ = a₁ + (n - 1)daₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹
    sum of n termsSₙ = (n/2)(a₁ + aₙ)Sₙ = a₁(1 - rⁿ)/(1 - r)
    infinite sumdoes not convergeS = a₁/(1 - r), only if |r| < 1
    Example 1 — arithmetic

    For 7, 11, 15, 19, ... find the 30th term and the sum of the first 30 terms.

    a₁ = 7, d = 11 - 7 = 4 a₃₀ = 7 + (30 - 1)(4) = 7 + 29(4) = 7 + 116 = 123 S₃₀ = (30/2)(7 + 123) = 15(130) = 1950
    Example 2 — geometric, finite and infinite

    For 12, 6, 3, 3/2, ... find the 8th term, the sum of 8 terms, and the infinite sum.

    a₁ = 12, r = 6/12 = 1/2 a₈ = 12(1/2)⁷ = 12/128 = 3/32 S₈ = 12(1 - (1/2)⁸)/(1 - 1/2) = 12(1 - 1/256)/(1/2) = 12(255/256)(2) = 765/32 = 23.90625 Infinite sum: |r| = 1/2 < 1, so it converges. S = 12/(1 - 1/2) = 12/(1/2) = 24

    Complex numbers

    i = √-1, i² = -1, i³ = -i, i⁴ = 1, then it repeats. Divide the exponent by 4 and use the remainder.
    Example 1 — arithmetic and powers

    Simplify (3 + 2i)(4 - 5i) and i³⁷.

    FOIL: 12 - 15i + 8i - 10i² 12 - 7i - 10(-1) ← i² becomes -1 12 - 7i + 10 22 - 7i i³⁷: 37 ÷ 4 = 9 remainder 1 → i³⁷ = i¹ = i
    Example 2 — dividing, and complex roots

    Simplify (2 + i)/(3 - i), then solve x² + 4x + 13 = 0.

    Multiply by the CONJUGATE of the denominator, (3 + i): (2 + i)(3 + i) 6 + 2i + 3i + i² 6 + 5i - 1 5 + 5i -------------- = ----------------- = ---------- = ------ (3 - i)(3 + i) 9 - i² 9 + 1 10 = (5 + 5i)/10 = 1/2 + (1/2)i Quadratic: a = 1, b = 4, c = 13 b² - 4ac = 16 - 52 = -36 x = (-4 ± √-36)/2 √-36 = √36 · √-1 = 6i x = (-4 ± 6i)/2 = -4/2 ± 6i/2 ← divide EACH term by 2 = -2 ± 3i

    Complex roots always arrive as conjugate pairs when the coefficients are real.

    Polar coordinates

    x = r cos θ    y = r sin θ    r² = x² + y²    tan θ = y/x
    Example 1 — polar to rectangular

    Convert (4, 2π/3) to rectangular coordinates.

    x = 4 cos(2π/3) = 4(-1/2) = -2 y = 4 sin(2π/3) = 4(√3/2) = 2√3 (-2, 2√3)
    Example 2 — rectangular to polar

    Convert (-3, 3) to polar coordinates with r > 0 and 0 ≤ θ < 2π.

    r = √(9 + 9) = √18 = 3√2 tan θ = 3/(-3) = -1 Reference angle π/4. The point (-3, 3) is in Quadrant II, so θ = π - π/4 = 3π/4. (3√2, 3π/4)
    Always check the quadrant. tan⁻¹(-1) returns -π/4, which is in Quadrant IV. The point is not there.

    Mixed review — additional topics

    1. Solve x² - 4x ≤ 0
    2. Solve (x + 2)/(x - 3) > 0
    3. Solve (x - 1)(x + 4)² ≥ 0
    4. For f(x) = 2x if x < 1, x² + 1 if x ≥ 1: find f(0), f(1), and say whether it is continuous at 1
    5. Solve the system 2x - y = 5, x + 3y = 6
    6. Solve the nonlinear system y = x² - 1, y = 3x + 3
    7. 10th term and sum of the first 10 terms of 3, 10, 17, ...
    8. Infinite sum of 20, 5, 5/4, ...
    9. Evaluate Σ from k=1 to 12 of (2k + 5)
    10. Simplify (4 - 3i)(2 + i)
    11. Solve x² - 2x + 10 = 0
    12. Simplify i⁸³
    13. Given a = 9, b = 12, C = 50°, find c
    14. Given a = 6, b = 10, A = 30°, how many triangles?
    15. Convert (2, -2) to polar
    16. Convert r = 2 sin θ to rectangular
    17. How many petals does r = 5 sin(4θ) have?
    Answers

    1. x(x - 4) ≤ 0, critical 0 and 4, negative between → [0, 4]

    x² - 4x ≤ 0 → x(x - 4) ≤ 0 Zeros 0 and 4 (closed, ≤) x = -1: (-1)(-5) = 5 + x = 1: (1)(-3) = -3 - x = 5: (5)(1) = 5 + Keep - and the zeros → [0, 4]

    2. Critical -2 and 3; positive outside → (-∞, -2) ∪ (3, ∞)

    Top 0: x = -2; bottom 0: x = 3 (both open, >) x = -3: (-1)/(-6) = 1/6 + x = 0: (2)/(-3) = -2/3 - x = 4: (6)/(1) = 6 + (-∞, -2) ∪ (3, ∞)

    3. Critical 1 and -4. The squared factor never changes sign, so the expression is negative only on (-∞, 1) except at -4 where it is zero. Answer {-4} ∪ [1, ∞)

    Zeros: 1 and -4 (x + 4)² ≥ 0 always, so the sign follows (x - 1) x = -5: (-6)(1) = -6 - x = 0: (-1)(16) = -16 - x = 2: (1)(36) = 36 + Keep + and both zeros (≥) → {-4} ∪ [1, ∞)

    4. f(0) = 0; f(1) = 2. The left rule approaches 2 and the right rule gives 2, so it is continuous at 1

    f(0): 0 < 1 → 2x → 2(0) = 0 f(1): 1 ≥ 1 → x² + 1 → 1 + 1 = 2 Left rule at 1: 2(1) = 2; right rule gives 2 They match → continuous at 1

    5. Multiply the first by 3: 6x - 3y = 15; add: 7x = 21 → x = 3, y = 1. Answer (3, 1)

    Multiply 2x - y = 5 by 3: 6x - 3y = 15 Add x + 3y = 6: 7x = 21 → x = 3 y = 2(3) - 5 = 1 (3, 1)

    6. x² - 1 = 3x + 3 → x² - 3x - 4 = 0 → (x - 4)(x + 1) = 0. Points (4, 15) and (-1, 0)

    x² - 1 = 3x + 3 x² - 3x - 4 = 0 (x - 4)(x + 1) = 0 → x = 4 or -1 x = 4: y = 3(4) + 3 = 15 x = -1: y = 3(-1) + 3 = 0 (4, 15) and (-1, 0)

    7. d = 7; a₁₀ = 3 + 9(7) = 66; S₁₀ = 5(3 + 66) = 345

    d = 10 - 3 = 7 a₁₀ = 3 + (10 - 1)(7) = 3 + 63 = 66 S₁₀ = (10/2)(3 + 66) = 5(69) = 345

    8. r = 1/4; S = 20/(3/4) = 80/3

    r = 5/20 = 1/4; |r| < 1 → converges S = a₁/(1 - r) = 20/(3/4) = 20 · 4/3 = 80/3

    9. 2Σk + Σ5 = 2[12(13)/2] + 60 = 156 + 60 = 216

    Σ(2k + 5) = 2Σk + Σ5 Σk = 12(13)/2 = 78 → 2(78) = 156 Σ5 = 12 · 5 = 60 156 + 60 = 216

    10. 8 + 4i - 6i - 3i² = 8 - 2i + 3 = 11 - 2i

    FOIL: 8 + 4i - 6i - 3i² = 8 - 2i - 3(-1) = 8 - 2i + 3 = 11 - 2i

    11. x = (2 ± √(4 - 40))/2 = 1 ± 3i

    a = 1, b = -2, c = 10 b² - 4ac = 4 - 40 = -36 √(-36) = 6i x = (2 ± 6i)/2 = 1 ± 3i

    12. 83 ÷ 4 = 20 remainder 3 → i³ = -i

    83 ÷ 4 = 20 remainder 3 i⁸³ = i³ = -i

    13. c² = 81 + 144 - 216cos50° ≈ 86.16, c ≈ 9.28

    c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C = 81 + 144 - 2(9)(12)cos 50° = 225 - 216(0.642788) ≈ 225 - 138.84 = 86.16 c ≈ 9.28

    14. sin B = 10 sin30°/6 = 0.8333 → B₁ ≈ 56.4°, B₂ ≈ 123.6°. Both give A + B < 180, so two triangles

    sin B = b sin A/a = 10 sin 30°/6 = 5/6 ≈ 0.8333 B₁ = sin⁻¹(0.8333) ≈ 56.4° B₂ = 180° - 56.4° = 123.6° 30 + 56.4 < 180 ✓; 30 + 123.6 = 153.6 < 180 ✓ Two triangles

    15. r = 2√2; QIV, reference π/4 → (2√2, 7π/4)

    r = √(2² + (-2)²) = √8 = 2√2 tan θ = -2/2 = -1, reference π/4 (2, -2) is in QIV → θ = 2π - π/4 = 7π/4 (2√2, 7π/4)

    16. Multiply by r: r² = 2r sin θ → x² + y² = 2y, or x² + (y - 1)² = 1

    Multiply both sides by r: r² = 2r sin θ x² + y² = 2y x² + y² - 2y + 1 = 1 x² + (y - 1)² = 1

    17. n = 4 is even → 2n = 8 petals

    r = a sin(nθ) with n = 4 n even → 2n = 8 petals (each of length 5)

    Graphing a piecewise function

    1Take one piece at a time. Ignore the others completely.
    2Graph that piece as if it ran forever, then erase everything outside its interval.
    3At each boundary, plug the boundary value into both neighboring rules to get the two endpoint heights.
    4Closed dot for the piece whose inequality includes the boundary, open dot for the one that excludes it. Exactly one piece owns each boundary.
    Example — a three-piece function

    Graph f(x) = x + 3 for x < -1; x² for -1 ≤ x < 2; 4 for x ≥ 2. State the domain and range.

    PIECE 1: y = x + 3, only left of -1 Endpoint at x = -1: -1 + 3 = 2 Inequality is x < -1, strict → OPEN dot at (-1, 2) Ray going down-left from there. PIECE 2: y = x², from -1 up to 2 At x = -1: 1. Inequality includes -1 → CLOSED dot at (-1, 1) At x = 2: 4. Inequality excludes 2 → OPEN dot at (2, 4) Parabola arc dipping to (0, 0) in between. PIECE 3: y = 4, from 2 rightward At x = 2: 4. Inequality includes 2 → CLOSED dot at (2, 4) Horizontal ray to the right. BOUNDARY CHECK At x = -1: piece 1 approaches 2, piece 2 gives 1. They disagree → JUMP. At x = 2: piece 2 approaches 4, piece 3 gives 4. They agree → CONTINUOUS. Domain: all real numbers, no gaps Range: piece 1 gives (-∞, 2), piece 2 gives [0, 4), piece 3 gives {4} Union: (-∞, 4]
    Two closed dots stacked at the same x would break the vertical line test. Check every boundary: one open, one closed, or a single shared point.

    Solving inequalities graphically

    f(x) > g(x) asks: where is the graph of f above the graph of g? Find the intersections, then read off the x-intervals. f(x) > 0 is the same question with the x-axis as g.
    Example — reading the answer off a picture

    f(x) = x² - 1 and g(x) = 3. Solve f(x) > g(x) and f(x) ≤ g(x).

    Intersections: x² - 1 = 3 x² = 4 x = -2, 2 The parabola opens up, so it is ABOVE the line y = 3 outside the intersection points and BELOW between them. f(x) > g(x): (-∞, -2) ∪ (2, ∞) f(x) ≤ g(x): [-2, 2] ← includes the intersections because of the ≤

    Same answer as the sign chart in the inequality section above. The graph is faster when you can already picture the shape.

    Summation notation

    Σ from k = 1 to n of aᵏ means add up aᵏ for every integer k from 1 through n.
    PropertyFormula
    Constant multipleΣ c·aᵏ = c Σ aᵏ
    Sum splitsΣ (aᵏ + bᵏ) = Σ aᵏ + Σ bᵏ
    Constant termΣ from 1 to n of c = nc
    First n integersΣ k = n(n+1)/2
    First n squaresΣ k² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6
    First n cubesΣ k³ = [n(n+1)/2]²
    Example 1 — expanding and evaluating

    Evaluate Σ from k = 1 to 5 of (2k - 1).

    Substitute each k in turn. k=1: 2(1) - 1 = 1 k=2: 2(2) - 1 = 3 k=3: 2(3) - 1 = 5 k=4: 2(4) - 1 = 7 k=5: 2(5) - 1 = 9 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25
    Example 2 — using the properties instead of adding

    Evaluate Σ from k = 1 to 20 of (3k² + 2).

    Split the sum and pull out the constant: Σ(3k² + 2) = 3Σk² + Σ2 Σk² from 1 to 20 = 20(21)(41)/6 = 17220/6 = 2870 Σ2 from 1 to 20 = 20 · 2 = 40 3(2870) + 40 = 8610 + 40 = 8650
    Σ2 is not 2. You are adding the number 2 twenty separate times. Constants inside a sum get multiplied by the number of terms.

    Proof by mathematical induction

    1Base case. Show the statement is true for n = 1.
    2Inductive hypothesis. Assume it is true for n = k. Write out exactly what that assumption says.
    3Inductive step. Using that assumption, prove it for n = k + 1.
    4Conclude. True for 1, and each case forces the next, so it is true for all positive integers.
    Example — the sum of the first n integers

    Prove that 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2 for every positive integer n.

    BASE CASE, n = 1 Left side: 1 Right side: 1(2)/2 = 1 They match. ✓ HYPOTHESIS, assume true for n = k 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k + 1)/2 ← this is the tool for the next step INDUCTIVE STEP, prove it for n = k + 1 Target: 1 + 2 + ... + k + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2 Start with the left side and substitute the hypothesis for the first k terms: [1 + 2 + ... + k] + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) ← the hypothesis replaced the bracket Common denominator 2: = k(k + 1)/2 + 2(k + 1)/2 = [k(k + 1) + 2(k + 1)]/2 Factor out (k + 1): = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2 ← matches the target ✓ CONCLUSION True at n = 1, and true at k implies true at k + 1. Therefore true for all positive integers n.
    The one move that matters. In the inductive step you must actually use the hypothesis, by swapping it in for the first k terms. A proof that never substitutes the assumption is not an induction proof.

    Converting polar and rectangular equations

    Use x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, r² = x² + y², and tan θ = y/x. Going to polar, substitute for x and y. Going to rectangular, manufacture the pieces you need, usually by multiplying both sides by r.
    Example 1 — rectangular to polar

    Convert x² + y² = 6x to polar form.

    Substitute: x² + y² = r² 6x = 6r cos θ r² = 6r cos θ Divide both sides by r (allowed for r ≠ 0, and r = 0 is already on the curve): r = 6 cos θ

    This is the circle of radius 3 centered at (3, 0). Polar form makes it a one-line equation.

    Example 2 — polar to rectangular

    Convert r = 4 sin θ and θ = π/3 to rectangular form.

    PART A: r = 4 sin θ There is no bare "sin θ" substitution. Manufacture r sin θ = y by multiplying BOTH SIDES by r. r² = 4r sin θ x² + y² = 4y Optional: complete the square to see the shape. x² + y² - 4y = 0 x² + (y - 2)² = 4 circle, center (0,2), radius 2 PART B: θ = π/3 Take the tangent of both sides. tan θ = tan(π/3) = √3 y/x = √3 y = √3 x A line through the origin with slope √3.
    The multiply-by-r trick. Whenever you see a lone sin θ or cos θ, multiply through by r. That converts it into y or x and turns the r on the other side into r², which is x² + y².

    Graphing polar equations

    EquationGraphNotes
    r = acircle radius a at the origin
    θ = aline through the origin
    r = a cos θcircle, diameter a, along the x-axiscenter (a/2, 0)
    r = a sin θcircle, diameter a, along the y-axiscenter (0, a/2)
    r = a ± a cos θcardioidheart shape, cusp at the origin
    r = a ± b cos θ, a > blimacon, no inner loopdimpled if a < 2b
    r = a ± b cos θ, a < blimacon with an inner loop
    r = a cos(nθ)rosen odd → n petals; n even → 2n petals
    r² = a² sin(2θ)lemniscatefigure eight
    Symmetry tests. Replace θ with -θ and the equation is unchanged → symmetric about the polar axis (x-axis). Replace θ with π - θ and it is unchanged → symmetric about the line θ = π/2 (y-axis). Replace r with -r and it is unchanged → symmetric about the pole. Cosine equations are x-axis symmetric, sine equations are y-axis symmetric.
    Example 1 — a cardioid

    Graph r = 2 + 2cos θ.

    a = 2, b = 2, and a = b → CARDIOID Cosine → symmetric about the x-axis, so plot the top half and mirror it. Table of key angles: θ = 0 r = 2 + 2(1) = 4 → point (4, 0) θ = π/3 r = 2 + 2(1/2) = 3 → 3 units out at 60° θ = π/2 r = 2 + 2(0) = 2 → point (0, 2) θ = 2π/3 r = 2 + 2(-1/2) = 1 θ = π r = 2 + 2(-1) = 0 → the CUSP, at the origin Mirror the top half below the x-axis. Widest point 4 units right, cusp touching the origin on the left.
    Example 2 — a rose

    Graph r = 3 sin(2θ).

    n = 2, which is EVEN → 2n = 4 petals Petal length = |a| = 3 Find where petals peak: sin(2θ) = ±1 2θ = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2 θ = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4 Find where r = 0 (petal edges): sin(2θ) = 0 2θ = 0, π, 2π, 3π θ = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 Four petals of length 3, tips pointing at 45°, 135°, 225°, 315°, each petal tucked between two consecutive multiples of 90°.
    Odd n gives n petals, even n gives 2n. The even case traces each petal once going around; the odd case retraces the same petals on the second lap, so you do not get twice as many.

    Practice set — piecewise, sums, induction, SSA, polar

    1. For f(x) = -x if x ≤ 0, √x if x > 0: is it continuous at 0? Give the range.
    2. Solve x² - 4 < 5 graphically
    3. Evaluate Σ from k=1 to 6 of k²
    4. Evaluate Σ from k=1 to 30 of (4k - 1)
    5. Set up the base case and hypothesis for proving Σk³ = [n(n+1)/2]²
    6. a = 12, b = 9, A = 55°. How many triangles?
    7. a = 7, b = 9, A = 35°. How many triangles?
    8. Convert y = 5 to polar
    9. Convert r = 6 cos θ to rectangular
    10. How many petals does r = 4cos(5θ) have, and how long?
    Answers

    1. Left rule at 0 gives 0; right rule approaches 0. Continuous. Range [0, ∞)

    At x = 0: left rule -x gives -0 = 0 Right rule √x approaches √0 = 0 Match → continuous -x on x ≤ 0 gives [0, ∞); √x on x > 0 gives (0, ∞) Range [0, ∞)

    2. x² = 9 at x = ±3; parabola is below y = 5 between them → (-3, 3)

    Intersections: x² - 4 = 5 → x² = 9 → x = ±3 Parabola opens up → below y = 5 between them Strict < → (-3, 3)

    3. 6(7)(13)/6 = 91

    1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36 = 91 (formula: 6(7)(13)/6 = 91)

    4. 4Σk - Σ1 = 4[30(31)/2] - 30 = 4(465) - 30 = 1830

    Σ(4k - 1) = 4Σk - Σ1 Σk = 30(31)/2 = 465 4(465) - 30 = 1860 - 30 = 1830

    5. Base: n=1 gives 1³ = 1 and [1(2)/2]² = 1. Hypothesis: assume 1³ + ... + k³ = [k(k+1)/2]², then show the sum through (k+1)³ equals [(k+1)(k+2)/2]²

    Base, n = 1: left 1³ = 1; right [1(2)/2]² = 1² = 1 ✓ Hypothesis: assume 1³ + ... + k³ = [k(k + 1)/2]² Goal: show 1³ + ... + k³ + (k + 1)³ = [(k + 1)(k + 2)/2]²

    6. sin B = 9 sin55°/12 = 0.61436 → B₁ ≈ 37.9°, B₂ ≈ 142.1°. But 55 + 142.1 = 197.1 > 180, so the second fails. One triangle

    sin B = 9 sin 55°/12 ≈ 9(0.819152)/12 ≈ 0.61436 B₁ ≈ 37.9° B₂ = 180° - 37.9° = 142.1° 55 + 142.1 = 197.1 > 180 → second fails One triangle

    7. sin B = 9 sin35°/7 = 0.73745 → B₁ ≈ 47.5°, B₂ ≈ 132.5°. 35 + 132.5 = 167.5 < 180, both work. Two triangles

    sin B = 9 sin 35°/7 ≈ 9(0.573576)/7 ≈ 0.73745 B₁ ≈ 47.5° B₂ = 180° - 47.5° = 132.5° 35 + 132.5 = 167.5 < 180 → both work Two triangles

    8. r sin θ = 5 → r = 5/sin θ = 5 csc θ

    y = r sin θ r sin θ = 5 → r = 5/sin θ = 5 csc θ

    9. Multiply by r: r² = 6r cos θ → x² + y² = 6x, or (x - 3)² + y² = 9

    Multiply by r: r² = 6r cos θ x² + y² = 6x x² - 6x + 9 + y² = 9 (x - 3)² + y² = 9

    10. n = 5 is odd → 5 petals, each of length 4

    r = a cos(nθ) with n = 5, a = 4 n odd → 5 petals Petal length |a| = 4

    12 = 2·2·3, 8 = 2·2·2 → LCD 24 5/12 = 10/24, 3/8 = 9/24 10/24 - 9/24 = 1/24

    5. √(49 · 2 · x⁶ · x) = 7x³√(2x)

    30. (2x⁴ + 1)/x² = 2x² + 1/x², so the end-behavior asymptote is the parabola y = 2x². VA x = 0

    Split the fraction: 2x⁴/x² + 1/x² = 2x² + 1/x² As x → ±∞, 1/x² → 0 → parabola y = 2x² Bottom zero at x = 0 → VA x = 0

    31. 5²⁽ˣ⁻¹⁾ = 5³⁽ˣ⁺²⁾ → 2x - 2 = 3x + 6 → x = -8

    25 = 5², 125 = 5³ 5²⁽ˣ⁻¹⁾ = 5³⁽ˣ⁺²⁾ 2x - 2 = 3x + 6 -8 = x

    32. 2ˣ = 25 → x = log 25/log 2 ≈ 4.6439

    2ˣ = 25 ÷ 4 x log 2 = log 25 x = log 25/log 2 ≈ 1.397940/0.301030 ≈ 4.6439

    33. x(x - 3) = 10 → x² - 3x - 10 = 0 → (x - 5)(x + 2) = 0. Reject -2. x = 5

    ln[x(x - 3)] = ln 10 x(x - 3) = 10 x² - 3x - 10 = 0 (x - 5)(x + 2) = 0 x = -2 gives ln(-2): reject x = 5

    34. log(√x · z / y³)

    (1/2)log x - 3 log y + log z = log √x - log y³ + log z = log(√x · z) - log y³ = log(√x · z / y³)

    35. cos(5π/6) = -√3/2; tan(300°) = -√3; sin(4π/3) = -√3/2 so csc(4π/3) = -2/√3 = -2√3/3

    cos(5π/6): QII, ref π/6 → -√3/2 tan(300°): QIV, ref 60° → -√3 sin(4π/3): QIII, ref π/3 → -√3/2 csc(4π/3) = -2/√3 = -2√3/3

    36. Start from sin² + cos² = 1 and divide every term by cos²θ: tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ. Rearranged, sec²θ - tan²θ = 1

    sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 Divide every term by cos²θ: tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ sec²θ - tan²θ = 1 ✓

    37. QIII, both sine and cosine negative. 7-24-25 triangle → cos θ = -24/25. cos 2θ = 1 - 2sin²θ = 1 - 2(49/625) = 527/625

    sin θ = -7/25 in QIII → cosine negative cos θ = -√(1 - 49/625) = -√(576/625) = -24/25 cos 2θ = 1 - 2sin²θ = 1 - 2(49/625) = 1 - 98/625 = 527/625

    38. Factor: 5cos(2(x + π/4)) - 1. Amplitude 5, period π, shift π/4 LEFT, midline y = -1

    Factor 2: 2x + π/2 = 2(x + π/4) y = 5cos(2(x + π/4)) - 1 x + π/4 = x - (-π/4) → shift π/4 LEFT Amplitude 5; period 2π/2 = π; midline y = -1

    39. (2sin x - 1)(sin x - 1) = 0. sin x = 1/2 → π/6, 5π/6; sin x = 1 → π/2. Answer π/6, π/2, 5π/6

    u = sin x: 2u² - 3u + 1 = 0 ac = 2, add -3 → -2 and -1 (2u - 1)(u - 1) = 0 sin x = 1/2 → π/6, 5π/6 sin x = 1 → π/2 π/6, π/2, 5π/6

    40. r = √(9 + 16) = 5 → (x - 2)² + (y + 5)² = 25

    r = distance from (2, -5) to (-1, -1) Δx = -3, Δy = 4 → r = √(9 + 16) = 5 (x - 2)² + (y + 5)² = 25
    Scoring. Count by part. A part where you missed more than a third tells you exactly which unit review to redo. Part 1 or Part 2 weakness outranks everything else — fix those first, because the later parts sit on top of them.
