    Glossary

    Plain-English meaning of every term the course uses. Each one links to the place it is taught.

    ABCDEFGHILMNOPQRSTUVZ

    A

    Absolute value
    Distance from zero, so it is never negative. |x| = 4 means x = 4 or x = -4. Core Algebra · Absolute value
    AC method
    Factoring ax² + bx + c by finding two numbers that multiply to a·c and add to b, then splitting the middle term and grouping. Factoring · AC method
    Ambiguous case (SSA)
    Given two sides and an angle not between them, there can be zero, one, or two triangles. Check sin B and the supplement 180° - B. Sec 12 · The ambiguous case (SSA)
    Amplitude
    Half the distance from the maximum to the minimum of a sine or cosine graph. In y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D it is |A|. Sec 7 · Sine and cosine form
    Angle of depression
    Angle measured down from a horizontal line to an object below. Sec 4 · Angles of elevation and depression
    Angle of elevation
    Angle measured up from a horizontal line to an object above. Sec 4 · Angles of elevation and depression
    Arc length
    Length along a circle: s = rθ, with θ in radians. Sec 5 · Arc length, sector area, and velocity
    Arithmetic sequence
    A list where you add the same number d each time: aₙ = a₁ + (n - 1)d. Additional · Sequences and series
    Asymptote
    A line a graph approaches but does not reach (or, for horizontal and slant ones, approaches at the far ends). Sec 2 · Asymptotes
    Average rate of change
    Slope between two points on a graph: [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a). Sec 1 · Average rate of change

    B

    Base (exponential or log)
    The number being raised to a power: b in bˣ and in log_b x. It must be positive and not 1. Sec 3 · Exponential form
    Binomial theorem
    Formula for expanding (a + b)ⁿ using the coefficients C(n, k). Appendix · Binomial theorem

    C

    Change of base
    log_b x = log x / log b. Lets the calculator do any base using LOG or LN. Sec 3 · Change of base
    Circle (equation)
    (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², center (h, k), radius r. Coordinate Geometry · Circle
    Coefficient
    The number multiplying a variable. In -3x², the coefficient is -3. Polynomial Skills · Degree and leading term
    Cofunction
    Pairs like sin and cos whose values swap for complementary angles: sin θ = cos(90° - θ). Sec 4 · Cofunctions and complementary angles
    Common denominator
    A shared bottom number needed before fractions can be added or subtracted. Fractions · Adding/subtracting fractions
    Completing the square
    Adding (b/2)² to x² + bx to make a perfect square, used to solve quadratics and find vertices and circle centers. Quadratics · Completing the square
    Complex number
    A number a + bi, where i = √-1. Additional · Complex numbers
    Composition
    (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)). Do the inside function first. Sec 2 · Composition
    Compound interest
    A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt): interest added n times a year. Sec 3 · Compound interest
    Conic section
    A curve made by slicing a cone: circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola. Appendix · Conic sections beyond the circle
    Conjugate
    The same two terms with the middle sign flipped, as in a + √b and a - √b. Multiplying by it clears radicals or simplifies identities. Exponents & Radicals · Rationalizing
    Continuous compounding
    A = Pe^(rt): interest added constantly. Sec 3 · Continuous compounding
    Cosecant (csc)
    Reciprocal of sine: csc θ = 1/sin θ. Sec 6 · Reciprocal trig functions
    Cosine (cos)
    Adjacent ÷ hypotenuse in a right triangle; the x-coordinate on the unit circle. Sec 4 · SOH–CAH–TOA
    Cotangent (cot)
    Reciprocal of tangent: cot θ = cos θ / sin θ. Sec 6 · Reciprocal trig functions
    Coterminal angles
    Angles that end in the same place. Add or subtract 360° (or 2π). Sec 5 · Angles in standard position

    D

    Degree (of a polynomial)
    The highest exponent in the polynomial. Polynomial Skills · Degree and leading term
    Degrees, minutes, seconds (DMS)
    Angle units where 1° = 60′ and 1′ = 60″. Sec 5 · Degrees, minutes, and seconds
    Descartes' rule of signs
    Counting sign changes in f(x) and f(-x) gives the possible numbers of positive and negative real zeros. Polynomial Skills · Descartes' rule of signs
    Determinant
    For a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] it is ad - bc. Appendix · Matrices and determinants
    Difference of squares
    a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b). Factoring · Difference of squares
    Discriminant
    b² - 4ac. Positive: two real roots; zero: one; negative: none real. Quadratics · Discriminant
    Distance formula
    d = √((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²). Coordinate Geometry · Distance
    Domain
    Every input x a function allows. Watch for zero denominators, negative even roots, and logs of non-positive numbers. Sec 1 · Domain
    Double-angle formulas
    sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ; cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ. Sec 10 · Double angle

    E

    End behavior
    What the graph does as x → ∞ and x → -∞, set by the leading term. Polynomial Skills · End behavior shortcut
    Exponent laws
    Rules like xᵃ·xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ, (xᵃ)ᵇ = xᵃᵇ, x⁻ᵃ = 1/xᵃ. Exponents & Radicals · Exponent laws
    Exponential function
    f(x) = a·bˣ. Growth when b > 1, decay when 0 < b < 1. Sec 3 · Exponential form
    Extrema
    Maximum and minimum values of a function. Sec 1 · Increasing, decreasing, and extrema

    F

    Factor theorem
    If f(c) = 0, then (x - c) is a factor of f(x). Polynomial Skills · Factor theorem
    Function
    A rule giving exactly one output for each input. Sec 1 · Function notation

    G

    GCF (greatest common factor)
    The largest factor every term shares. Always pull it out first. Factoring · GCF
    Geometric sequence
    A list where you multiply by the same ratio r each time: aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹. Additional · Sequences and series
    Grouping
    Factoring four terms in pairs, then pulling out the shared binomial. Factoring · Grouping

    H

    Half-angle formulas
    sin(θ/2) = ±√[(1 - cos θ)/2], cos(θ/2) = ±√[(1 + cos θ)/2]. The quadrant of θ/2 picks the sign. Sec 10 · Half-angle formulas
    Heron's formula
    Area from three sides: √(s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)), where s is half the perimeter. Sec 12 · SSS: finding angles, and Heron's formula
    Hole
    A missing point on a rational graph where a factor cancels from top and bottom. Sec 2 · Hole coordinates
    Horizontal asymptote
    The y-value a graph levels off toward at the far ends. Found by comparing degrees. Sec 2 · Horizontal asymptote: compare degrees
    Hypotenuse
    The side opposite the right angle; the longest side. Sec 4 · SOH–CAH–TOA

    I

    Identity
    An equation true for every allowed value of the variable, such as sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Sec 9 · Pythagorean identities
    Increasing / decreasing
    Rising or falling as you read the graph left to right. State it with x-intervals. Sec 1 · Increasing, decreasing, and extrema
    Induction
    A proof method: show a base case, then show case k implies case k + 1. Additional · Proof by mathematical induction
    Inequality
    A statement with <, ≤, >, or ≥. Flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative. Core Algebra · Inequalities
    Intercept
    Where a graph crosses an axis. x-intercepts: set y = 0. y-intercept: set x = 0. Sec 2 · The full order
    Interval notation
    Writing a set of numbers with brackets and parentheses, like [2, ∞). Brackets include the endpoint; parentheses do not. Sec 1 · Domain
    Inverse function
    f⁻¹ undoes f. Swap x and y, then solve for y. Exists only if f is one-to-one. Sec 2 · Inverse functions
    Inverse trig functions
    sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹: give an angle back from a ratio, within restricted ranges. Sec 8 · Inverse trigonometric functions

    L

    Law of Cosines
    c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C. Use for SAS and SSS triangles. Sec 12 · Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
    Law of Sines
    a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use for AAS, ASA, and SSA triangles. Sec 12 · Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
    Leading coefficient
    The coefficient of the highest-degree term. Polynomial Skills · Degree and leading term
    Like terms
    Terms with exactly the same variable part, such as 3x² and -5x². Only these combine. Core Algebra · Combine like terms
    Linear equation
    An equation whose variable is only to the first power, like 3x + 7 = 19. Core Algebra · Linear equations
    Log rules
    log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a - log b; log(aⁿ) = n log a. Sec 3 · Log rules
    Logarithm
    The exponent: log_b x = y means bʸ = x. Sec 3 · Logs are inverse exponents

    M

    Matrix
    A rectangular grid of numbers. Appendix · Matrices and determinants
    Midline
    The horizontal center line of a sine or cosine graph: y = D. Sec 7 · Sine and cosine form
    Midpoint
    ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Coordinate Geometry · Midpoint
    Multiplicity
    How many times a zero repeats. Even: the graph touches and turns. Odd: it crosses. Polynomial Skills · Multiplicity

    N

    Natural log (ln)
    Log base e ≈ 2.718. TI-30XIIS · Logs

    O

    One-to-one
    Each output comes from only one input. Passes the horizontal line test. Sec 2 · Inverse functions
    Order of operations
    Parentheses, exponents, multiply/divide left to right, add/subtract left to right (PEMDAS). Arithmetic & Signs · Order of operations

    P

    Parent function
    The basic graph a family is built from, like y = x², y = √x, y = |x|. Sec 1 · The graphs you must know cold
    Perfect square trinomial
    a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)². Factoring · Perfect square trinomial
    Period
    Horizontal length of one full cycle. 2π/|B| for sine and cosine, π/|B| for tangent. Sec 7 · Sine and cosine form
    Phase shift
    Horizontal shift C in y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D. Factor B out first. Sec 7 · Sine and cosine form
    Piecewise function
    A function defined by different formulas on different intervals. Additional · Piecewise functions
    Polar coordinates
    A point given as (r, θ): distance from the origin and angle. Additional · Polar coordinates
    Polynomial
    A sum of terms axⁿ with whole-number exponents. Polynomial Skills · Degree and leading term
    Pythagorean identities
    sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ. Sec 9 · Pythagorean identities

    Q

    Quadrant
    One of the four regions of the plane, I to IV counterclockwise from upper right. Sec 6 · Quadrant signs
    Quadratic formula
    x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / 2a. Quadratics · Quadratic formula

    R

    Radian
    Angle where the arc equals the radius. 180° = π radians. Sec 5 · Degrees and radians
    Radical
    A root sign, such as √ or ∛. Exponents & Radicals · Simplifying radicals
    Range
    Every output y a function actually produces. Sec 1 · Vertical line test, domain and range from a graph
    Rational function
    A fraction of polynomials, N(x)/D(x). Sec 2 · Rational functions
    Rationalizing
    Removing a radical from a denominator by multiplying by a suitable form of 1. Exponents & Radicals · Rationalizing
    Reciprocal
    1 divided by the number. The reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2. Fractions · Dividing fractions
    Reference angle
    The acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis. Sec 5 · Reference angles
    Reflection
    A flip. -f(x) flips over the x-axis; f(-x) flips over the y-axis. Sec 1 · Function transformations
    Root / zero
    An x-value that makes f(x) = 0; an x-intercept. Quadratics · Zero-product property

    S

    Secant (sec)
    Reciprocal of cosine: sec θ = 1/cos θ. Sec 6 · Reciprocal trig functions
    Sector area
    A = ½r²θ, with θ in radians. Sec 5 · Arc length, sector area, and velocity
    Sign chart
    A number line marking where an expression is positive or negative, used for inequalities. Additional · Polynomial and rational inequalities
    Simple harmonic motion
    Back-and-forth motion modeled by d = a sin(ωt) or a cos(ωt). Sec 7 · Simple harmonic motion
    Sine (sin)
    Opposite ÷ hypotenuse in a right triangle; the y-coordinate on the unit circle. Sec 4 · SOH–CAH–TOA
    Slant (oblique) asymptote
    A tilted line asymptote when the top degree is exactly one more than the bottom. Found by division. Sec 2 · Slant asymptote
    Slope
    Steepness: rise over run, m = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁). Coordinate Geometry · Slope
    SOH-CAH-TOA
    Memory aid: Sine = Opp/Hyp, Cosine = Adj/Hyp, Tangent = Opp/Adj. Sec 4 · SOH–CAH–TOA
    Special right triangles
    45-45-90 (1 : 1 : √2) and 30-60-90 (1 : √3 : 2). Sec 6 · Special triangles
    Standard position
    An angle with its vertex at the origin and its initial side along the positive x-axis. Sec 5 · Angles in standard position
    Sum and difference formulas
    sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B; cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B. Sec 10 · Sum and difference
    Summation (sigma) notation
    Σ means add the terms for each index value in the given range. Additional · Summation notation
    Synthetic division
    A shortcut for dividing a polynomial by x - c. Polynomial Skills · Synthetic division
    System of equations
    Two or more equations solved together. Use substitution or elimination. Additional · Systems of equations

    T

    Tangent (tan)
    Opposite ÷ adjacent; sin θ / cos θ. Sec 4 · SOH–CAH–TOA
    Terminal side
    The ray where an angle in standard position ends. Sec 5 · Angles in standard position
    Transformation
    A shift, stretch, compression, or reflection of a parent graph. Sec 1 · Function transformations
    Trig equation
    An equation with a trig function of the unknown. Solve for the angle, then list all solutions in the interval. Sec 11 · Solving trig equations

    U

    Unit circle
    Circle of radius 1 centered at the origin. Point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ). Sec 6 · Core first-quadrant values

    V

    Vector
    A quantity with size and direction, written ⟨a, b⟩. Appendix · Vectors
    Vertex (of a parabola)
    The turning point. For y = ax² + bx + c, x = -b/(2a). Quadratics · Graphing a quadratic from scratch
    Vertical asymptote
    A vertical line x = a where the remaining denominator is zero after canceling. Sec 2 · Vertical asymptote
    Vertical line test
    A graph is a function if no vertical line hits it twice. Sec 1 · Vertical line test, domain and range from a graph

    Z

    Zero-product property
    If A·B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0. Quadratics · Zero-product property

    Do not try to memorize the whole guide at once. Build it in layers.

    The formulas worth memorizing first

    a2-b2 =(a-b)(a+b)
    x= -b±b2-4ac2a
    sin2θ+cos2θ=1
    180°=π
    If Stages 1–6 become automatic, precalculus becomes dramatically easier. Most later mistakes come from algebra underneath the new material, not from the new concept itself.

    Appendix: More Topics

    Conic sections beyond the circle

    ConicStandard formKey features
    Parabola (vertical)(x - h)² = 4p(y - k)vertex (h,k); focus p above; opens up if p>0
    Ellipse(x-h)²/a² + (y-k)²/b² = 1center (h,k); c² = a² - b²; larger denominator is the major axis
    Hyperbola(x-h)²/a² - (y-k)²/b² = 1center (h,k); c² = a² + b²; opens toward the POSITIVE term
    Telling them apart from the general equation. No squared term on one variable → parabola. Both squared, same sign, different coefficients → ellipse. Both squared, opposite signs → hyperbola. Both squared, identical coefficients → circle.
    Example 1 — ellipse

    Analyze (x - 2)²/25 + (y + 1)²/9 = 1.

    Center (2, -1). Larger denominator 25 is under x → major axis is HORIZONTAL. a² = 25 → a = 5 (semi-major) b² = 9 → b = 3 (semi-minor) c² = 25 - 9 = 16 → c = 4 Vertices: (2 ± 5, -1) = (7, -1) and (-3, -1) Co-vertices: (2, -1 ± 3) = (2, 2) and (2, -4) Foci: (2 ± 4, -1) = (6, -1) and (-2, -1)
    Example 2 — hyperbola

    Analyze y²/16 - x²/9 = 1.

    Center (0, 0). The POSITIVE term is y, so it opens UP and DOWN. a² = 16 → a = 4 (a always belongs to the positive term) b² = 9 → b = 3 c² = 16 + 9 = 25 → c = 5 (hyperbolas ADD) Vertices: (0, ±4) Foci: (0, ±5) Asymptotes: y = ±(a/b)x = ±(4/3)x
    Ellipse subtracts, hyperbola adds. c² = a² - b² versus c² = a² + b². And for a hyperbola, a is whichever denominator sits under the positive term, even if it is the smaller number.

    Vectors

    A vector ⟨a, b⟩ has magnitude ‖v‖ = √(a² + b²) and direction angle θ = tan⁻¹(b/a), adjusted for the quadrant. Dot product: u · v = a₁a₂ + b₁b₂. A dot product of 0 means the vectors are perpendicular.
    Example 1 — magnitude, direction, operations

    u = ⟨3, -4⟩, v = ⟨-1, 2⟩. Find ‖u‖, 2u - 3v, and u · v.

    ‖u‖ = √(3² + (-4)²) = √25 = 5 2u = ⟨6, -8⟩ 3v = ⟨-3, 6⟩ 2u - 3v = ⟨6 - (-3), -8 - 6⟩ = ⟨9, -14⟩ u · v = (3)(-1) + (-4)(2) = -3 - 8 = -11
    Example 2 — from magnitude and angle back to components

    A force of 50 N acts at 120° from the positive x-axis. Write it in component form.

    a = ‖v‖ cos θ = 50 cos 120° = 50(-1/2) = -25 b = ‖v‖ sin θ = 50 sin 120° = 50(√3/2) = 25√3 ≈ 43.3 v = ⟨-25, 25√3⟩ Check: √(625 + 1875) = √2500 = 50 ✓

    Binomial theorem

    (a + b)ⁿ = Σ C(n, k) aⁿ⁻ᵏ bᵏ, where C(n, k) = n!/[k!(n-k)!]. The (k+1)th term is C(n, k) aⁿ⁻ᵏ bᵏ.
    Example 1 — full expansion

    Expand (x + 2)⁴.

    Coefficients from Pascal's triangle row 4: 1 4 6 4 1 x powers count DOWN from 4; the 2 powers count UP from 0. 1·x⁴·2⁰ = x⁴ 4·x³·2ⁱ = 8x³ 6·x²·2² = 24x² 4·xⁱ·2³ = 32x 1·x⁰·2⁴ = 16 (x + 2)⁴ = x⁴ + 8x³ + 24x² + 32x + 16
    Example 2 — one specific term

    Find the term containing x³ in (2x - 1)⁵.

    Here a = 2x, b = -1, n = 5. Term is C(5, k)(2x)⁵⁻ᵏ(-1)ᵏ. We need the x power to be 3, so 5 - k = 3, meaning k = 2. C(5, 2) = 5!/(2!3!) = 10 (2x)³ = 8x³ (-1)² = 1 10 · 8x³ · 1 = 80x³
    TI-30XIIS. C(5,2) is 5 PRB (select nCr) ENTER 2 ENTER → 10 Press PRB unshifted, select nCr with the arrow keys, and press ENTER to insert it before entering r. 2nd PRB is F↔D conversion; execute that conversion with ENTER.

    Matrices and determinants

    For a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]]: determinant = ad - bc, and the inverse is (1/det)·[[d, -b], [-c, a]]. A determinant of 0 means no inverse exists.
    Example 1 — determinant and inverse

    A = [[3, 1], [5, 2]]. Find det A and A⁻¹.

    det = (3)(2) - (1)(5) = 6 - 5 = 1 Inverse: swap a and d, negate b and c, divide by det. A⁻¹ = (1/1)[[2, -1], [-5, 3]] = [[2, -1], [-5, 3]]
    Example 2 — Cramer's rule

    Solve 3x + y = 9, 5x + 2y = 16.

    D = |3 1; 5 2| = 6 - 5 = 1 Dˣ = replace the x column with the constants: |9 1; 16 2| = 18 - 16 = 2 Dʸ = replace the y column with the constants: |3 9; 5 16| = 48 - 45 = 3 x = Dˣ/D = 2/1 = 2 y = Dʸ/D = 3/1 = 3 Check: 3(2) + 3 = 9 ✓ 5(2) + 2(3) = 16 ✓

    Practice set — appendix topics

    1. Center, vertices, and foci of x²/36 + y²/11 = 1
    2. Center, vertices, foci, and asymptotes of x²/9 - y²/16 = 1
    3. Vertex and focus of (x - 1)² = 8(y + 2)
    4. Identify the conic: 4x² + 9y² - 36 = 0
    5. Identify the conic: y² - 4x² = 16
    6. ‖⟨-5, 12⟩‖
    7. u = ⟨2, -1⟩, v = ⟨3, 4⟩. Find 3u + 2v and u · v.
    8. Are ⟨4, 6⟩ and ⟨-3, 2⟩ perpendicular?
    9. A 60 N force acts at 210°. Component form?
    10. Determinant and inverse of [[2, 5], [1, 3]]
    11. Solve by Cramer's rule: 4x - y = 7, 2x + 3y = 7
    12. Coefficient of x² in (x + 3)⁵
    13. Expand (2x - 1)⁴
    Answers

    1. Center (0,0); a = 6 horizontal; vertices (±6, 0); c² = 36 - 11 = 25, foci (±5, 0)

    Larger denominator 36 is under x → horizontal a² = 36 → a = 6; b² = 11 Vertices (±6, 0) c² = a² - b² = 36 - 11 = 25 → c = 5 Foci (±5, 0)

    2. Center (0,0); positive term is x so it opens left/right; a = 3, b = 4; vertices (±3, 0); c² = 9 + 16 = 25, foci (±5, 0); asymptotes y = ±(4/3)x
